sections.heading: Introduction: A Telescope Trained on the Wrong Star
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a story about “focus”.

An amateur astronomer spent the better part of a year’s savings on a telescope. When night fell, he set it up on his balcony, adjusted the angle, adjusted the focus, and did everything with meticulous care. Yet however he adjusted it, all he could see was a blurry haze of light. He changed the eyepiece, cleaned the lenses, recalibrated the tripod, and fiddled for two hours before he finally found the problem — his finderscope had never been lined up in the first place. Nothing was wrong with the equipment, nothing was wrong with his technique, nothing was wrong with his effort. Only the focus was wrong. And when the focus is wrong, the harder you try, the further you get from your target.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what we are going to talk about today.

Today’s church does not lack equipment, methods or strategies. We hold conferences, run camps, write plans and set goals. None of these is a bad thing. But we have to stop and ask the most fundamental question of all: who is our focus aimed at?

Let me tell you something else that really happened.

It was 24 December 1968, Christmas Eve. The spacecraft Apollo 8 was orbiting the moon — the first time in human history that people had left the pull of the earth and travelled round to the far side of the moon. As the spacecraft came out from behind the moon, the astronaut Bill Anders looked out through the window and suddenly saw a sight no one had ever seen before: above the grey, desolate horizon of the moon, a blue planet was slowly rising. He quickly grabbed his camera and took the photograph that would later stun the whole world — “Earthrise”.

That night, in a live television broadcast, the three astronauts read the first chapter of Genesis to the whole earth: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.”

Brothers and sisters, notice what happened at that moment. They flew three hundred and eighty thousand kilometres to look at the moon; and what they truly saw was the earth, was creation, was God. They went looking for one thing, and on the way they were seized by a far greater focus.

This is revival.

The end time revival is not about showcasing any one person, any one church or any one method. There is only one true focus: Jesus Christ. The source of revival is Jesus, the power of revival comes from Jesus, and the purpose of revival is to let Jesus receive all the glory.

When the end time revival comes, what people see should not be the reputation of certain spiritual leaders, nor the size of a church, nor some special strategy. It should be the Lord who laid down his life for us and rose from the dead — Jesus. He is the centre of God’s Kingdom, the head of the church, and the focal point of every believer’s life.

What does Paul say? He says, “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ” (Philippians 3:7).

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the role model we follow; he is the worth and direction of our lives. What we need today is not the revival of a particular system, nor the revival of a particular form, but the restoration of our love for Jesus, our trust in him and our obedience to him.

In this lesson we will look at two things: Jesus is the focal point of the Bible, and Jesus is the focal point of the universe. Having seen these, we will practise together letting Jesus become the focal point of our daily living.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: One Man’s Profit-and-Loss Statement
sections.html:
To understand Philippians chapter 3, we first need to get to know the writer, the readers and the times.

The writer is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally dated to AD 61–62, written from Rome. Paul was then under house arrest in rented lodgings, chained and guarded by Roman soldiers. He did not know whether his trial would end in release or in beheading. It was in that situation that he wrote Philippians, the letter known as “the epistle of joy”, in which “joy” and “rejoice” appear again and again. How could a man in chains rejoice? Because his focus was not on the chains.

The readers are the church in Philippi. Philippi was in Macedonia, and it was the first church Paul planted in Europe. Acts chapter 16 records how it happened: in Troas Paul saw a vision in the night, a man of Macedonia standing and begging him, “Come over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9). And so the gospel crossed the Aegean Sea and entered Europe for the first time. In Philippi, the first to believe was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth; next came the jailer who, after hearing Paul and Silas singing praises to God at midnight and after the great earthquake, turned to the Lord with his whole household.

Philippi was a Roman colony. In 42 BC, Antony and Octavian defeated Caesar’s assassins on the plain of Philippi, and after the battle they settled veterans there. The people of the city took enormous pride in holding Roman citizenship. “Status” and “glory” were in the very air of that city.

Once we understand this, we can read Philippians chapter 3. There Paul lists his own “assets”: “circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; concerning the law, a Pharisee; concerning zeal, persecuting the assembly; concerning the righteousness which is in the law, found blameless” (Philippians 3:5–6).

Brothers and sisters, this is a breathtaking CV. Pure bloodline, a noble tribe, a first-class education, a strict religious party, unrivalled zeal, a blameless moral record. In today’s terms, he was the kind of man who came from a distinguished family, graduated from a top school, trained under a famous pastor, had a solid theological grounding and a brilliant record of ministry.

And then he wrote verse 7: “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.”

The Greek for “gain” here is κέρδος (kerdos), meaning “profit, surplus”; “loss” is ζημία (zēmia), meaning “deficit, loss”. These are two standard terms of commercial bookkeeping. Paul is drawing up a profit-and-loss statement. He takes the things he had once entered in the “assets” column, strikes them out one by one, and moves every one of them to the “liabilities” column.

Why? Not because those things were bad in themselves. His bloodline was not bad, the law was not bad, zeal was not bad. It was because, once they became the focus, they blocked out Jesus. Anything that blocks out Jesus is, in Paul’s ledger, entered as a loss.

Verse 8 goes further: “for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ.” The Greek for “refuse” is σκύβαλον (skybalon), meaning the scraps thrown out from the table, rubbish tossed to the dogs. Paul uses an extremely blunt word. What he wants to say is this: compared with knowing Christ, the things I used to be so proud of are not even worth keeping.

Brothers and sisters, this is not asceticism; it is a shift of focus. When a man has fallen in love with the sun, the candle in his hand naturally seems superfluous.

This lesson also quotes two other important passages, so let me give their background too.

One is John chapter 5. John’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 85 and 95, in Ephesus, by the apostle John. Chapter 5 records the Lord Jesus healing, at the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years — and that day was the Sabbath. The religious leaders were furious. At the climax of this dispute, the Lord Jesus spoke an extremely weighty word to people who had spent their whole lives studying the Scriptures: “You search the Scriptures (or: Search the Scriptures), because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:39–40).

The other is Colossians chapter 1. Colossians, like Philippians, is one of Paul’s prison letters. At the time, the church in Colossae was being troubled by a kind of syncretistic teaching: these people talked about angels, about secret knowledge, about all kinds of rules, and they demoted Jesus to just one level among many spiritual tiers. Paul wrote this letter to put Jesus back in his rightful place — “that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? From the first century to today, Satan’s tactics have never changed. He rarely tells people outright to deny Jesus. He just keeps nudging Jesus, constantly and gently, from the centre to the side. He lets Jesus stay in your faith, but he won’t let Jesus stay in your focus.

So there is only one thing this lesson sets out to do: to move the focus back.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Is the Focal Point of the Bible
sections.html:
“You search the Scriptures (or: Search the Scriptures), because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me” (John 5:39).

Brothers and sisters, the main thread and core of the whole Bible exist to bear witness to Jesus.

The Greek word for “search” is ἐραυνάω (eraunaō). It was originally used of hunters — a hunter bending low, tracking inch by inch the footprints his prey has left behind — and also of miners — a miner going deep underground, digging out a seam layer by layer. It describes an extremely earnest, extremely strenuous kind of searching.

The Lord Jesus acknowledges that those scribes and Pharisees were in earnest. They could recite the books of the law, they could count how many letters there were in the Scriptures, and they read through the five books of Moses several times a year. Their effort was no less than that of the amateur astronomer who spent two hours cleaning his lenses.

So where did it go wrong? The Lord said, “These are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life.”

They spent their whole lives tracking the footprints, yet refused to recognise the One standing in front of them. They spent their whole lives digging in the mine, their hands full of stones, and tossed the diamond aside.

Brothers and sisters, what a solemn warning this is. Reading a great deal of Scripture is not the same as knowing Jesus. The accumulation of knowledge can sometimes even become an obstacle to knowing him.

sections.heading: 1. He Is the Centre of the Four Gospels
sections.html:
The four Gospels record the Lord Jesus’ life on earth, his teaching, his cross and his resurrection.

At the end of his Gospel, the apostle John states in his own words why he wrote it: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

Notice that the four Gospels are not four biographies. A biography usually gives a balanced account of a person’s whole life, but the four Gospels devote an enormous amount of space to the last week of the Lord Jesus’ life. Mark’s Gospel has sixteen chapters, and six of them are about Passion Week. That is why the German theologian Martin Kähler described the Gospels as “passion narratives with extended introductions”.

Why? Because the cross and the empty tomb are the focus of the focus.

Paul puts it with absolute firmness: “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).

Brothers and sisters, this verse deserves to be pondered again and again. Corinth was a Greek city that prized debate and wisdom. Paul could easily have shown off his learning there. But he says, “I determined.” “Determined” is a decision, an act of focusing. He blurred out everything else in the lens and left only one sharp image: Christ crucified.

sections.heading: 2. He Is the Protagonist of the New Testament
sections.html:
What the apostles preached was Jesus Christ and him crucified.

In Acts chapter 4, Peter stands before the Sanhedrin and says, “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!” (Acts 4:12).

Paul writes to the church in Corinth, “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

Brothers and sisters, listen to this phrase: “we don’t preach ourselves.”

This is the great watershed between revival and religious movements. Religious movements preach themselves — their own experiences, their own methods, their own results. Revival preaches Jesus. When a religious movement is over, what people remember is the speaker; when a revival has passed, what people remember is the Lord.

John the Baptist put this most clearly of all: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

In the original these are two very simple verbs: one rising, one falling, like a see-saw. Brothers and sisters, our problem is often that we want both ends to rise. We want Jesus to be glorified, and we also want to be seen ourselves. But a see-saw doesn’t work like that. There is only one focus.

sections.heading: 3. He Is the Messiah to Whom Old Testament Prophecy Points
sections.html:
On the day the Lord Jesus rose again, on the road to Emmaus, he did something for two discouraged disciples: “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

That same evening he said to the disciples, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44).

Brothers and sisters, “the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” was the Jewish way of naming the whole Old Testament. The Lord Jesus was in effect saying: the whole Old Testament speaks about me.

Let’s look at a few examples.

After humanity’s fall, God announced the first gospel right there in the Garden of Eden: “I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). “Her offspring” — the offspring of the woman — is a foreshadowing that points to a Son born of a virgin.

In the eighth century BC Isaiah wrote, “But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Seven hundred years later, on the hill of Golgotha, these words were fulfilled to the letter.

The psalmist says, “Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come. It is written about me in the book in the scroll’” (Psalm 40:7). The writer of Hebrews puts these words directly into the mouth of Christ: “Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come (in the scroll of the book it is written of me) to do your will, O God’” (Hebrews 10:7).

Brothers and sisters, what does “it is written about me in the scroll” mean? It means: the whole scroll is about me.

The title “Christ” is Χριστός (Christos) in Greek, corresponding to the Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (Mashiach); both mean “the anointed one”. In the Old Testament three kinds of people were anointed: prophets, priests and kings. In the Old Testament no one ever held all three offices fully at once — until Jesus came. He is the perfect Prophet, bringing God’s word to people; he is the perfect Priest, bringing people to God; he is the perfect King, reigning for ever.

Peter says too, “Concerning this salvation, the prophets sought and searched diligently. They prophesied of the grace that would come to you, searching for who or what kind of time the Spirit of Christ, which was in them, pointed to, when he predicted the sufferings of Christ, and the glories that would follow them” (1 Peter 1:10–11).

Even the Old Testament prophets themselves did not fully understand what they were writing. It was as if they were working on a giant jigsaw puzzle, each holding only a few pieces. Only when Jesus came was the picture on the box lid revealed.

sections.heading: 4. The Bible Has Only One Theme
sections.html:
Down the ages, many theologians have tried to find a single unifying theme for the whole Bible. Some say it is “promise”, running from the covenant with Abraham all the way to its fulfilment in the New Testament. Some say it is “covenant”: God makes a covenant with humanity, humanity breaks it, and God makes covenant again. Some say it is “Kingdom”: the Kingdom of God sets out from Eden and finally comes down in the new heaven and new earth.

Each of these has its value, and each has a basis in Scripture. But brothers and sisters, all of these themes finally flow together into one centre — Jesus Christ, the Lord who became flesh and has been exalted.

Who is the content of the promise? Christ. Who is the mediator of the covenant? Christ. Who is the King of the Kingdom? Christ.

Revelation puts it most thoroughly of all: “for the testimony of Jesus is the Spirit of Prophecy” (Revelation 19:10).

From Genesis to Revelation — sixty-six books, more than forty authors, spanning over fifteen hundred years and written in three languages — together they tell only one story: the coming, the salvation and the glory of Jesus.

Martin Luther is generally credited with saying, “The whole of Scripture everywhere speaks only of Christ.” And in The Bondage of the Will, written in 1525, he left these ringing words: take Christ out of the Scriptures, and what more will you find in them?

Spurgeon, too, has a widely quoted piece of teaching: from every village and every town in England there is a road that leads to London; in the same way, from every text of Scripture there is a road that leads to Christ.

sections.heading: 5. A Scientific Reminder: You Can’t See What You Aren’t Looking For
sections.html:
In 1999 the psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris published a famous experiment in the journal Perception. They asked participants to watch a video in which two teams were passing basketballs, and the participants’ task was to count exactly how many passes the team in white made. Halfway through the video, a person in a gorilla suit walked through the middle of the scene, even stopping to thump its chest, for about nine seconds in all.

The result? About half the participants did not see the gorilla at all.

Psychologists call this phenomenon “inattentional blindness”. It tells us one thing: although a person’s eyes are wide open, they see only what they are looking for.

It is the same physiologically. In the human eye, only a small area at the centre of the retina, called the “fovea”, can see clearly; the rest of the picture is blurred. In other words, when God made us, he determined that we must choose what to look at. Wherever your attention falls, that is the only place that is clear.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the tragedy of John 5:39. Those scribes were not failing to read the Scriptures; they were failing to look for Jesus. They were counting the passes, and so the gorilla walked right in front of them and they could not see it.

So the key to reading the Bible is not how many times you have read it, but who your heart is looking for when you open it.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: From Information to Revelation
sections.html:
The second of the Three Foundations of 321 says: the Bible is my standard.

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Bible is the standard not because it is an ancient book, but because it bears witness to the living Lord. A standard cut off from the Lord turns into legalism; the Lord cut off from the standard turns into doing whatever we please. The two cannot be separated.

The Lord Jesus said, “Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:40). The Bible exists not to add to our knowledge, but so that, in doing the word, we may know him, follow him and live out his likeness.

321 speaks of the eight stages of changing our mindset. The first stage is “Information”, and the second is “Revelation”. Brothers and sisters, the difference between these two stages is the difference between the scribes and the disciples.

Information is: I know John 3:16.

Revelation is: I know God loves “me”, so much that he gave his one and only Son for “me”.

Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Many people have read the Bible all their lives and are still stuck at the first stage, because when they read, their eyes are looking for answers, not for the Lord.

Let me give you a very simple practice that will change your devotional life for good: tomorrow morning, before you open your Bible, be still for ten seconds and pray one sentence — “Lord, today please reveal yourself to me in this passage.” Then, whether you are reading the sacrificial regulations of Leviticus, the palace intrigues of Kings or the love poetry of the Song of Songs, ask the same question:

How does this passage help me know Jesus better?

Brothers and sisters, you will find that the sin offering in Leviticus speaks of him, the Passover lamb speaks of him, the rock in the wilderness speaks of him, the bronze serpent speaks of him; Joseph sold, imprisoned and exalted foreshadows him; Boaz as the kinsman-redeemer foreshadows him; Jonah’s three days and three nights in the belly of the fish foreshadow him.

Then the Bible will no longer be a hard-to-understand ancient book, but a love letter — a love letter sent from the cross, with your name written on it.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Jesus Is the Focal Point of the Universe
sections.html:
“For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen” (Romans 11:36).

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is not only the core of our faith; he is the centre of the entire universe.

In the original, Romans 11:36 uses three prepositions, like three pillars holding up the whole universe:

The first is ἐξ (ek), “out of, from” — he is the source of all things.

The second is διά (dia), “through, by means of” — he is the way and the sustainer of all things.

The third is εἰς (eis), “into, towards” — he is the destination of all things.

The starting point is him, the process is him, and the end point is him too. Brothers and sisters, this verse is the doxology that bursts out of Paul once he has finished the first eleven chapters of Romans on salvation. After eleven chapters of theology, there is only one thing left to say: glory to him.

And immediately, in chapter 12, verse 1, Paul says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). Brothers and sisters, did you see that “therefore”? Because all things are from him, through him and to him, “therefore” I offer myself. Knowing the focal point inevitably leads to offering ourselves. This is what 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life.

sections.heading: 1. He Is the Lord of Creation
sections.html:
“All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3).

John says the same thing twice, once positively and once negatively, sealing off every possible exception. There is not a single created thing that was not made through him.

Hebrews says, “has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds” (Hebrews 1:2).

Colossians declares even more: “For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:16–17).

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to this phrase: “and for him.”

Creation is not only “through” him; even more, it is “for” him. The universe is not some work that has nothing to do with him; the universe exists for him. The galaxies turn for him, the seasons change for him, and your heart beats for him.

This answers one of humanity’s oldest questions: why am I here?

In the first book of his Confessions, Augustine wrote the words that have been repeated for sixteen hundred years: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

sections.heading: 2. He Is the Lord Who Is Heir of All Things and Upholds All Things
sections.html:
Colossians 1:17 says, “in him all things are held together.” This phrase “held together” is συνέστηκεν (synestēken) in Greek, meaning “bound together, held in place so they do not fall apart”.

Hebrews says, “His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

Brothers and sisters, “upholding” is not a one-off action; it is a continuous one. The original uses a present participle, meaning “he keeps on holding them up”.

On the Areopagus in Athens, Paul said to the Greek philosophers, “For in him we live, move, and have our being” (Acts 17:28).

The Lord Jesus himself said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Jesus is not only the craftsman of creation in the beginning; he is also the Lord who keeps the universe running now. Without him, nothing could exist; without him, we could not live.

Brothers and sisters, we often treat Jesus as “one part of life”. He is one item in our daily living, ranked after work, family, health and finances, or perhaps before them — but in any case he is “one of the items”.

No. He is not an item; he is the table holding up the whole list. He is not one part of our faith; he is the very reason and centre of our living.

sections.heading: 3. A Revolution in Astronomy Is a Shift of Perspective
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, I want to use a piece of the history of science to show just how important this matter of “focus” is.

From Ptolemy in the second century AD, for fourteen hundred years, humanity believed the earth was the centre of the universe, with the sun, the moon and all the stars revolving around it. This “geocentric” model sounded perfectly reasonable, because every day we see with our own eyes the sun rise in the east and set in the west.

The trouble was the planets. Seen from the earth, Mars would sometimes be moving along and suddenly go “backwards”, and then after a while move forwards again. This is called “retrograde motion”. To explain it, astronomers had to add a small circle on top of the circular orbit, called an “epicycle”; when that still didn’t work, they added another layer. The whole system became astonishingly complicated, and still it couldn’t predict accurately.

In 1543 Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, putting forward a proposal so simple it was unsettling: put the sun at the centre.

Once it was put in the right place, everything fell into place. The planets’ retrograde motion no longer needed dozens of layers of epicycles to explain it — it was simply the visual effect of the earth overtaking them on the inside track.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: Ptolemy’s astronomers were not lazy; they worked harder than anyone. Their mathematics was extremely ingenious, and their observations extremely careful. They got only one thing wrong — they put the wrong thing at the centre. And with the wrong thing at the centre, the harder they worked, the more complicated the model became, the more weary the people grew, and the less accurate the answers were.

Our lives are very often just like that. We read the Bible, attend meetings, serve and give, adding layer upon layer of “epicycles” — one more meeting, one more course, one more method — and yet inside our sums still don’t add up; we are still uneasy, still tired.

Because the centre hasn’t changed.

Here is a figure, by the way: the sun accounts for 99.86 per cent of the total mass of the solar system. In other words, put all eight planets, all the moons, all the asteroids and all the comets together, and they make up less than two-thousandths of the solar system. Brothers and sisters, the sun is the centre not because the earth graciously stepped aside, but because that is simply how things are.

In the same way, Jesus has the first place not as a courtesy we extend to him, but because that is how things are. “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together” (Colossians 1:17). What we call “letting Jesus be King” is not, in fact, lifting him up onto the throne; it is us getting down off his throne and returning to the place where we belong.

321 puts it precisely: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

sections.heading: 4. A Lesson from Flying: Don’t Trust Your Feelings
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, here is one more thing to do with focus.

In pilot training there is an extremely important lesson called “instrument flying”. When an aircraft enters cloud, or is flying over the sea at night with no horizon outside to refer to, the vestibular system in the inner ear produces serious illusions — you are clearly turning, yet you feel you are flying level; you are clearly descending, yet you feel you are climbing. This is called “spatial disorientation”. The training materials of the US Federal Aviation Administration stress again and again that in such a situation the only way to survive is to trust the instruments, not your feelings. History holds far too many tragic accidents, all with the same cause: the pilot moved his focus from the instruments to his own feelings.

Brothers and sisters, our lives also have times when we fly into cloud. The day the diagnosis comes, the day your child storms out and slams the door — the fog closes in on every side, and you can’t see the horizon. At those times our feelings will tell us: God doesn’t love you any more; it’s all over.

At those times the only way to survive is to move our focus from our feelings back to the instruments — back to God’s word, back to the Lord who sits on the throne.

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2).

The Greek word for “looking” is ἀφοράω (aphoraō). It is made up of two parts: “away from” plus “to look at”. It means taking your eyes off everything else and fixing them on him alone.

Brothers and sisters, looking to Jesus is an act that involves a choice. You cannot fix your eyes on Jesus and on other people’s opinions at the same time. To gaze at this One, you have to turn away from those other things.

sections.heading: 5. Confirmation from Psychology: When the Focus Is on Ourselves, We Suffer
sections.html:
Psychology also offers corroborating evidence on this.

In 2002 the researchers Nilly Mor and Jennifer Winquist published in Psychological Bulletin a meta-analysis drawing together more than two hundred studies. Their conclusion was clear: “self-focused attention” is significantly and consistently associated with negative emotions such as depression and anxiety. The more persistently people keep their attention on themselves, the deeper their emotional suffering.

The Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman put forward the “focusing illusion”: nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.

Brothers and sisters, these two findings are not teaching spiritual truths, but from the side they confirm what Scripture said long ago.

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

What is the self-centred life? It is putting yourself at the centre. People who put themselves at the centre live exhausting lives. Because when you are the centre, the whole weight of the universe presses down on your shoulders. You have to prove yourself, defend yourself, compare yourself, protect yourself. Every day you are calculating: How do others see me? Have I lost? Am I good enough?

What is selflessness? 321 puts it well: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the move from an earth-centred to a sun-centred universe. “It is no longer I who live” — I have stepped down from the centre; “but Christ lives in me” — he is now at the centre.

Once it is put in the right place, everything falls into place.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Four Shifts of Perspective
sections.html:
Once the truth that Jesus is the focal point of the universe gets into our hearts, it brings about what 321 calls the four shifts of perspective:

From “man’s” perspective to “God’s” perspective. I used to ask: how do other people see this? Now I ask: how does God see it? “For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

From an “earthly” perspective to a “heavenly” perspective. “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

From a “temporal” perspective to an “eternal” perspective. Paul counted his brilliant record as refuse, because he had seen a much longer timeline.

From a “worldly” perspective to a “godly” perspective. The worldly asks, “What’s in this for me?” The godly asks, “Can this let Jesus be glorified?”

Brothers and sisters, 321 also says: our focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances.

When the focus is on ourselves, we become proud or we feel inferior — in fact these are the same disease, both a matter of staring into the mirror.

When the focus is on other people, we compare or we resent — your joy is placed in someone else’s hands.

When the focus is on our circumstances, we fear or we complain — circumstances change every day, so you are shaken every day.

When the focus is on Jesus, we become strong, settled and full of hope — because he is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

Only when we put our focus on Jesus can we stand unshaken, never lose our way, and be more than conquerors in all things.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Everything Comes Back to the One
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the whole framework of 321 is really the unfolding of a single sentence: let Jesus become the focus.

First, look at the Three Foundations.

One: Jesus is my role model. The focus is his life — as he lived, so I live.

Two: the Bible is my standard. The focus is his word — as he says, so I do.

Three: the Holy Spirit is my guide. The focus is his Spirit — the Lord Jesus said, “He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you” (John 16:14).

Brothers and sisters, notice the third one. The work of the Holy Spirit is to bring the focus onto Jesus. So a person truly filled with the Holy Spirit will not exalt his own gifts, experiences or promptings; he will only exalt Jesus. Any “prompting” that moves the focus away from Jesus, we must test carefully.

Next, look at the Two Core Values.

One: let Jesus be King. This is exactly what the second practice in the lesson text speaks of: turning to Jesus and making the choice of sovereignty.

Two: let Jesus receive all the glory. This is exactly what the lesson text said at the very start: the purpose of revival is to let Jesus receive all the glory.

Then look at the Goal: establish God’s system.

What is God’s system? It is a system that runs with Jesus at its centre. By contrast, the Babylonian system is a system that runs with “self” at its centre. The difference between the two is not in outward appearance, nor in how many activities there are, but in who is at the centre.

321 also says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

Change begins with the mindset. When the mindset that “Jesus is the focal point” truly gets into the heart, life changes with it; when life has changed, daily living changes; when daily living has changed, relationships change; when relationships have changed, ministry changes.

Brothers and sisters, this order cannot be reversed. Many people do it backwards: they rush into ministry first, then patch up relationships, and only last of all think about life. The result is that the bigger the ministry grows, the emptier the life becomes. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Relationships have their order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If the focus isn’t first aimed at God, the other three levels of relationship will all go askew.

As for the 920 practice, it is especially meaningful in this lesson. 920 says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; we are to practise living a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions towards them — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, fruit is for others to eat, not for the tree to eat itself. When, at home, at the office or in your chat groups, you shift your focus from “I want to be seen” to “let Jesus be seen”, those nine graces will grow naturally. Because selflessness is exactly the soil in which fruit grows.

As for 235 relationships: find a brother or sister who is also pursuing selflessness and become a “2”, spiritual companions reminding each other where the focus belongs; then, above and below you, establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally, together with co-workers of the five ministry gifts, become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

And the Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible shines its light on me, Jesus becomes my life, and so I am able to let Jesus be King, and finally let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? From beginning to end, not one part of 321 has “me” at the centre.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Fixing the Focus Firmly with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s take them one at a time, and use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to fix them firmly in place.

Practice 1: Jesus Is the Focus of Our Daily Devotions

Each day, quieten your heart, and when you open the Bible, don’t just read the words; look for the heart of Jesus. Whichever book you are reading, ask yourself: how does this passage help me know Jesus better?

How do we do this in concrete terms? I suggest three steps, which take only five to ten minutes.

Step one: before you read, pray one sentence: “Lord, please reveal yourself to me in this passage today.” This is lining up the finderscope.

Step two: after you read, write down one sentence: what kind of Lord the Jesus I saw today is. Don’t write your feelings, don’t write plans; write only “who he is”.

Step three: carry that one sentence into the day. Think it over once while you wait at a red light, and again before you go to sleep.

Brothers and sisters, these three steps look very small, but after thirty days you will find that your Bible has grown thicker and your heart has grown softer.

Looking at this practice through the eight stages:

Information: I have learned that “the whole Bible bears witness to Jesus”.

Revelation: one day as I read the Bible, the Holy Spirit suddenly let me see the Lord’s face in a passage I had read ten times, and my heart burned within me, just as the two disciples on the road to Emmaus said: “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

Conviction: I begin to believe that the purpose of reading the Bible is not to keep to a schedule, but to meet the Lord.

Implementation: for thirty days in a row, I write down one sentence each day about “the Jesus I came to know today”.

Evaluation: on day twelve I notice I have started rushing to keep up with the schedule again, and the sentences I write are all clichés.

Correction: I cut my daily reading in half. Better to read five verses and take them in deeply than to read five chapters and come away empty.

Repetition: I keep going, so that it moves from effort to habit, and from habit to second nature.

Multiplication: I teach this method to my spouse, to my children, and to a new friend in my small group.

Practice 2: Turning to Jesus, Making the Choice of Sovereignty

In daily living, ask Jesus’ will first in everything. No longer make decisions on your own, but practise entrusting, looking to him and obeying in everything.

The lesson text gives two examples; let’s unpack them.

The first example: when facing conflict, choose forgiveness and love.

Brothers and sisters, conflict is the touchstone of our focus. When someone hurts me, my focus instantly and automatically snaps back to myself — I’ve been wronged, I’ve been misunderstood, I want justice. That is instinct.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

What did the Lord Jesus do on the cross? He said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Brothers and sisters, at that moment his focus was not on his own suffering, but on the Father’s will and on people’s salvation.

So the next time a conflict arises, don’t first ask, “How should I respond?” First ask, “How can this bring Jesus glory?” With that one question, the focus has shifted.

The second example: in financial planning, seek the Lord’s will rather than acting on your own ideas.

Money is the most honest indicator of our focus. The Lord Jesus said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

So before every financial decision, be still and ask: Lord, is this money building your Kingdom, or building my name?

Looking at it through the eight stages:

Information: I know that sovereignty belongs in Jesus’ hands.

Revelation: once, I made a decision by my own judgement and came away battered and bruised. At that moment I truly understood: I am not God.

Conviction: I decide I will no longer be my own king.

Implementation: before every decision, I begin to be still for thirty seconds and ask the Lord first.

Evaluation: a month later I notice that the smaller the matter, the more easily I forget to ask; the more urgent the matter, the more easily I decide by myself.

Correction: I ask a spiritual companion — my “2” — to ask me once a week: which decision this week did you ask the Lord about first?

Repetition: time after time, until “asking the Lord first” becomes a reflex.

Multiplication: I share this practice in my small group and help someone else begin doing it too.

Practice 3: Letting Jesus Be Glorified through Our Actions

Every day, look for one thing through which people can see Jesus in you. It might be a word of comfort, an act of help, a choice. Be willing to turn the spotlight onto Jesus, not seeking to be seen yourself, but letting Jesus alone be lifted up.

Brothers and sisters, here is a very practical exercise, which I call “one light a day”: before each day ends, think back over whether there was one thing today through which someone saw Jesus. If there was, write it down and thank the Lord; if there wasn’t, make up for it tomorrow.

Research by the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that participants who regularly wrote down things they were grateful for each week were noticeably more optimistic than those who recorded their troubles, complained of fewer physical symptoms, and even exercised more.

Brothers and sisters, please note that this is only supporting evidence from psychology, not our reason for doing it. Our reason for doing it is the Lord Jesus’ own words: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Look carefully at the order: the light shines out, people see the good works, and the glory goes to the Father. If the light shines out, people see the good works, and the applause comes to me — then it isn’t light at all; it’s a stage spotlight.

Looking at it through the eight stages:

Information: I know my daily living should glorify God.

Revelation: one day someone said to me, “You’re different from other people,” and I suddenly realised that it wasn’t that I was good; it was the Lord in me.

Conviction: I no longer need other people’s applause, because I already have the Lord’s acceptance.

Implementation: I begin doing one small thing each day, and deliberately give the credit to the Lord.

Evaluation: I notice that sometimes I am “performing humility”, while deep down I still want to be praised.

Correction: I switch to doing things no one will ever know about — anonymous giving, prayers I never mention.

Repetition: day after day, until lifting up Jesus becomes instinct.

Multiplication: I bring a spiritual child alongside me to do it together, and at the weekend we share with each other: “How did you let Jesus be seen this week?”

Brothers and sisters, these three practices help us not only to acknowledge in our heads that Jesus is the focal point, but to lift Jesus up as King in our actual daily living. This is the very starting point and key of the end time revival.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Him Have First Place
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that telescope at the very beginning.

Nothing was wrong with the equipment, nothing was wrong with the technique, nothing was wrong with the effort. Only the focus was wrong.

Today many people are praying for revival. We pray for numerical growth, for an outpouring of anointing, for signs and wonders. There is nothing wrong with these prayers in themselves. But Scripture tells us that the source of revival is Jesus, the power of revival comes from Jesus, and the purpose of revival is to let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Lord Jesus said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).

Brothers and sisters, if what is lifted up is a method, people will follow the method; if what is lifted up is a person, people will follow that person — and people fall. Only when it is Jesus who is lifted up will people be drawn to him, and never be disappointed.

So this morning I want to issue this call:

Move him back to the centre.

In your devotions, move him back to the centre — don’t just read the words; look for his heart.

In your decisions, move him back to the centre — don’t just follow your own ideas; ask his will first.

In your reputation, move him back to the centre — don’t seek to be seen yourself; let him alone be lifted up.

In your church, move him back to the centre — boast not in size, not in strategy, not in any one person, but boast only in Christ.

One day, every focus will return to the same place: “I heard every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, and everything in them, saying, ‘To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!’” (Revelation 5:13).

Brothers and sisters, that day will surely come. Since that is how it all ends, why not begin this very morning, and take our place there now?

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–11).

keyVerses: “However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ. Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8).

“He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:17–18).
practices: Make Jesus the focus of your daily devotions
Turn to Jesus and make the choice of sovereignty
Let Jesus be glorified through your actions
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. Thank you that you are not merely one part of our faith; you are the very reason and centre of our living.

Lord, we confess that we often push you to the side. We are busy reading the Bible, yet we do not meet you; we are busy serving, yet we do not look to you; we are busy being seen by others, and we forget that you alone are worthy of the glory. Lord, please forgive us.

Cleanse our eyes today, we pray, and move our focus back onto you. When we open the Bible, reveal yourself to us between the lines; when we face decisions, help us to ask your will first; when we do anything good, help us to turn the spotlight onto you.
Lord, may the end time revival come among us — not to showcase any one person, any one church or any one method, but only so that you may receive all the glory.
May you have the first place in our lives, in our families, in our church, and in all things.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “You search the Scriptures (or: Search the Scriptures), because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:39–40). Think back over your Bible reading this past month: have you been “searching”, or “meeting”? Please share a time when you truly saw Jesus in a passage of Scripture. How did that experience change your daily living that day?

“For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen” (Romans 11:36). In your life right now, is there some matter, some relationship or some goal that is still sitting in the “centre” of your heart? This week, what concrete choice are you willing to make to give that place back to Jesus?
l011.title: The Focus of Revival Is Jesus
l011.subtitle: Let Jesus Have First Place in Everything
l011.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: Jesus Is Not an Option but the Focus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to do something very simple: close your eyes for three seconds, then open them and look at the room in front of you.

You’ll notice something remarkable. Although your eyes “see” the whole room, the only part that is truly sharp is the small patch you are looking straight at. That isn’t an illusion; it’s a fact of the Creator’s design. On the retina of the human eye there is a tiny area called the fovea centralis — less than a millimetre across — and yet it holds the great majority of the cells that give us high-resolution sight. In other words, the field we truly see clearly at any one moment is only about one or two degrees wide — roughly the size of your thumbnail held at arm’s length.

God never made the human eye to “see everything clearly at once”. He made it to “focus clearly on one”.

But what kind of age are we living in? It’s an age that leans on reason, prizes efficiency, and is crammed with images and noise. The phone lights up and a dozen red dots pop up at once; we open the computer and twenty tabs are waiting for us. Our hearts are easily scattered, our eyes easily blurred — and even in our faith we have slipped into the confusion of having many focal points.

We need to admit something honestly: for many Christians, the problem isn’t that we fail to see Jesus; it’s that we see too much. He hasn’t disappeared — he has simply been pushed to one side. He has gone from being “the only one” to being “one of many”.

Where does Jesus rank on the list of our lives? Family, work, health, finances, relationships, dreams … and then Jesus. We haven’t denied him; we’ve just filed him under “also very important”.

But brothers and sisters, the Bible reminds us plainly: Jesus is not an optional extra on the journey of faith, nor is he some kind of spiritual supplement. He is not one dish on the platter of our lives; he is the host of the whole table. He is the centre of our lives, the one focus we should be fixing our eyes on every day.

Astronomers describe the solar system like this: the sun makes up about 99.8 per cent of the total mass of the entire solar system. That isn’t a religious claim; it is basic astronomical data. It is precisely because the sun’s mass is so overwhelming that every planet is held firmly in its orbit. If one day the sun were moved out of place, the solar system wouldn’t merely become less convenient — it would collapse altogether.

As early as 1609, the German astronomer Johannes Kepler set out, in his New Astronomy, the first law of planetary motion: a planet travels around the sun in an elliptical orbit, with the sun at one “focus” of that ellipse. Notice that word — focus. An orbit is an orbit not because the planet runs well, but because the focus is where it is. Shift the focus and the orbit is thrown into chaos.

Our lives are just the same. We often think our spiritual problem is “I’m not trying hard enough”, when far more often it is “my focus has drifted”. With the wrong focus, the harder you try, the further you stray; with the right focus, your whole life naturally falls back into place.

Today’s message comes down to one sentence: Jesus is not an option; he is the focus. May we refocus on him this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Scene on the Mount of Transfiguration
sections.html:
Our theme verse today is Matthew 17:8. To really understand this verse, we first need to know something about this book, its author, and the passage around it.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by the apostle Matthew, whose former name was Levi. He had been a tax collector in Capernaum, and when the Lord called him he followed him (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written somewhere between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish readers. That is why Matthew keeps quoting the Old Testament and repeatedly uses phrases like “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet”. His aim was to prove one thing to his fellow Jews: this Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — the Son of David, the offspring of Abraham, the King.

Once we grasp that purpose, we understand why the scene on the Mount of Transfiguration matters so much to Matthew.

In time, the transfiguration follows hard on the heels of a major event. In Matthew 16, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16) The Lord commended him, saying that flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but his Father in heaven.

Yet in that very same chapter, the Lord began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and be raised on the third day. Peter immediately took hold of him and rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” And the Lord turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, take note of those words. The same Peter who one moment received revelation from the Father was, the next moment, being used by Satan. What made the difference? The Lord himself put it plainly: “You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” That is exactly a problem of focus — a shift from God’s point of view to man’s.

Then Matthew 17:1 says, “After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:1–2)

“After six days” — these three words are not thrown in casually. They bind the transfiguration tightly to the battle over focus that came just before. The disciples had just stumbled over their focus, and the Lord took them up the mountain to refocus them himself.

Geographically, tradition places the transfiguration on Mount Tabor in Galilee, but the context suggests it was more likely Mount Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi — around 2,800 metres high and the tallest mountain in that region. Whichever it was, the point is that they went up “into a high mountain by themselves” — away from the crowds, away from the noise, away from every distraction, until only the Lord and these three disciples remained.

Culturally, the appearance of Moses and Elijah carried deep meaning for the Jews. Moses stood for the law: he led Israel out of Egypt and met God on Mount Sinai. Elijah stood for the prophets: he heard the gentle whisper on Mount Horeb and was later taken up by chariots and horses of fire. “The Law and the Prophets” was how the Jews referred to the whole of the Old Testament.

So the meaning of this scene is this: here the entire Old Testament hands the baton to this one man, Jesus.

Then three things happened, and they form the heart of today’s lesson. First, Peter proposed making three tents. Second, a bright cloud overshadowed them and the Father himself spoke. Third, the disciples lifted up their eyes and saw no one, except Jesus alone.

Brothers and sisters, this is not a romantic religious experience; it is a “refocusing operation” performed by God himself. This morning, let us go up the mountain together.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Jesus Is the Centre of History and Eternity
sections.html:
Jesus is not merely a great man within one stretch of history; he is the source and the end of history.

Paul says it with great clarity in Colossians: “For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.” (Colossians 1:16–17)

Notice the three prepositions here: “created through him”, “created for him”, and “held together in him”. The first speaks of origin, the second of purpose, the third of continuance. All things come from him, all things exist for him, all things hold together in him. Once those three statements are spoken, there is no way left to put Jesus in the position of “one among many”.

The word for “held together” in Greek is sunistemi, meaning “to bring together and keep from falling apart”. In today’s language, Jesus is the power that keeps all things from flying to pieces. Scientists tell us that the positively charged protons in the nucleus of an atom repel one another, yet some force binds them tightly together; they call it the “strong nuclear force”. The Bible doesn’t teach us physics, but it does tell us who it is that holds everything in his hand — “in him all things are held together”.

In the chronology of world history there is a well-known fact: most civilisations number their years from the birth of Jesus. The years before his birth are called “before Christ” (BC), and those after it “AD” — from the Latin Anno Domini, “in the year of the Lord”. This way of reckoning was proposed in AD 525 by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus. It gradually spread throughout the world, and to this day it remains the international standard for dating.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: today, whether or not a person believes in Jesus, the moment they write down the date they are already acknowledging one thing — that history divides at the birth of this man. Jesus did not merely influence one religion; he has touched the course and the very core of all human history.

More importantly, Jesus is not only the focus of the past. The writer of Hebrews says, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8)

We often take this verse to comfort ourselves that the Lord does not change. That is certainly true. But its deeper meaning is that all three dimensions of time — past, present and future — are centred on him. He is not a single point living within history; he is the line that runs through the whole of it.

In the days to come, he will be the focus before whom every nation and people bows in worship: “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:10–11)

In eternity he will still be the centre of worship. John saw the New Jerusalem in Revelation, and he said: “The city has no need for the sun or moon to shine, for the very glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb.” (Revelation 21:23)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? In eternity even the sun leaves the stage, because by then the true source of light has come in person. The Lord himself says, “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.” (Revelation 22:13)

Let me use an everyday picture. Have you ever played with a magnifying glass in the sunshine? The same sunlight, spread out, only gives warmth; gathered to a single point, it can start a fire. The sun’s energy hasn’t increased — only the focus has changed.

Many Christians today are not short of grace; their grace is simply too scattered. Our time, energy and passion are all there; they just aren’t focused on one person. The Bible says “in him all things are held together”, and our lives are the same: when Jesus becomes the focus, everything that was scattered begins to come together; when Jesus is not the focus, everything that was together begins to fall apart.

Seen through the eyes of the 321 vision, this is exactly “a shift of perspective”. Our natural perspective is human, earthly, temporary and worldly: I look at my years of service, I look at the difficulties in front of me, I look at whether this season is a success or a failure. God wants us to turn to a perspective that is divine, heavenly, eternal and of God: I look to the Lord who is the author and perfecter, I look to the Christ who never changes, I look to the kingdom that is coming.

Once our perspective shifts, our life begins to change. As the 321 vision puts it so well: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: See No One but Jesus
sections.html:
Now we come to the heart of this lesson.

Matthew 17 records a supremely glorious scene. The Lord took Peter, James and John up the mountain and was transfigured before them; his face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Then, “Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him.” (Matthew 17:3)

Brothers and sisters, try to picture the scene. Three fishermen from Galilee, who had read the law and heard the prophets all their lives, suddenly find the giver of the law and the representative of the prophets standing before their eyes — and their Teacher standing in the middle, his face shining like the sun.

Peter’s response was deeply human, and deeply sincere. He said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)

Peter meant no harm. He was eager; he wanted to hold on to this glory. When Luke records the event, he adds a very honest comment: “not knowing what he said.” (Luke 9:33)

So where was the problem? It lay in the number — three tents.

Three tents means three focal points. Peter put Moses, Elijah and Jesus on the same level. He didn’t reject Jesus; he simply made Jesus “one of the three”.

Brothers and sisters, this is the mistake we make most often and notice least. We rarely deny Jesus outright; we just keep “pitching tents” for other people and other things. We pitch a tent for our achievements, a tent for our family, a tent for some spiritual mentor, and then a tent for Jesus too — usually the finest one of all. We think this is honouring him; in fact it is losing our focus.

How did the Father respond? The Bible says: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5)

Notice two actions. The first is “overshadowing”. The Father didn’t argue with Peter or explain theology; he simply covered everything with the cloud. The second is “speaking”. He moved the disciples’ attention from their eyes to their ears, from the scene to the word.

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” — the Father had already said this once, at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17). But this time the Father added three more words: “Listen to him.”

Those three words have a long history behind them. In Deuteronomy, Moses had long ago prophesied: “Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from among you, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.” (Deuteronomy 18:15)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The “Listen to him” the Father spoke on the mountain points to the very one Moses himself had pointed to more than a thousand years earlier. Moses never wanted people to listen to Moses; he wanted them to listen to the prophet who was to come. So when the Father said, “Listen to him”, Moses’ task was complete.

Then verse 8: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”

This is no coincidence; it is a deliberate revelation from God. Even Moses, the representative of the law, even Elijah, the representative of the prophets, had to leave the stage, because now the focus belonged to Jesus alone.

Hebrews describes this as a grand history of salvation: “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.” (Hebrews 1:1–2)

John says as well: “For the law was given through Moses. Grace and truth were realized through Jesus Christ.” (John 1:17)

Paul puts it more vividly still: “So that the law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” (Galatians 3:24)

The word “tutor” in Greek is paidagogos: in a Greek or Roman household, the servant whose job was to take the children to school and bring them home. His task was to bring the child safely to the teacher and then step aside. He was important, but he was not the teacher. Moses and Elijah are the servant who brings us to Jesus. Once the child stands before the teacher, if the servant is still standing in the middle, he is in the way.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God covered Moses and Elijah not because they weren’t good, but precisely because they were so good. It is exactly because they were glorious enough, weighty enough and worthy enough of honour that they were the most likely to steal our gaze from Jesus.

Even spiritual leaders, signs of grace and great figures of the past — if they rob us of our focus on Jesus, God himself will cover them and remind us: “Listen to him.”

There is a tender detail here that we often miss. When the disciples heard the Father’s voice, “they fell on their faces, and were very afraid.” Then the Bible says, “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’” (Matthew 17:6–7)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord of glory who made them afraid is the same Jesus who came and touched them. Refocusing is not a frightening thing. When everything else is covered over, what remains is not judgement but a hand resting on your shoulder, and the words, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”

Paul says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

This is the single most important verse in the whole Bible on “gazing”. It tells us a spiritual law: what you gaze upon, you become. On the mountain the disciples saw the Lord transfigured; after they came down, they themselves began to be transformed.

Psychology offers an interesting confirmation. A study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, with wide variation between individuals. This reminds us that gazing on Jesus isn’t accomplished by one moving moment on a mountain; it takes refocusing day after day.

Seen through the eyes of the 321 vision, Peter’s “three tents” are an expression of the self-centred life. Being self-centred doesn’t necessarily mean doing evil; very often it means “I’ve got a good idea”. Within Peter’s zeal lay his own arrangements, his own plans, the glory he himself wanted to hold on to. And the Father’s cloud came to cover that “self”, so that a selfless life might be revealed.

The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. When all three tents are taken down and only one Christ remains, that is not a loss; it is entering into fullness without limit. Paul says, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

This is precisely the 321 vision’s Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. “See no one but Jesus” is the most beautiful picture of those Two Core Values.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: When Our Focus Drifts, We Easily Lose Our Way
sections.html:
Our spiritual life often isn’t without the Lord; it’s that we see too many “other people”.

We follow those who teach us, we admire the servants God uses, we honour the spiritual elders who led us to faith. All of these are good; all of them are grace God has given. But if they cause us to put our focus in the wrong place, our faith has lost its focus.

The church in Corinth is the clearest example. Paul says: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” (1 Corinthians 1:12)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Corinthians’ problem wasn’t that they were unspiritual but that they were too spiritual — every one of them was clutching a very impressive name. Paul, Apollos, Cephas — which of them wasn’t good? Which of them wasn’t a servant God greatly used? Yet when these names were put in the place of focus, the church split apart.

Paul’s answer is utterly decisive: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him? I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:5–7)

“Neither he who plants is anything” — that is how Paul speaks of himself. This isn’t low self-esteem; it’s clear-sightedness. Paul knew he was the “tutor”: his task was to bring people to Jesus and then step aside.

John the Baptist took this to its very limit: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

There is a phenomenon in psychology that helps us understand how scarce focus is. In 1953 Colin Cherry, a scholar at Imperial College London, conducted a classic experiment that later gave its name to the “cocktail party effect”. He found that in a room full of voices, a person can lock on to one voice and listen intently — but at the cost of hearing almost nothing of what the other voices are saying; and the moment their attention is pulled away, the original voice immediately grows blurred.

That tells us something very important: human attention is a limited resource, not something that can be shared out without end. So “listening closely to Jesus” is not an emotional form of piety; it is a choice that costs something — if you choose to listen to him, you must stop listening to other things at the same time.

The Lord himself puts it even more directly: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

He also says: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.” (Matthew 6:22)

The word “sound” in Greek is haplous, which literally means “single, undivided, simple”. The Lord’s meaning is that if the eye is single, the whole body is full of light. The Danish thinker Kierkegaard wrote a book whose title is Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. He was right — a pure heart is a single-minded heart.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask an honest question: this morning, who takes up the most space in your heart?

Is it the person who hurt you? The message that still hasn’t had a reply? The test result that still hasn’t come back? The co-worker who is moving ahead faster than you?

When our focus drifts, it isn’t necessarily because we love the world. More often it’s because we care too much — too much about what people think, too much about our own performance, too much about the changes in our circumstances.

The 321 vision has a saying that hits the mark exactly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

When the focus is on ourselves, we fall into pride or into feelings of inferiority — two sides of the same coin, both of them the self-centred life. When the focus is on other people, we fall into comparison and criticism — which was exactly the state of the church in Corinth. When the focus is on our circumstances, we fall into fear and anxiety — which is the story of Peter on the sea that we’ll come to shortly.

The Lord’s heart comes down to one sentence: “Listen to him.” Only Jesus is worthy of our whole-hearted gaze, our single-minded following and our complete obedience.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: How to Actually Live a Life That Sees “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
“Jesus alone” isn’t a romantic religious slogan; it is a deliberately chosen way of life.

This doesn’t mean we no longer see anyone else. The Lord hasn’t told us to close our eyes; he has told us to fix our focus. Truly seeing “Jesus alone” means having a clear centre within: I live for him; I act relying on him; I think with my eyes fixed on him.

Paul describes this life in full: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

The word “set your mind” in Greek is phroneo. It doesn’t mean thinking of something now and then, but “continually orienting the mind towards it”. It speaks of a habit of the mind, an inner compass needle pointing north.

He also says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, there’s a beautiful picture that can help us here. Why don’t ballet dancers get dizzy when they spin? They use a technique called “spotting”: the body keeps turning, but the eyes stay locked on a single point on the wall; when the body can turn no further, the head whips round and the eyes find that same point again. The body spins, but the focus doesn’t move.

Brothers and sisters, our lives are often spinning just like that. Our schedules spin, our emotions spin, our relationships spin, the times we live in spin. God has never promised that we won’t spin, but he has promised that we can have a fixed point that doesn’t move.

David says, “I have set Yahweh always before me. Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.” (Psalm 16:8)

He also says, “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.” (Psalm 27:4)

“One thing.” Not ten things, not three things — one thing. Paul says the same: “but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

C. S. Lewis is generally credited with saying something like this in Mere Christianity: aim at heaven and you will get earth thrown in; aim at earth and you will get neither. That captures the secret of seeing “Jesus alone” — it isn’t giving up everything on earth, but first fixing our aim on the One in heaven, and then everything else falls into its proper place.

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Brothers and sisters, this order must not be reversed. Many weary servants are worn out not because they are doing too much but because their order is upside down — first things, then people, and only then God. By the time God’s turn comes, there is no strength left.

Seeing “Jesus alone” means setting the order right. When he is in first place, everything else returns to where it belongs.

A Gentle Reminder: Focus Comes Not by “Effort” but by “Turning”

Before we move on to putting this into practice, there is one vital reminder.

Focusing on Jesus doesn’t come from staring at him anxiously; it comes from turning to him straight away whenever you notice your focus has drifted.

There is a scene in the Bible that makes this as clear as it could be. The Lord was walking on the water, and Peter said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.” The Lord said, “Come!” And the Bible records: “Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:29–30)
