Brothers and sisters, notice that Peter didn’t sink because the wind and waves got bigger. The wind and waves had been there from the moment he stepped out of the boat. He sank because “he saw that the wind was strong”. His eyes changed what they were looking at.

And how did the Lord respond? “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31)

“Immediately.” The Lord didn’t wait until Peter had sunk to the bottom before giving him a lecture; he stretched out his hand at once. Brothers and sisters, how gentle our Lord is towards those who lose their focus.

So it isn’t about how spiritual you are; it’s about whether you are willing to keep “coming back to him one more time”.

Hebrews gives us the whole movement: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)

Lay aside, throw off, persevere, run — and finally, “looking”. The word for “looking” in Greek is aphorao. The prefix apo means “away from”, and horao means “to see”. So the word literally means: to take your eyes off everything else and fix them on one thing.

True looking to Jesus always includes the act of “looking away”.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Seeing Jesus Alone Is 321
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is in fact the most central picture of the whole 321 vision.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. On the mountain the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.” That one sentence establishes three things at once: Jesus is the role model we are to follow; his word is the standard we are to listen to; and the one who enables us truly to hear him and truly to recognise him is the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The words “see no one but Jesus” are a picture of those Two Core Values. When my eyes see only him, he reigns as King in my heart; when my lips proclaim only him, all the glory goes to him.

The Goal — establish God’s system. God’s system is not propped up by one very strong leader; it is built together by a company of people who “see no one but Jesus”. Any system propped up by a person collapses when that person falls; only a system with Christ as its cornerstone will never fall.

Now look at the self-centred life and selflessness. Peter wanting to build three tents was the self-centred life; the Father covering it with the cloud was turning the self-centred life into selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Moses and Elijah leaving the stage is the most beautiful demonstration of “returning to our originally intended position”. They were not rejected; they simply returned to the place of creatures and servants.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Think of Matthew 16: Peter set his mind on the things of men, and the Lord said, “Get behind me, Satan!” Six days later, on the mountain, the Father himself dealt with the same problem through the cloud. What Satan fears most is not that we are busy, but that our eyes turn away from everything he has laid out and back to Jesus.

Now look at the five-fold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today’s lesson starts with mindset — Jesus is not an option; he is the focus. Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. The order cannot be reversed, nor can any step be skipped.

Now look at the shift of perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to what is of God. On the mountain Peter was “not knowing what he said”, because he was still viewing the scene from a human perspective. Many years later he wrote 2 Peter, and said: “For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.” (2 Peter 1:17–18) Years later, he finally understood. A shift of perspective is the lesson of a lifetime.

Now look at the 920 practice. Every person we are in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living a selfless (0) life, we can bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions in these relationships. Brothers and sisters, think about it: why are we so easily hurt in relationships? Often it’s because we look for our focus in those relationships — I need to be seen, I need to be affirmed, I need to be understood. But when our focus is on Jesus alone, we no longer need to take anything from other people; instead we are able to give. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control — all nine of these fruits grow naturally out of a life that is in focus.

Finally, look at the 235 relationships. With selfless people we become a “2” — spiritual companions who hold each other up; we build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; we become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, notice how many people were on the Mount of Transfiguration — the Lord took three disciples up the mountain. He didn’t take one, nor did he take twelve. The spiritual mountaintop experience is never meant to be enjoyed by a lone bird; it is to be experienced together among companions, witnessed together, and carried down the mountain together into service.

And after coming down the mountain? From Matthew 17:14 onwards, at the foot of the mountain a boy possessed by a demon was waiting for them. The glory on the mountain was for the service below it. The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Receiving life on the mountain, building relationships among companions, doing ministry at the foot of the mountain — the order is perfectly clear.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Make Jesus Your Focus Every Day
sections.html:
In an age with too many voices and too many options, “focusing on Jesus” is not just an emotional longing; it is a spiritual rhythm that has to be deliberately cultivated.

One classic study deserves our attention. In research published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford University found that when a store displayed only six kinds of jam, the proportion of people who stopped to taste and went on to buy was far higher than when it displayed twenty-four. The more options people had, the harder they found it to decide, and the less satisfied they were with their decision.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the spiritual situation of our generation. We’re not short of options; what we’re short of is focus.

Here are three concrete practices to help you refocus in everyday life and live as a disciple who sees “Jesus alone”. We’ll deepen each practice through the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Your First Glance in the Morning Goes to Jesus

When you get up each day, don’t rush to check your phone, scroll social media or dive into your schedule. First be still for one minute and give your heart to Jesus.

You can say to him quietly, “Lord Jesus, today I long to see you alone, and not to let anyone or anything take my eyes off you.”

This is a deliberate beginning — letting faith define your day instead of letting the world define it. Let Jesus be the first focus of your day, so that even as the sun is rising, your heart has already turned towards him.

The Lord himself did exactly this: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” (Mark 1:35)

David did the same: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.” (Psalm 5:3)

Lamentations says, “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.” (Lamentations 3:23)

Brothers and sisters, your first glance in the morning sets the direction of your day.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — recognise a fact: the focus of your day is decided in its first ten minutes.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see that every morning you are already worshipping something, though it may not be the Lord.

Stage 3, Conviction — say sincerely in your heart: I believe that a day that begins by seeing Jesus and a day that begins by seeing my phone are two completely different days.

Stage 4, Implementation — today, move the place where your phone charges out of reach of your bed, and put a Bible by your bedside.

Stage 5, Evaluation — in the evening, ask honestly: whom did I give my first glance to this morning?

Stage 6, Correction — if you failed, don’t condemn yourself; simply turn again tomorrow.

Stage 7, Repetition — keep it up for at least forty days. Remember that study: forming a new habit takes an average of sixty-six days.

Stage 8, Multiplication — find a brother or sister, make a commitment together, remind each other, and pass this practice on.

Practice 2: When Facing a Choice, Pause and Ask Jesus

Before you make any important decision, give Jesus thirty seconds.

Whether it’s a choice at work, how to respond to someone, or an emotional reaction, you can ask in your heart, “Lord Jesus, how do you want me to choose? How do you see this?”

This simple pause is an act of surrender and refocusing. You aren’t reacting on emotion; you are choosing to invite Jesus in and let his will lead you forward. Very often he will give you unexpected guidance through a verse of Scripture, a word, or a sense of peace.

The Bible says, “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

James also says, “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.” (James 1:5)

The 321 vision puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll worry, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. Those thirty seconds are the switch that moves you from relying on the brain to relying on the heart.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — know that you make far more decisions every day than you think, and that most of them are made out of habit.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Lord to shine his light so you can see what you most often base your decisions on: fear, saving face, efficiency — or the Lord.

Stage 3, Conviction — believe that the Lord has a will for every small decision you make today; he isn’t a God who only cares about the big things.

Stage 4, Implementation — pick the situation where you most easily lose control, such as “wanting to reply at once to a message that has made me angry”, and deliberately pause for thirty seconds there.

Stage 5, Evaluation — after a week, look back: which times did I pause? What turned out differently?

Stage 6, Correction — shorten or lengthen the thirty seconds until you find a length you can really keep to.

Stage 7, Repetition — let the pause become a reflex.

Stage 8, Multiplication — share a testimony in your small group: “I paused for thirty seconds, and it turned out differently.”

Practice 3: After Sunset, Review Whether You Saw “Jesus Alone”

Before the day ends, set aside five minutes to look back quietly over your walk with the Lord. Ask yourself three questions:

First, at what moment today was I especially fixed on Jesus, especially drawn to him?

Second, at what moments did my eyes drift from the Lord and fix instead on what people thought of me, on the pressure of work, or on my own emotions?

Third, in which situation of daily living am I willing, tomorrow, to fix my eyes on Jesus more simply?

This kind of spiritual review will help you gradually develop a sensitivity of life that is “alert to Jesus”. You’ll find that the more often you review, the more easily you “see” him in everyday life.

David’s prayer can serve as the pattern for our review: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Lamentations also says, “Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to Yahweh.” (Lamentations 3:40)

Notice the order: first search, then turn again. The purpose of review isn’t condemnation; it is turning back.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Stage 1, Information — recognise that this kind of review is a spiritual tradition of the saints through the ages, not a new invention.

Stage 2, Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of the truly decisive moments of your day, not just the most dramatic one.

Stage 3, Conviction — believe that an unexamined life will, without your noticing, be refocused by the world.

Stage 4, Implementation — try five minutes tonight; three lines written down is enough.

Stage 5, Evaluation — at the weekend, look over the week’s notes and find the patterns of losing focus that keep recurring.

Stage 6, Correction — for that pattern, ask the Lord for a verse to be your “fixed point”.

Stage 7, Repetition — let the review become the full stop of your day, as natural as switching off the light.

Stage 8, Multiplication — in the 920 practice, pray for every “2” around you, asking the Lord to let them see Jesus too.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: May Your Whole Life See “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the central reminder of this whole course rests on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. But the deeper aim is that we would not merely know about Jesus, but see “Jesus alone” every day.

Knowing him is a matter of the head; seeing him alone is a matter of the eyes and the heart. Many people have known about Jesus for years, yet have seldom truly “seen” him.

May we not let achievement steal our focus, nor relationships, nor service, nor expectations, pressure or disappointment — but keep our eyes fixed on him always.

When Stephen was martyred, the Bible says: “But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God.” (Acts 7:55) Brothers and sisters, the stones were raining down on him, yet he saw Jesus. When a person truly sees “Jesus alone”, not even death can take away their focus.

Those Greeks who came to Philip spoke words that have become the cry of the church through every age: “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” (John 12:21)

This morning, that is our cry too.

May our families let people see Jesus; may our church let people see Jesus; may our workplaces let people see Jesus; and when we come to the end of this life, may those who look back on it see no one but Jesus.

Because — he is worthy of all our focus and all our worship.

In his vision John heard the song of heaven: “To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!” (Revelation 5:13)

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: First glance in the morning: fix your eyes on Jesus
Facing a choice: pause and ask Jesus
After sunset: review whether you saw “Jesus alone”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that this morning you have brought us up the mountain.

Lord, we confess that our hearts are so often scattered and our eyes so often blurred. Like Peter, we have eagerly wanted to pitch tents for many people and many things, and without even noticing we have made you just one among them. Please forgive us.
We ask you, like that bright cloud, to cover everything in our lives that steals our focus; and we ask you, like the voice of the Father, to speak to us: This is my beloved Son; listen to him.
Lord, when we see that the wind is strong and we begin to sink, stretch out your hand at once and take hold of us.

Holy Spirit, help us, from tomorrow morning onwards, to give our first glance to you; to pause and ask you before every choice; and at the close of every day to look back quietly and turn to you once again.

May our mindset be changed by you, our life changed by you, our daily living changed by you, our relationships changed by you, and our ministry changed by you too. Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours.
We lift up our eyes and see no one else; we long to see only you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 17:4: “Peter answered, and said to Jesus, ‘Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’” Take a quiet moment to reflect: in your life right now, which “tent” stands side by side with Jesus? It may be an achievement, a person, an expectation, or a sense of security. Share with your group, and pray together, asking the Lord to cover it with his cloud.

Matthew 14:30: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” Which “wind” has lately been most likely to pull your eyes away from the Lord? Which concrete practice (your first glance in the morning, thirty seconds before a decision, a review after sunset) do you plan to use to help yourself turn back? Make a commitment to one another in your group, and become each other’s spiritual companion.
l012.title: See No One but Jesus
l012.subtitle: Jesus Is the Focus of Everything (Part 2)
l012.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: A Shadow That Hid the Sun
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Today I’d like to begin with something that happens in the sky.

The sun is about 1.39 million kilometres across; the moon is about 3,474 kilometres across. The sun is roughly four hundred times the size of the moon. Yet every so often people on earth witness something astonishing: broad daylight suddenly turns dark, birds fly back to their nests, the temperature plunges, and stars appear on the horizon. And what has blotted out the sun entirely is that very moon, four hundred times smaller.

Why? Because the sun is about 150 million kilometres from the earth and the moon about 384,000 kilometres — and the first distance is also roughly four hundred times the second. Four hundred times the size, four hundred times the distance, so that to our eyes the two look exactly the same size. As long as the moon stands on that line between them, it can cover the whole sun completely.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to what this is telling us. The moon gives off no light of its own; every bit of its light is borrowed. A rock like that — giving no light, not burning, with no source of energy at all — can nonetheless hide the sun. Not because it is big, but because it is “standing in the wrong place”.

That is what today’s lesson has to say to us. Each of us is like that moon: we have no light of our own; all our light is borrowed from the Lord. But the moment we stand in the wrong place — the moment we move ourselves in between the Lord and the people — we can hide the Lord, who is infinitely greater than we are, so that people can no longer see him.

What a solemn thing that is. We don’t have to be big to block out Jesus; all we have to do is stand in the wrong place.

Let me tell you something closer to our everyday lives.

A brother led worship in his church for the first time. That day the presence of the Holy Spirit was unmistakable: the congregation wept, and some people repented. After the service everyone gathered round him and said, “You sang so beautifully today!” “Your voice really carries an anointing!” He modestly brushed it off, but inside, something quietly warmed.

The second week, he started paying attention to whether he was in tune. The third week, he started noticing the angle at which he stood on the platform. The fourth week, he found that when he prayed, what came to mind was not the face of the Lord but the applause of the congregation.

Later, with tears in his eyes, he said, “I didn’t fall. I just slowly moved myself into the middle.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the quietest drift of all, and the hardest to detect. No great sin, no scandal — just moving, step by step, from the side into the middle; just slowly lifting your head amid the cheers of the crowd.

Today we are going up the Mount of Transfiguration together. When the cloud has lifted and the voice has fallen silent, and the disciples raise their eyes from the ground, the Bible records a short but stunning sentence:

“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

No one. Except Jesus alone.

That is the direction of our whole lives.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Tents on the Mountain
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of that sentence, we first need to look at the setting of the passage.

The Gospel of Matthew is generally held to have been written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector, sometime around AD 60, mainly for Jewish believers. Matthew’s aim was to prove that this Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the Son of David, the King who was to come. That is why the book particularly emphasises the kingship of Jesus and how he fulfils the Law and the Prophets.

The transfiguration is recorded at the beginning of Matthew 17. Matthew says, “After six days.” From when are those six days counted? From the end of chapter 16.

Three major things happened in chapter 16. First, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, Peter recognised Jesus and said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16) Second, Jesus foretold that he would be killed and rise on the third day, but Peter tried to stop him, and the Lord rebuked him: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23) Third, the Lord went on to say, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24)

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Peter, who had only just received revelation, became a stumbling block in the blink of an eye. Why? Because he slid from “setting his mind on the things of God” to “setting his mind on the things of men”. Once the focus drifts, everything drifts. And the remedy the Lord gave comes down to a single phrase: deny yourself — which is the most direct biblical basis for the 321 vision’s teaching that “the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless”.

Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain (traditionally thought to be Mount Hermon, north of Caesarea Philippi). There Jesus “was changed”.

The verb “to be changed” — transfigured — is metamorphoō (μεταμορφόω) in Greek, meaning “to change the outward form from within”. Jesus’ glory was not a halo added from outside; it shone out from his very being. He had always been that glorious; ordinarily it was veiled by his flesh, but in that moment a corner of the tent was drawn back.

Next, Moses and Elijah appeared to them.

Who were these two? Moses represented the law, and Elijah the prophets; the Jews often spoke of “the Law and the Prophets” as a name for the whole Old Testament. Moses led Israel out of Egypt and received the law on Mount Sinai; Elijah stood alone on Mount Carmel against four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and was finally carried up to heaven by chariots and horses of fire. They are the two loftiest peaks in the history of the Old Testament.

If we are talking about human greatness, who could be greater than they? Yet how does the Bible describe Moses? “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) And what did Elijah say under the juniper tree? “It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.” (1 Kings 19:4)

These two giants — one very humble, the other confessing he was no better than his fathers. They knew who they were: they were vessels.

But Peter didn’t understand. The moment he saw the three of them together, he blurted out, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)

Three tents. The same size, the same height, side by side in a row.

Peter meant no harm; he spoke out of excitement, out of eagerness. But hidden in what he said was a fatal distortion: he set the Creator alongside the created, the master alongside the servants, the source of light alongside the things that merely reflect it.

How did God respond?

“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5)

God the Father interrupted Peter; he didn’t wait for him to finish. This is the second time in Matthew’s Gospel that the Father speaks in person (the first was at Jesus’ baptism, Matthew 3:17), and this time he adds three words: “Listen to him.”

Not to Moses, not to Elijah — to him.

Then the cloud lifted.

“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

Moses was gone; Elijah was gone. Not because they didn’t matter, but because their task was to point to that One.

Brothers and sisters, this is the final destiny of everyone God uses, and also their greatest glory: to bring people to Jesus, and then to step aside.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: People Are Not the Focus — Jesus Is the Focus
1. Every One of Us Is a Vessel
sections.html:
The lesson states its theme from the very start: each of us, however gifted or capable, is ultimately a vessel in the hands of Jesus. That isn’t belittling people; it’s recognising who we are. Paul says it most clearly: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7)

The word for “clay” in Greek is ostrakinos (ὀστράκινος), meaning earthenware fired from clay. In Paul’s day it was the cheapest, most ordinary kind of container. Every household had them, and nobody grieved when one broke.

Why did God put “this treasure” in clay vessels? Paul gives the answer himself: “that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.”

Brothers and sisters, if the treasure were put in a golden vessel, people’s eyes would stop at the gold; put it in a clay jar, and people can see the treasure. God uses ordinary people precisely so that his glory is beyond dispute.

sections.heading: 2. A Vessel’s Worth Is Not in the Vessel Itself
sections.html:
The lesson puts it very precisely: a vessel has no worth in itself; it is “who uses it” that determines its glory and its function.

Think of an ordinary wooden staff. It’s worth next to nothing. But when that staff was in Moses’ hand and stretched out over the Red Sea, the waters parted; from then on the Bible calls that staff “God’s rod” (Exodus 4:20). Did the staff change? No. What changed was “who was holding it”.

Brothers and sisters, our gifts, our eloquence, our music, our organising ability — they are all that staff. In themselves they cannot save a single person; they have worth because they are held in the Lord’s hand.

sections.heading: 3. When God Uses Us, Are We Still Humble?
sections.html:
The lesson asks a very pointed question: when God uses us, are we still humble? When people praise us, follow us and notice us, do we turn the glory towards Jesus — or do we unwittingly “block his light”?

The Bible has one example that is truly alarming.

In the wilderness the Israelites grumbled against God, and God sent fiery serpents among the people. The people cried out, and God gave Moses instructions: “Moses made a serpent of bronze, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived.” (Numbers 21:9) This bronze serpent was a vessel God commanded and God used, and it saved thousands upon thousands of lives.

But more than seven hundred years later, King Hezekiah did something: “He removed the high places, and broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah. He also broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it.” (2 Kings 18:4)

Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase: the children of Israel burned incense to the bronze serpent. The bronze serpent that had once saved lives ended up as an idol. A vessel God had used was lifted up by people into the place of God, and so a godly king had no choice but to smash it to pieces.

A vessel that is exalted will sooner or later be broken. That is a principle of Scripture — and it is also God’s mercy.

sections.heading: 4. The Spotlight Effect: We Overestimate How Much We Are Noticed
sections.html:
Psychology offers us a very interesting piece of supporting evidence.

Around 1999 and 2000, the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky at Cornell University in the United States described what they called the “spotlight effect”. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, and then asked them to estimate how many people had noticed the shirt. The participants’ estimates came out at roughly twice the actual number.

The conclusion: people systematically overestimate how much others notice them, because we live at the centre of our own consciousness and find it very hard to step outside and see things from someone else’s point of view.

Brothers and sisters, this research carries two reminders. The first: we are not as important as we imagine; the people in the congregation are not staring at us all the time, as we suppose. The second goes deeper: since we are naturally inclined to turn the spotlight on ourselves, “not exalting ourselves” will never happen automatically. It has to be a deliberate, daily choice made by relying on the Holy Spirit.

Our old self is a planet spinning on its own axis, forever revolving around itself — unless a greater gravity takes hold of us. That greater gravity is Jesus.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
The 321 vision says it with complete clarity: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. That is exactly how Satan’s fall began: he was not content to be a created shining star; he said, “I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:14)

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

A vessel returning to the place of a vessel: that is humility.

The nineteenth-century South African spiritual leader Andrew Murray says in his book Humility that humility is nothing other than the creature taking its rightful place before God. Humility isn’t putting yourself down or saying, “I can’t do anything.” Humility is standing in the right place — not an inch further forward, not an inch further back.

That’s why the 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, an empty clay jar isn’t a loss; it’s a readiness. Only when it is empty can it hold the treasure; only when we are selfless can we contain Christ.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Lesson of the Donkey’s Colt — Being Used Is No Reason to Be Exalted
1. The Lord Needs Him
sections.html:
The lesson uses a wonderfully vivid picture: a donkey’s colt. Let’s put it back into its biblical setting.

On Palm Sunday, Jesus was about to enter Jerusalem. Mark records that he “said to them, ‘Go your way into the village that is opposite you. Immediately as you enter into it, you will find a young donkey tied, on which no one has sat. Untie him, and bring him. If anyone asks you, “Why are you doing this?” say, “The Lord needs him;” and immediately he will send him back here.’” (Mark 11:2–3)

Notice these four words: “The Lord needs him.”

Those four words were the only credentials that colt ever had. It was no thoroughbred, no warhorse; no one had ever ridden it; it had no training and no track record at all. It was tied up at the entrance to the village, waiting for someone to come and untie it.

Its only worth was this: “The Lord needs him.”

Brothers and sisters, it’s the same with you and me. We were chosen not because we were good enough; we are used not because we are strong enough. All we can lean on for our whole lives are those four words: the Lord needs him.

And this had been prophesied some five hundred years earlier: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! Behold, your King comes to you! He is righteous, and having salvation; lowly, and riding on a donkey, even on a colt, the foal of a donkey.” (Zechariah 9:9)

Zechariah spoke these words around 520 BC. Five hundred years later, a nameless donkey’s colt fulfilled that prophecy.

sections.heading: 2. That Day, Whom Were the Crowds Welcoming?
sections.html:
“A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road. Others cut branches from the trees, and spread them on the road. The multitudes who went in front of him, and those who followed, kept shouting, ‘Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!’” (Matthew 21:8–9)

Clothes spread on the road, branches spread on the road, shouts of praise shaking the whole city.

The lesson asks a simple but piercing question: whom were the people welcoming? The colt, or Jesus?

The answer could not be more obvious: Jesus.

The colt walked right in the middle of it all — cloaks on its back, branches under its hooves, cheering in its ears. It was present for all the pageantry; not one bit of the glory was its own.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the situation of everyone who serves: we stand right in the middle, applause in our ears, eyes upon us — and yet not one bit of it belongs to us.

sections.heading: 3. If the Colt Lifts Up Its Head
sections.html:
The lesson goes on to say something sobering: if the colt had lifted up its head amid the crowd’s cheers, Jesus would have fallen off its back, and the focus would have changed.

The colt’s job is to keep its head down, to carry the load, to keep walking forward. If its head comes up, its back tilts, and the one riding on it can’t sit steady.

Brothers and sisters, the posture of our service determines whether the Lord can sit steady.

When our heads are down, the Lord sits steady and people see the King; when our heads come up, the Lord sways and people see the donkey.

And the most dangerous thing is this: when the colt lifts its head, it feels as though it is “being affirmed”, “being effective”, “being used by God”. It doesn’t feel that it is sinning. It has just … slowly raised its head a little higher.

The lesson is right: today we are just like that colt. If, while we are being used, we “lift ourselves up”, people will no longer be able to see Jesus.

sections.heading: 4. The Lesson of the Moon
sections.html:
Let’s go back to the moon we began with. It’s a dim rock that gives no light, yet humanity has sung its praises for thousands of years and written it into countless poems. Why? Because it stands in the right place and reflects the sun’s light to people in the night.

But that same moon, once it moves in between the sun and the earth, is no longer reflecting — it is eclipsing. The same moon, the same size, the same substance — change its position, and its effect is completely reversed.

Brothers and sisters, this is the mystery of service. We don’t glorify God by “trying harder”; we glorify God by “standing in the right place”.

John the Baptist summed this up in the most concise sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Lord commended him: “Among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer.” (Matthew 11:11) Yet the motto of this greatest of the prophets for his whole life was “I must decrease.”

Decreasing isn’t failure; decreasing is completing the task. When the moon fades at sunrise, it hasn’t been defeated — the day has dawned.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. It also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice, rely on the brain and you’ll worry.

The colt has no brainpower to rely on; it can only follow the one leading it — and that turns out to be its protection. Our problem is often that we think too much: Did I preach well today? What do people think of me? Will they ask me again next time? The moment we rely on the brain and on ourselves, worry comes, and our focus shifts from the Lord to ourselves.

The 321 vision also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Ministry comes last not because it is unimportant, but because ministry must grow out of life. If we put ministry first, ministry becomes our identity, and we start using results to prove our worth — and at that moment, we have lifted our heads.

The colt doesn’t need to prove itself to anyone. It only has to remember: the Lord needs him.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Right Attitude in Service — Head Down, Not Head Up
1. The Glory Is Not to Add Points to Our Name
sections.html:
The lesson says: being used by the Lord is an immense honour, but that honour is not to add points to our name; it is so that Jesus is glorified. Our mission is not to make people remember us but to help people meet the Lord.

These are two roads. One is: I serve, and people remember me — and the further I go, the heavier it gets, because keeping up a name is exhausting. The other is: I serve, and people meet the Lord — and the further I go, the lighter it gets, because I don’t have to carry anything that doesn’t belong to me. Paul chose the second road: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” (2 Corinthians 4:5)

“We don’t preach ourselves” — those words are worth reading every morning.

sections.heading: 2. Three Questions to Ask Yourself
sections.html:
The lesson offers a very practical exercise: every time a prayer is answered, every time our service bears fruit, every time we lead someone to salvation, we should ask ourselves: am I bearing witness to Jesus, or am I emphasising “me”?

I’ve broken that question down into three, so we can use them to examine ourselves every day. First: when I talk about this, who is the subject of the sentence? Is it “what God did” or “what I did”? Second: where are my listeners being led? To the Lord, or to me? Third: if my name were removed from this, would I still be willing to do it?

Brothers and sisters, that third question cuts the deepest; a great deal of service is exposed for what it really is in front of it.

Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) What people see is our “good works”; whom they glorify is “your Father who is in heaven”. Our responsibility is to handle the “turn” in between.

sections.heading: 3. True Humility Does Not Deny What God Has Done
sections.html:
The lesson contains one very important sentence that steers us away from a common mistake: true humility is not denying what God has done; it is knowing clearly that it is Jesus who is doing the work through me.

Some brothers and sisters mistakenly think that humility means answering everything with “No, no, it wasn’t me.” When someone says, “You spoke really well,” they hurry to say, “I spoke terribly.” That isn’t actually humility; it’s another form of self-preoccupation, because the conversation is still revolving around “me”.

So what is true humility? It is Paul’s sentence: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Paul didn’t deny the fact that “I worked more than all of them”. He acknowledged the fact — but immediately added, “yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

That is the standard sentence pattern of humility: acknowledge the facts, give back the glory.

The lesson puts it well: the beauty of the vessel comes from Jesus living within it.

sections.heading: 4. The Window and the Mirror: A Study in Management
sections.html:
The American management scholar Jim Collins, in his 2001 book Good to Great, recorded a research project that lasted five years. From more than 1,400 publicly listed companies, he and his team identified eleven that had made the leap from “good” to “great”, and looked for what they had in common. The result surprised even him: the leaders of these companies were almost never the celebrity figures the public knew. He called them “Level 5 leaders” — people combining extreme personal humility with intense professional will.

Collins used a very telling image, which he called “the window and the mirror”. He found that when their companies did well, these leaders would look out of the window, giving the credit to outside factors and to their colleagues; when their companies did badly, they would look in the mirror and take the responsibility on themselves. The leaders in the comparison companies did exactly the opposite: they looked in the mirror when things went well and out of the window when things went badly.

Brothers and sisters, even research in the world has found that truly lasting excellence comes from people who don’t turn the spotlight on themselves.

So in the kingdom of God, isn’t this principle doubly true?

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

“Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Humility Inspires Humility
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

You can see this every day in a ministry team. When a co-worker with his head held high joins the team, the others immediately feel the pressure and start raising their heads too: competing over gifts, over results, over who gets noticed. On the surface it all looks lively, but underneath it’s a war of attrition, and in the end both sides lose. Conversely, when a co-worker who keeps his head down joins the team, the others relax and are able to speak the truth. Humility is a kind of quiet contagion; it makes a team a safe place.

And the 321 vision’s priority of relationships tells us: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Why does “with ourselves” come before “with others”? Because a person who hasn’t yet made peace with himself will always be grasping when he is among others. Only when a person’s identity has been settled before God — I am loved; I am a chosen vessel — can he stand firm amid applause, and stand firm when he is overlooked.

This is what the 321 vision means by selflessness: not having no sense of worth, but no longer building our worth on how people see us.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: What Happens When the Church Starts “Exalting People”
1. The Lesson’s Reminder
sections.html:
The lesson says: today many church conferences are full of celebrity speakers and eye-catching events. That in itself isn’t wrong, but if we’re not watchful, we may, without even noticing, put people in the place of focus.

Notice the lesson’s sense of proportion: that in itself isn’t wrong. Gifts come from God, and careful preparation is a mark of faithfulness. The question isn’t “whether there are people involved” but “whether people have been put in the place of focus”.

sections.heading: 2. The Factions in Corinth
sections.html:
The clearest case in the New Testament happened in the church at Corinth.

“For when one says, ‘I follow Paul,’ and another, ‘I follow Apollos,’ aren’t you fleshly?” (1 Corinthians 3:4)

Paul’s response is razor-sharp: “Who then is Apollos, and who is Paul, but servants through whom you believed, and each as the Lord gave to him? I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.” (1 Corinthians 3:5–7)

Paul says it twice over: they are nothing to speak of.

The word “servant” in Greek is diakonos (διάκονος), originally meaning “a servant, one who waits at table”. At a banquet, no guest remembers who carried the dishes in; what everyone remembers is the taste of the food and the host’s hospitality. Paul is saying: we are the ones carrying the dishes.

Brothers and sisters, the division in Corinth didn’t happen because Paul or Apollos did anything wrong, but because the congregation put its focus on people. Exalting people never leads to unity; it leads to factions.

Because if the focus is Jesus, the whole church has only one focus; if the focus is people, there are as many focal points as there are popular people — and many focal points means division.

The lesson puts it superbly: once the focus is scattered, it is no longer a focus.

sections.heading: 3. The Cry at Lystra and the End of Herod
sections.html:
The book of Acts contains two scenes in sharp contrast.

The first is in Lystra. Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth, and the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes (Acts 14:11–12). How did the two apostles react? “But when the apostles, Barnabas and Paul, heard of it, they tore their clothes, and sprang into the multitude, crying out, ‘Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men of like passions with you.’” (Acts 14:14–15)

They tore their clothes and sprang into the crowd. This was no polite declining; it was fierce resistance. They would rather look foolish than stand in that place.

The second scene is in Caesarea. King Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne and made a speech to the people. “The people shouted, ‘The voice of a god, and not of a man!’ Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:22–23)

The same kind of cry, two responses, two endings. Paul tore his clothes; Herod put on his robes. Paul said, “We also are men”; Herod said nothing at all — the Bible says only that “he didn’t give God the glory”.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Herod’s sin was not “seizing the glory” but “not giving the glory”. He didn’t do anything; he simply didn’t turn the glory back. Silence can sometimes be consent.

Even the angels understand this. When the apostle John fell down to worship the angel who showed him the visions, the angel said, “Look! Don’t do it! … Worship God.” (Revelation 19:10)

sections.heading: 4. After the Conference Is Over
sections.html:
The lesson asks two questions that make us fall quiet: when the conference is over, whom are people talking about — Jesus or the speaker? What do people remember — the anointing or the performance?

Those two questions aren’t only for speakers; they are for every one of us who listens. Try a very simple test: after a meeting, what is the conversation in the car on the way home?

If we’re talking about “That illustration of his was so funny” or “His voice is so lovely”, then however fervent the meeting was, the focus has drifted. If we’re talking about “So that’s what this verse means” or “Tomorrow I’m going home to apologise to my father”, then the focus is right.

The lesson says: we are not denying people’s gifts and service; we are reminding ourselves that the church exists not to promote people but to exalt Christ.

“He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision: Establish God’s System
sections.html:
The Goal of the 321 vision is to establish God’s system — a system in which Jesus is King and all the glory goes to Jesus.

Then what is the Babylonian system? It is a system centred on people, run on human reputation and human methods. Babylon’s slogan was: “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves.” (Genesis 11:4)

“Let’s make a name for ourselves” — that is the engine of Babylon.

Brothers and sisters, the frightening thing is that Babylon’s engine can be fitted inside the shell of a church. The same building, the same songs, the same pulpit — if the engine is “making a name for ourselves”, then it is Babylon, not the temple.

The 321 vision says: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

“All” — not ninety-nine per cent, not keeping a little back for ourselves.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: What Draws People Is Not Us but Jesus Lifted Up
1. If I Am Lifted Up from the Earth
sections.html:
The lesson quotes the Lord’s own words: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32)

The very next verse adds an explanation: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.” (John 12:33)

Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: the first meaning of the Lord’s “lifted up” is being lifted up on the cross. That is a tremendous reversal. What the world calls “being exalted” is being put up high and looked up to; what the Lord calls “being lifted up” is being nailed to wood, rejected by people, laying down his life for them.

The word “draw” in Greek is helkuō (ἑλκύω), meaning “to pull, to drag”, like hauling a boat up onto the shore with a rope, or like a magnet drawing iron. The word stresses an active, powerful pull.

What truly draws people’s hearts is the cross. Not the stage, not the lighting, not the pageantry — but the Lord who was lifted up for us.

In John 3 the Lord also said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” (John 3:14–15) How were the people in the wilderness healed? Simply “when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived” (Numbers 21:9). The bronze serpent had no power in itself; its function was to turn people’s eyes away from their wounds and their pain to the one point God had appointed.

Brothers and sisters, this is the whole meaning of our service: to turn people’s eyes to Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. Events Wear Us Out; Glory Brings Lasting Transformation
sections.html:
The lesson says: if a church relies only on events to draw people, it will wear itself out; but if it relies on the glory of Jesus to draw people, the result is a revival that is real, lasting and transforms hearts.

There’s a very practical logic in that sentence: people drawn by events are loyal to the events; people drawn by a speaker are loyal to the speaker; people drawn by the atmosphere are loyal to the atmosphere. All of these pass, so you have to keep putting on another one — bigger, fresher, more exciting. That’s what wearing yourself out looks like.

Only people drawn by Jesus are loyal to Jesus — and Jesus is the same yesterday, today and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

History bears this out. The Welsh Revival of 1904 and the Great Pyongyang Revival of 1907 had features in common, and none of them was innovation in method; they were deep confession, repentance and worship before God. Revival has never been something you can organise; revival is the natural result of the Lord being lifted up.

sections.heading: 3. The Moment of Totality
sections.html:
Let’s go back to that astronomical phenomenon from the beginning and finish the story.

During a total solar eclipse, the moon blocks the sun’s photosphere and the sky grows dark. Yet it is precisely at that moment that the naked eye can see something normally invisible — the sun’s corona, that ring of silvery-white light. During the total eclipse of 29 May 1919, the British astronomer Arthur Eddington took advantage of that very covering to observe starlight being bent as it passed close to the sun.

Brothers and sisters, there is a beautiful spiritual lesson here: when our “self” is covered, nailed to the cross and made quiet, people see a glory they normally cannot see — not our glory, but the Lord’s.

Our selflessness is the Lord’s revealing.

sections.heading: 4. Applying the 321 Vision: From the Temporary to the Eternal
sections.html:
The 321 vision says our perspective must shift — from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to what is of God.

Human applause is temporary: when a meeting ends, the applause stops; when a generation passes, the names are forgotten. But God’s glory is eternal: “the Lord’s word endures forever.” (1 Peter 1:25)

Everything done so that people will remember me will pass away; everything done so that people will meet the Lord will last for ever.

“If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.” (1 Peter 4:11)

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: See No One but Jesus
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the framework of the 321 vision and see clearly where it sits in the whole picture.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations All Point the Same Way
sections.html:
Jesus is my role model. He is the Son of God, yet he “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

The word “emptied” in Greek is kenoō (κενόω), meaning “to pour out, to make empty”. If the Lord of the universe emptied himself, what do we clay jars have left to cling to?

The Bible is my standard. God says it with complete clarity: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another.” (Isaiah 42:8) Who receives the glory is not a matter of style; it is a matter of truth.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. The Lord said of the Holy Spirit, “He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you.” (John 16:14) Notice this: even the Holy Spirit does not exalt himself. The work of the Holy Spirit is to glorify Jesus.

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King, and Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
sections.html: This lesson is practically an unfolding of those two sentences. Let Jesus be King — where is the King? On the colt’s back, so the colt must keep its head down. Let Jesus receive all the glory — “all” means that even the one per cent of “I deserve a little credit too” has to be handed over.

sections.heading: 3. The Goal: Establish God’s System
sections.html: To establish God’s system is to establish a system that “sees no one but Jesus”: gifts are treasured, but gifts are not worshipped; leaders are respected, but leaders are not deified; people are valued, but people do not occupy the place of God.

sections.heading: 4. The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless
sections.html:
The colt in this lesson is the most vivid picture of selflessness.

The colt carries the King, so it walks in the middle; the colt carries the King, so it has no need to raise its head.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. What can a donkey’s colt possibly have? All it has is the King on its back — and that King is everything. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me: that isn’t a loss; it’s an upgrade.

sections.heading: 5. The Five-Fold Change
sections.html:
The 321 vision says: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

Today’s lesson begins precisely with mindset: I am not the star; I am a vessel. I am not the source of light; I am a reflector. I am not the destination; I am a bridge.

Change the mindset, and the life changes — I no longer need applause to live on. Change the life, and daily living changes — I no longer do things in order to be seen, nor am I hurt when I go unseen. Change daily living, and relationships change — there’s no more secret comparison between me and my co-workers. Change relationships, and ministry changes — ministry is no longer my stage but the Lord’s workshop.

sections.heading: 6. The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; we are to practise living a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

In this lesson the 920 practice has a very concrete use: when your “2” praises you, how do you respond? That is exactly the moment to practise the “0”. You can say one sentence that turns the glory back: “This really is the Lord’s grace; I couldn’t have done it myself.” That isn’t mere politeness; it’s a declaration. Say it often enough, and it moves from your lips into your heart.

The 235 relationships say: with selfless people we become a “2” — spiritual companions; we build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; we become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Notice the condition: we become spiritual companions with selfless people. Because if you work alongside a self-centred person, you’ll be drawn into comparison; if you work alongside a selfless person, you’ll be drawn into freedom.

Brothers and sisters, find a companion who can say to you, “You just lifted your head.” A companion like that is worth more than a hundred compliments.

sections.heading: 7. The Shift of Perspective
sections.html: From the human to the divine: people look at the pageantry; God looks at the heart. From the earthly to the heavenly: on earth it’s about reputation; in heaven it’s about faithfulness. From the temporary to the eternal: applause lasts three seconds; the reward lasts for ever. From the worldly to what is of God: the world asks, “Who are you?” God asks, “Who is in you?”

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Cultivating a Life That Exalts Jesus Alone
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices, plus a gentle reminder. We’ll use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive each one deep, one at a time.

Practice 1: Give the Glory to Jesus Straight After You Serve

The lesson says: when you’ve finished any act of service — preaching, praying, sharing, counselling, visiting — go straight back to your inner room and say to the Lord, “Lord, you did all this, not me. The glory is yours.”

Information: first recognise the fact — the glory was never mine to begin with (Isaiah 42:8).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit, after some particular act of service, to let you see that faint longing in your heart to be praised. Seeing it is grace.

Conviction: admit from the heart that giving the glory to the Lord isn’t losing out; it’s returning to your originally intended position, and it is safe.

Implementation: within ten minutes of finishing your service, find a quiet place and say that sentence. Don’t leave it past that evening.

Evaluation: every Sunday evening, spend five minutes looking back: how many times did I serve this week? How many times did I give back the glory straight away? How many times did I forget, or not want to let it go?

Correction: if you find yourself enjoying praise more and more, write your thanks down, and make it specific: Lord, that sister’s tears today — you touched her; it wasn’t what I said.

Repetition: this isn’t a one-off decision; it’s a lifelong habit. Practise it for at least forty days in a row, until it becomes a reflex.

Multiplication: teach your co-workers to do the same. After a meeting, two or three of you bow your heads together: “Lord, you did all of this.” A team like that is hard for pride to break into.

Practice 2: After a Meeting, Ask, “Do I Love Jesus More?”

The lesson says: next time you attend a conference, listen to a sermon or watch a Christian film, try asking yourself — do I know Jesus better now? Or do I only remember the speaker, the lines and the atmosphere?

Information: simply knowing there are these two possibilities is itself a protection. A meeting can help people see Jesus, or it can just give them a burst of excitement before they go back to where they started.

Revelation: ask the Lord to help you discern what is real anointing and what is merely charisma.

Conviction: accept a standard — the measure of a meeting is not “Was I moved?” but “Do I love Jesus more and obey him more?”

Implementation: after every meeting, write two lines. Line one: what did this meeting show me about Jesus? Line two: what is one thing I’m going to change this week because of it?

Evaluation: look back over them after a month. If, eight times out of ten, you couldn’t write the first line, it’s time to be on your guard.

Correction: cut back on content that only excites you, and take in more content that helps you know the Lord.

Repetition: build the habit of “two lines after every meeting” and keep it up for six months.

Multiplication: bring this habit into your small group. Before you part, ask one another, “What did today’s passage show you about Jesus?”

Practice 3: Each Week, Meditate on “I Am the Colt”

The lesson says: set aside some time each week to pray quietly and meditate on one sentence — “I am the colt.” Remind yourself that my worth lies not in what I have done but in the fact that Jesus is willing to use me.

The lesson also gives three questions to ask yourself: Were there times this week when I “lifted my head”? Did I block the glory of Jesus? Am I willing to become his vessel more humbly?

Information: read Mark 11:1–11 until you know the colt’s story well, and remember those four words: “The Lord needs him.”

Revelation: be still for ten minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to bring before your eyes the picture of the moment this week when you “lifted your head”.

Conviction: admit that my worth is not built on results but on the fact that “the Lord needs me”.

Implementation: choose a fixed time each week — Sunday evening, for example — and write down the lesson’s three questions and your answers.

Evaluation: after a month, see whether your list of “head-lifting” moments has a common pattern: is it when you’re praised? When you’re comparing yourself? Or when you’re overlooked?

Correction: for that pattern, prepare a one-line prayer: “Lord, this is yours, not mine; I am the colt, and you are the King.”

Repetition: let “I am the colt” become your silent prayer before you step up to the pulpit, before you speak, before you press “send”.

Multiplication: teach this sentence to the spiritual children you are discipling. One sentence can protect a person for a lifetime.

A Gentle Reminder: You Are Not the Star — You Are a Bridge

The lesson closes by reminding us: the church needs bridges, not stars on a stage. God wants to use you to bring people to Jesus, not to bring them to you. Remember — what people truly need is not you, but him.

A bridge has two characteristics. First, a bridge is there to be walked across: nobody holds a celebration in the middle of a bridge, and if people stop on the bridge and go no further, the bridge has failed.

Second, a bridge sits low. A bridge always spans the gap between two banks; it has to stoop over that chasm. The Lord Jesus himself is that bridge: he came down from heaven to the very lowest place, to carry us across to God.

Brothers and sisters, are you willing to be a bridge?

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Exalt Jesus Alone, and Revival Will Come
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words are beautiful: God has never looked for famous people; he looks for people willing to make Jesus famous.

Through the ages, the people God has used most mightily have often been those who “disappeared”. John the Baptist said, “I must decrease,” and then went down into prison. Paul said, “I am nothing to speak of,” and then wrote letters from a cell in Rome. The colt completed its task, and the Bible never so much as mentions where it went afterwards. They all disappeared — yet the One they pointed to is still praised by hundreds of millions two thousand years later.

The lesson says: if we are willing to lower ourselves and lift Jesus high, God’s glory will come, and our lives and our churches will experience revival.

Lowering and lifting are two sides of the same movement. Only when one end of the seesaw goes down can the other end come up.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to put this call before you.

If you are serving but find you’ve started paying attention to how people look at you — lower your head today. If you’ve been hurt, or have pulled back, because you weren’t noticed — today, take your eyes off people and come back to the Lord who saw you long ago. If you are praying for revival in your church, your small group, your family — start today by “not exalting people”. Because revival doesn’t begin with a bigger event; revival begins with a company of people willing to bow their heads.

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

See no one but Jesus — this is the Father’s heart, and the direction of our whole lives.

Let us declare together the lesson’s declaration of faith:

Lord, I am not the star. Be exalted, and may all people come to see you because of me!

keyVerses: “After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light. Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him. Peter answered, and said to Jesus, ‘Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.’ While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’ When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’ Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:1–8)
“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” (John 12:32)
practices: Give the glory to Jesus straight after you serve
After a meeting, ask: “Do I love Jesus more?”
Each week, meditate on “I am the colt”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We bow down before you. You are the Lord who was transfigured on the mountain; you are the King who rode into Jerusalem on a donkey’s colt; you are the Saviour who was lifted up from the earth for us.

Lord, forgive us. So often, while you are using us, we quietly lift our heads; we enjoy being remembered more than we enjoy people meeting you. Sometimes it isn’t that we snatch your glory — we simply forget to turn it back to you. Forgive us for that silence.
Lord, make us honest vessels who dare to say, “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” Keep us standing in the right place; don’t let us block your light, but let us reflect it.
Lord, we place our gifts, our names and our stages in your hands; we are willing to be the colt, the bridge, the clay jar. Have first place in our lives, in our homes and in our church.
No one else — only Jesus.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) Peter wanted to make three tents, putting Jesus side by side with Moses and Elijah. In your life or your service, are there any people, methods or experiences that you have, without realising it, set on the same level as Jesus? How will you take that “tent” down this week?

“But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Think back to the last time you were praised. What was your first reaction inside? Share with your group one sentence you will start using to “give back the glory”.
l013.title: Lift Up No One — Lift Up Only Jesus
l013.subtitle: I Am the Donkey’s Colt; He Is the King
l013.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: A Mountain That Can Fall, a Pillar That Can Run
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a picture all of us have seen.

In Italy there stands a world-famous bell tower: the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Construction began in 1173, and by the time the builders reached the third storey it had already started to lean, because the ground beneath it was soft alluvial soil. The workmen stopped, started again, stopped again; all told, the building took nearly two hundred years. Later craftsmen made the columns on the upper storeys taller on one side than the other, trying to “bend” the tower back into line, and the result was a tower shaped like a banana. By the end of the twentieth century the top had drifted more than four metres from the vertical, at an angle of about 5.5 degrees. In 1990 the Italian government closed the tower and brought in an international panel of experts. It took eleven years, drawing soil out from beneath the foundations on the north side, to pull it back to about 3.99 degrees.

Brothers and sisters, the surface of that tower is marble — finely carved and dazzling to behold. The problem was never the surface. The problem was the foundation.

Our elders have a little rhyme: “Lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall; lean on a man, the man may run; lean on the Lord Jesus — best of all.” It sounds like a folk saying, yet it touches the deepest truth of the human heart.

All our lives we are looking for something to lean on. As children we lean on our parents; as we grow up we lean on our qualifications; once we enter the working world we lean on our connections; in middle age we lean on our savings; in old age we lean on our children. We lean on systems, on positions, on a clean health-check report, on an insurance policy, on someone with a big name. These are not bad things, and God often provides for us through them. But brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: anything that can change cannot be a foundation.

You think “lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall” is an exaggeration? Mountains really do move. On 25 April 2015 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck Nepal, and nearly nine thousand people lost their lives. That earthquake even rewrote the terrain of the Himalayas. In December 2020 the governments of China and Nepal jointly announced a new official height for Mount Everest: 8,848.86 metres. Even the highest mountain on earth has to be measured again. Mountains move, mountains collapse, mountains have to be re-surveyed.

You think “lean on a man, the man may run” is too harsh? No. People don’t run away out of malice; people are simply limited. The one who loves you most will grow old; the one who backs you most will grow tired; the most faithful person you know will one day come to the end of their life. During his second imprisonment in Rome, Paul wrote to Timothy: “At my first defense, no one came to help me, but all left me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17). Paul didn’t blame them. He simply stated a fact: people will leave, and the Lord will stand by you.

So is there anything at all that doesn’t change?

Scientists, in fact, understand this problem better than anyone. Humanity once measured length by a metal bar. In 1889 the International Bureau of Weights and Measures cast the “International Prototype of the Metre” in platinum-iridium and stored it just outside Paris; every “metre” in the world was measured against it. But metal expands with heat and contracts with cold; it oxidises; it wears away. So in 1983 the General Conference on Weights and Measures decided to stop relying on that bar and to define the metre by the speed of light instead. Time is the same: since 1967, one second has been defined by the transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Even science admits that a standard cannot be built on something that changes. In the end, humanity had no choice but to anchor its standards to the most unchanging constants in the universe.

And what about our lives? Our families, our service, our churches? Where are we going to lay our foundation?

The Bible gives only one answer, and he is a Person: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8).

The title of today’s lesson is very direct: Rely on No One but Jesus. This is not about becoming solitary, refusing friends or refusing help. It is about moving the foundation back to where it belongs. People can be companions; they cannot be the foundation. Methods can be tools; they cannot be what we rely on. This morning, let’s move the whole weight of our lives off the mountain that can fall and the people who can run, and back onto the Rock that never changes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Multiple-Choice Question on the Eve of a Nation’s Fall
sections.html:
Our key passage today comes from Jeremiah chapter 17.

Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin. He was called in the thirteenth year of Josiah king of Judah, and he served right through to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon and the exile of the people — more than forty years in all. He is known as “the weeping prophet”, because the message he preached was exactly what his nation least wanted to hear.

What was Judah’s situation at the time? The Assyrian Empire was in decline, and two great powers, Egypt and the new Babylon, were locked in a tug-of-war up and down the corridor of Canaan. Little Judah was caught in the middle, and the royal court was split into two factions: one wanted to lean on Egypt, the other on Babylon. The hottest question in the whole nation was not “What does God say?” but “Whom should we rely on?” Long before Jeremiah, Isaiah had already warned: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, and rely on horses, and trust in chariots because they are many, and in horsemen because they are very strong, but they don’t look to the Holy One of Israel, and they don’t seek Yahweh!” (Isaiah 31:1).

Jeremiah 17 opens by naming the root of the problem: “The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, and with the point of a diamond. It is engraved on the tablet of their heart, and on the horns of your altars” (Jeremiah 17:1). The sin is not carved in stone; it is carved on the tablet of the heart. This is a problem of the heart, not a problem of strategy.

Then, in verses 5 to 8, God sets out a multiple-choice question. There are only two options. There is no third.

The first option: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh” (Jeremiah 17:5). The word for “flesh” here is the Hebrew basar: the body that perishes and wastes away. The Chinese Bible renders the phrase “an arm of flesh and blood”, and the arm stands for strength. Put together, it means strength that decays. God is not saying people have no strength; he is saying that human strength decays.

Notice the second half of verse 5: “whose heart departs from Yahweh.” That is the key. The real problem with relying on people is not that we “asked someone for help”; it is that our heart has left God. It is a question of order, a question of the throne — who sits on the throne of my heart.

And the result? “For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land” (Jeremiah 17:6). The “bush in the desert” is a small, stunted shrub of the wilderness. It isn’t dead; it is alive — but it can do no more than stay alive. Even if rain falls right beside it, it cannot feel it, because it stands in salt land, brackish ground where water won’t stay and roots can’t go deep.

The second option: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh” (Jeremiah 17:7). The Hebrew root behind “trust” here is batach: to put your whole weight down on something, to lean on it securely, to entrust yourself without a trace of wariness. The word does not describe intellectual agreement; it describes handing over the full weight of who you are.

And the result? “For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit” (Jeremiah 17:8).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: God did not say that those who trust in Yahweh will never meet the heat. The text says they “will not fear when heat comes.” Nor did he say there will be no year of drought; he said they “will not be concerned in the year of drought.” The same sun beats down on the desert bush and on the tree by the water. The difference is not the environment. The difference is where the roots go down.

Then verse 9 is the key verse of the whole chapter: “The heart is deceitful above all things and it is exceedingly corrupt. Who can know it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Why is it so easy for us to rely on people? Because the human heart is deceitful; it even deceives itself. With our lips we say “I trust the Lord”, while in our hearts we are working out a different plan. That is why in verse 10 God says: “I, Yahweh, search the mind. I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.”
