That is the background to this lesson: a nation on the eve of its fall, facing a multiple-choice question. And every morning when we wake up, we have to answer the same question all over again.

sections.heading: 1. Everything in the World Changes; Only Jesus Does Not
sections.html:
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” (Hebrews 13:8)

“For I, Yahweh, don’t change; therefore you, sons of Jacob, are not consumed.” (Malachi 3:6)

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

Brothers and sisters, in this fast-shifting world, no person, no system and no circumstance is truly reliable. Economies collapse, affections change, workplaces restructure, friendships drift apart; even the religious systems we know so well can fail us. That isn’t pessimism. That’s honesty.

James 1:17 uses a beautiful image from the sky. “The Father of lights” means the God who made the stars. “Turning shadow” in the Greek is literally “the shadow cast by turning”. Every light on earth shifts: the sun rises and sets, and shadows move from east to west; the moon waxes and wanes; the stars rise and set. But the One who made the light does not shift. There is not a trace of shadow on him, not a single degree of deviation.

We tend to think we are standing still. Yet as you sit there right now, the earth is carrying you round on its axis at about 1,670 kilometres an hour (near the equator), while orbiting the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second. We have not stopped for a single second. Life is the same: we think everything is just as it was, when in fact everything is moving.

Psychology measured the weight of “change” long ago. In 1967 two psychiatrists at the University of Washington, Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe, published the Social Readjustment Rating Scale, which turned life events into stress scores: the death of a spouse, 100 points; divorce, 73; being fired, 47; changing jobs, 36. Even “good things” like marriage, promotion and moving house add to the stress score. What wears us out is not only bad things; it is “change” itself. The human heart is made to long for a fixed point to stand on.

The classic study published in 1958 in the journal American Psychologist by Harry Harlow, a psychologist at the University of Wisconsin, is more direct still. He let infant monkeys choose between two surrogate mothers: one made of wire, with a feeding bottle attached; the other made of soft cloth, with no milk. The infant monkeys went to the wire mother only when hungry, for a few sips of milk; the vast majority of their time they spent clinging tightly to the cloth mother. When frightened, every one of them rushed to the cloth mother. Harlow’s conclusion: a creature’s need for something to “lean on” is not only about getting supplies; even more, it is about finding security.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly how God made us. We are created beings, made to live “leaning on” someone. The question was never “Should I lean on anything?” The question is “Whom do I lean on?”

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine prayed to God: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” In sixteen hundred years that sentence has never gone out of date, because the make-up of the human heart has not changed.

And what about Jesus? In the original of Hebrews 13:8, the three times — “yesterday, today, and forever” — are laid side by side with no verb at all — just one phrase, “the same” (ho autos), holding them together. The Jesus of the past, the Jesus of the present and the Jesus of eternity are one and the same. The power with which he turned water into wine at Cana has not faded. The compassion with which he touched the coffin at Nain has not cooled. The love with which he wept for you in Gethsemane has not lessened one bit.

The 321 vision speaks of the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, a foundation is called a foundation precisely because it does not move. However beautiful the marble of the Leaning Tower of Pisa, once the foundation gives way, everything is lost. If we lay the foundation of our lives on “people”, we are building our house on shifting sand. Only when we lay the foundation on Jesus — the One who does not move — can we stand firm.

So the first mindset that must change is this: not “the world is too chaotic for me to feel secure”, but “I have put my security in the wrong place.” Change the mindset and you change the life.

sections.heading: 2. Are You Looking for a Method, or for Jesus?
sections.html:
“Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.’” (John 14:6)

“God, you are my God. I will earnestly seek you. My soul thirsts for you. My flesh longs for you, in a dry and weary land, where there is no water.” (Psalm 63:1)

Brothers and sisters, when we face difficulties and problems, the first thing we usually look for is a “solution”: Who can help me? What should I do? Is there a success story I can copy?

That is human instinct. But what Jesus wants us to look for is not a method. It is himself.

Notice the grammar of John 14:6. Jesus did not say, “I point out the way”; he said, “I am the way.” He did not say, “I teach the truth”; he said, “I am the truth.” He did not say, “I give people life”; he said, “I am the life.” The Greek here uses the definite article three times over: the way, the truth, the life. Jesus is not the one who brings the answer. He is the answer itself.

The setting of these words is more moving still. It was the Last Supper, and the Lord had just told them he was going away. Thomas grew anxious and said, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?” (John 14:5). Thomas wanted a “route map”; the Lord gave him himself. Brothers and sisters, our prayers are often just like that: Lord, give me a method. And the Lord says: Child, I give you myself.

When David wrote Psalm 63, he was in the wilderness of Judah. That was real drought, a real lack of water, a real flight for his life. Yet look at what he says. He doesn’t say, “I thirst for water.” He says, “My soul thirsts for you.” What he sought in a land without water was not water but the source of life. That is the mark of spiritual maturity: in a dry land, the first thing you turn to is God, not a water supply.

Jeremiah puts it even more sharply: “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at the order of those two evils. The first: forsaking the spring of living water. The second: cutting out cisterns for themselves. Cutting cisterns is hard work; you hack away at the rock one blow at a time. People aren’t lazy. People work very hard — in the wrong direction. And however skilfully a cistern is cut, it will crack, because a cistern can only store water; it cannot produce it. Methods are the cistern. Jesus is the spring.

Second Chronicles records a heartbreaking example. As a young man, Asa king of Judah relied greatly on God. With five hundred and eighty thousand men he went out against an army of a million Cushites, and he prayed: “Yahweh, there is no one besides you to help, between the mighty and him who has no strength. Help us, Yahweh our God; for we rely on you, and in your name are we come against this multitude” (2 Chronicles 14:11). And God struck the Cushites down. But in his later years, when the northern kingdom of Israel came against him, he no longer sought God. Instead, he sent the silver and gold of the temple and the palace to Ben-Hadad king of Aram, borrowing outside power to break the siege. The prophet Hanani came to rebuke him: “For Yahweh’s eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. You have done foolishly in this; for from now on you will have wars” (2 Chronicles 16:9). Sadder still is the sentence that follows: “In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa was diseased in his feet. His disease was exceedingly great: yet in his disease he didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians” (2 Chronicles 16:12).

Please note: the Bible is not saying it is a sin to see a doctor. What it points out is that he “didn’t seek Yahweh, but just the physicians.” The problem lies in that word “just” — and in that “didn’t”. Methods are not sin. Putting a method in God’s place is.

The 321 vision teaches the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Our trouble today is often that we turn the whole order upside down — we deal with the task first, then look for people, and pray last of all. The result is that we rely on the brain and ourselves, and the more we think, the more we worry. The Bible says: “for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you find joy; rely on the brain and yourself, and you find worry.

So the second mindset that must change is this: not “I need an answer”, but “I need the One who is the Answer.”

sections.heading: 3. Revival Comes Not from Methods but from Jesus
sections.html:
“Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies. (Zechariah 4:6)

“Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Brothers and sisters, when many churches today pursue revival, they often imitate the models of successful churches, borrow the anointing language of whatever wave is current, and copy other people’s experiences and structures. These things are not necessarily wrong in themselves, but we can easily overlook a spiritual fact: what truly brings breakthrough and revival is not a model, not a strategy, not an event — it is Jesus.

The setting of Zechariah 4 fits this exactly. It was after the return from exile, and Zerubbabel was leading a weary people to rebuild the temple. They were few, they had little money, enemies harassed them, and the work had stalled for years. The angel showed the prophet a vision: a lampstand of pure gold, with two olive trees beside it, and oil flowing from the trees into the lampstand of its own accord. The meaning of the vision is plain: the lamp shines not because people keep carrying oil in, but because God himself supplies it without ceasing.

And so God spoke those famous words: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). “Might” in Hebrew is chayil — armies, wealth, the strength of a group. “Power” is koach — an individual’s physical strength, ability, skill. One is the resources of a team; the other is the ability of a person. In one stroke, God rules out both of the great categories people rely on.

Brothers and sisters, there is an important distinction here. The Lord is not saying “methods are sin”; he is saying “methods are not the source of power.” It is like an electric light. The switch matters, but the switch does not generate electricity. You could fill an entire wall with the most beautiful switches in the world, and the room would still be dark, because the electricity doesn’t come from the switch.

What’s more, someone else’s method is not necessarily the path God has prepared for us. The Bible has a fine example. When David was about to fight Goliath, Saul dressed him in his own armour, put a bronze helmet on his head and clothed him in a coat of mail. It was the best equipment of the day, fit for a king. But David said, “I can’t go with these; for I have not tested them” (1 Samuel 17:39). So he took them off, picked up his staff, five smooth stones and his sling, and went out in the name of Yahweh of Armies. Saul’s armour might have worked for Saul; for David it was a straitjacket.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly today’s temptation: we often put on someone else’s armour and walk someone else’s road, and in the end we look neither like ourselves nor like what God wants us to become. Every church’s road to revival should be the fruit of walking intimately with Jesus, receiving from him specifically, and responding to him genuinely.

Church history confirms this again and again. On 13 August 1727, at Herrnhut in Germany, the Moravian Brethren experienced an outpouring of the Holy Spirit during a communion service. Before that, this group of refugees from many different backgrounds had been quarrelling and splitting into factions. They did not rely on some new programme. Under the leadership of Count Zinzendorf, they confessed their sins, were reconciled and prayed with one heart. After the revival, they began a prayer watch in shifts; according to the Moravians’ own records, this round-the-clock prayer continued without a break for more than a hundred years and sent out hundreds of missionaries. The starting point of revival was not a strategy meeting. It was a group of people coming back before Jesus.

The 321 vision speaks of the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Brothers and sisters, when our eyes turn to “how to do it”, we drift, without noticing, away from “whom we rely on”. If revival is the credit of our methods, then the glory goes to the methods. If revival is Jesus’ own work, then the glory goes to Jesus. Which kind of revival do we want?

So the third mindset that must change is this: not “find the right model and revival will come”, but “return to the right Head, and only then will revival come.”

sections.heading: 4. Joshua’s Way to Victory in Battle: Relying Wholly on God
sections.html:
“When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood in front of him with his sword drawn in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, ‘Are you for us, or for our enemies?’ He said, ‘No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.’ Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, when the Israelites entered Canaan, they faced the combined armies of many nations, fortified cities and battles whose outcome no one could know. Yet they won one victory after another. Why? Their victories did not come from training and equipment; they came from relying wholly on God’s leading.

Look at this scene in Joshua chapter 5. Joshua had just led the people across the Jordan; they had been circumcised, they had kept the Passover, and the manna had stopped. Ahead of them lay Jericho — the first stronghold of Canaan. He went up close to the city alone, probably surveying the ground and thinking through his tactics. Suddenly a man with a drawn sword was standing in front of him.

Joshua asked a very “human” question: “Are you for us, or for our enemies?” That is the way of thinking we know best — divide people into two sides and see who is on mine.

The answer turned the whole question on its head: “No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army.”

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to that “No.” What the Lord means is: I have not come to join your side; I have come to take command. The question was never “Is God on my side?” The question is “Am I on God’s side?” It isn’t God coming to help me fight my battle; it is me joining God’s army to fight God’s battle.

Joshua’s response is beautiful. He didn’t argue; he didn’t explain. “Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and worshiped, and asked him, ‘What does my lord say to his servant?’” (Joshua 5:14).

Notice what he calls himself: servant. Who was he? He was Moses’ successor, the supreme commander of the whole army of Israel, the very man to whom God had personally promised, “Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go” (Joshua 1:9). He had every right to call himself commander. Yet he fell face down, gave up the commander’s place, and stepped back into the position of a servant.

The 321 vision puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. That is exactly what Joshua did outside Jericho. He laid down “I am the commander” and returned to “I am the servant.” The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is yielding up our limited self so that the infinite Commander can come in.

Then the commander said: “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy” (Joshua 5:15). These are the very words God had spoken to Moses at Horeb forty years earlier (Exodus 3:5). Taking off your sandals means dropping your own defences and your own stance; in the ancient Near East, removing your sandals also symbolised giving up your rights. The first step to victory is not putting on your battle boots. It is taking off your sandals.

And then, right at the opening of chapter 6, comes this: “Yahweh said to Joshua, ‘Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and the mighty men of valor’” (Joshua 6:2).

Brothers and sisters, notice the tense. God did not say, “I will give it to you.” God said, “I have given … into your hand.” The battle hadn’t been fought, yet the outcome was already settled — because the one fighting was not Joshua; it was Yahweh. And the battle plan that followed was even more outlandish: march round the city once a day for six days; on the seventh day, march round seven times, the priests blow the trumpets, and the people shout. That is not military tactics. It is a “training in obedience.” What God wanted his people to learn was this: the walls fall not because you shout loudly, but because God has spoken.

But if you keep reading, you will see a very important contrast.

Chapter 7: Ai. Ai was small. The spies came back and said: “Don’t let all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and strike Ai. Don’t make all the people to toil there, for there are only a few of them” (Joshua 7:3). So three thousand went up, and “they fled before the men of Ai” (Joshua 7:4). They won at Jericho, big as it was, yet lost at Ai, small as it was. Why? Apart from Achan’s sin, you will find this: before attacking Jericho they inquired of God; before attacking Ai they assessed the people.

Chapter 9: the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites put on worn-out clothes, brought dry, hard bread and came pretending to surrender. The text names Israel’s failure in a single sentence: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14). Without inquiring of God, they signed a treaty — and once signed, it was a permanent treaty, leaving trouble behind it for hundreds of years.

Brothers and sisters, put these three events side by side and the message is clear: inquire of God and you win; don’t inquire of God and you lose out. The difference is not the size of the matter. The difference is whether you have handed the commander’s place over to God.

In his 2001 book Good to Great, the leadership researcher Jim Collins studied eleven companies that went from mediocre to excellent, and found that the leaders at the very top level shared one trait: when things went well, they looked out of the window and gave the credit to others; when things went badly, they looked in the mirror and took the responsibility on themselves. Brothers and sisters, what the business world took decades of research to discover, Joshua acted out face down on the ground more than three thousand years ago.

In the same way, the Head of the church is Jesus — not the pastor, not the leaders, not the system.

sections.heading: 5. The Key to the Church: Who Is in Charge? Who Is Leading?
sections.html:
“For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the assembly, being himself the savior of the body.” (Ephesians 5:23)

“He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.” (Ephesians 1:22–23)

“He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

Brothers and sisters, the Bible says that Christ is the head of the church. The Greek word for “head” is kephalē: it means the head of a body, but also the source, the chief, the seat of authority. It is an image from the body, and it is also a declaration about how the church is ordered.

Think about it: what would happen if a body had two heads? The left foot heads east, the right foot heads west; the hand wants to grab, the mouth wants to let go. That isn’t richness; that’s a seizure. Much of the quarrelling, exhaustion and tearing apart in churches, traced back to its root, comes not from a lack of love but from too many heads.

The human body has a wonderful design. Your heartbeat, your breathing, your body temperature — none of them needs your willpower to direct it; the brainstem takes care of them for you. That is the function of the “head”: as long as the head is alive, the body has order. Conversely, the most terrible thing that can happen to a body is not an injured finger; it is a broken neck, with the signals cut off. That is called paralysis.

So the church’s greatest crisis is not a shortage of people, money or space. It is when the signal is cut — when we are no longer connected to the Head.

If a church is not led by Jesus but runs on human experience, ability or enthusiasm, then behind what looks like revival lies a crisis. Rely on human experience, and experience goes out of date; rely on human ability, and ability runs dry; rely on human enthusiasm, and enthusiasm cools. More dangerous still, when a whole group leans on one person, the moment that person falls, the whole system falls with them.

Jesus put it with complete clarity: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Notice that the Lord did not say, “Apart from me you will do a little less.” He said, “You can do nothing.” Not half the efficiency — zero.

What did the early church do? Before the Lord ascended, he commanded them: “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father” (Acts 1:4). Those hundred and twenty people were short on nothing so much as time, and nothing was more urgent to them than preaching the gospel. Yet the Lord told them to wait. So in the upper room they devoted themselves with one accord to prayer. They waited ten days; the Holy Spirit came; and in a single day three thousand people were baptised and turned to the Lord.

Later, when a great dispute broke out in the church over whether Gentiles must be circumcised, how did the letter recording the conclusion of the Jerusalem Council put it? “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you than these necessary things” (Acts 15:28). Look at the order: the Holy Spirit, and us. Not “we passed a resolution and then asked the Holy Spirit to bless it”, but “the Holy Spirit, and us.”

Brothers and sisters, what we truly need is not more resources or more talent, but more “relying on Jesus”: seeking him in our meetings, relying on him in our decisions, looking to him in our difficulties. As long as Jesus is in charge, the church will walk the road of victory.

Revelation chapter 3 paints a startling picture. The Lord says to the church in Laodicea: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). These are words the Lord speaks to a church. The church was meeting as usual, giving as usual, serving as usual — and the Lord was standing outside the door.

Brothers and sisters, this morning we must ask ourselves a very honest question: in my family, my small group, my service, is Jesus sitting on the throne, or standing outside the door?

The 321 vision speaks of the Goal: establish God’s system. The difference between God’s system and a human system is not size; it is who sits at the centre. A human system is a pyramid, with people at the top and God off to the side. God’s system is a set of concentric circles, with Jesus at the centre and all of us members of one body. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory — this is not a slogan. It is the blueprint of the system.

A Gentle Reminder: Methods Are Tools; Jesus Is the One We Rely On

“Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

Brothers and sisters, methods can be learned and strategies can be copied, but without the presence of Jesus, it is all just a spiritual performance.

Let me keep this balanced. We are not anti-intellectual, we are not against planning, and we are not saying that preparing sermons, rehearsing songs or planning the order of service is unspiritual. God is a God of order, and the Bible itself is a carefully structured book. The question is not “Do we have methods?” The question is “Which seat do our methods occupy?”

Methods are like the oars of a boat. Oars matter a great deal, but if you row in the desert, you can row till your hands bleed and you will never reach the shore. Where does the water come from? God gives the water. In the same way, where God is present, methods are vessels of grace; where God is absent, they are weary drudgery.

At the foot of Mount Sinai, Moses said something I love: “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). Moses would rather go without Canaan than have a Canaan without the presence of God.

Brothers and sisters, when you walk relying on Jesus, even a cup of water, a hug or a single prayer will bring God’s presence and bear fruit. The Lord himself said: “Whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink in the name of a disciple, most certainly I tell you he will in no way lose his reward” (Matthew 10:42). The method is small; the presence is great.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Methods to the Head
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at this lesson once more within the framework of 321.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he himself said: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). If even the Son of God lived on earth in complete dependence, how much more must we? The Bible is my standard — not other churches’ success stories, not the most popular courses online, but the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — not my intuition, not the consensus of the crowd, but the Counsellor himself.

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: that is the moment Joshua fell face down on the ground. Let Jesus receive all the glory: that is why the walls of Jericho had to fall by marching and shouting — a way of fighting that left no commander any credit to claim.

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The central question of any system is always “Who is at the centre?”

Now look at the core message. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. When the self-centred meet a difficulty, their first thought is “What am I going to do?” or “Whom do I know?” The selfless person’s first thought is “Lord, how do you see this?” The self-centred life leaves our originally intended position, seizes rights and wants to take God’s place; selflessness lays down our rights and returns to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. It is the same in the church: when I insist on my method and you insist on yours, pride provokes pride and both sides lose. When together we fall face down and say, “Lord, how do you see this?”, humility inspires humility and both sides win.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — entering the limitless and living out the limitless. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Relying on Jesus does not mean shrinking ourselves down to zero. It means connecting our limited self to the limitless God.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change is the link furthest upstream — the mindset. If the mindset doesn’t change, all we will change is our methods, not what we rely on. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; when daily living changes, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry bears genuine fruit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The shift in perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly system to God’s. “Lean on a mountain, the mountain may fall” is earthly and temporary; “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever” is heavenly and eternal.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living out the “0” of selflessness, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice this: the fruit of the Spirit is not produced by “methods”; it is produced by “life”. Fruit is never wrung out by force; it grows on branches that stay joined to the vine.

The 235 relationships: become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with selfless people; build the “3”, a legacy of spiritual parents and spiritual children; become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Someone may ask: doesn’t this lesson say “Rely on no one”? Why build relationships, then? Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the vital distinction. Not relying on people is not the same as not walking with people. 235 relationships are not about leaning on one another; they are about holding one another up as together we rely on Jesus. A true spiritual companion doesn’t make you more dependent on them; every time you meet, they bring you closer to the Lord. If a relationship makes you less and less able to do without a particular person while you draw near to Jesus less and less, something has gone wrong with that relationship.

The Path of Serving is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. You see, every stage of this path is the unfolding of one and the same thing: rely on no one but Jesus.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Training a Rhythm of Faith That Relies on Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if a mindset is to touch the ground, it has to become a rhythm. The three practices below are the concrete assignments the lesson gives us; we will then use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to deepen each one, layer by layer.

Practice 1: Every morning, declare, “Lord, today I will rely on you!”

Each day when you wake up, before you start fretting over today’s to-do list, first declare one sentence in your heart or out loud: “Lord Jesus, today I will not rely on myself or on people; I will rely on you alone!”

This sentence is not just an attitude. It is a spiritual switch, reminding us that today’s road is walked by relying on you.

Information: first put the truth into your head. Memorise three passages — Psalm 20:7, Proverbs 3:5–6 and Hebrews 13:8. Knowledge is the starting point; without information there is no material for the Holy Spirit to use.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn these words into something you truly see. You might pray: “Lord, show me what I actually relied on yesterday.” Revelation is often very specific; he may point to a name, a bank balance, a job title.

Conviction: move from “I know” to “I believe”. A practical test: when panic rises in your heart, where does your hand reach first — for your phone, or for prayer?

Implementation: tomorrow morning, speak before your feet even touch the floor. Make that declaration. Don’t wait until you feel like it; feelings follow behind actions.

Evaluation: take three minutes each evening to recall which thing today you pushed through by your own strength. Don’t condemn yourself; just be honest.

Correction: bring that thing back before the Lord and entrust it to him again, saying, “Lord, in that moment I forgot you. Now I hand it back to you.”

Repetition: keep this practice up for twenty-one days in a row. Neuroscience tells us the human brain has plasticity (neuroplasticity): repeated behaviour strengthens the corresponding neural connections. Spiritual training works the same way; the Lord Jesus himself entered the synagogue “as was his custom” (Luke 4:16). Spiritual habits are channels of grace.

Multiplication: find one person, teach them this declaration, and ask them about it once a week. What you teach others is what truly becomes your own.

Practice 2: When you need help, pray first, then ask

When you run into a problem, don’t immediately message a friend or search online for a solution. Stop first, be still for one minute and pray to Jesus: “Lord, you are my ever-present help. I turn to you now; please show me what to do.”

Let Jesus be the first one you ask, no longer just the last resort.

Brothers and sisters, please note: this practice is not telling us not to ask people for help. God often provides for us through people. What this practice changes is the order. Praying first and then asking for help, versus asking for help and then praying — the difference looks like a matter of minutes, but in reality it is the difference of a throne.

Information: remember Psalm 46:1 — “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1).

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you your own “default reaction”. Under pressure, everyone has an automatic first move: some reach for the phone to call someone, some start scrolling, some head for the kitchen.

Conviction: believe that God’s delays are not God’s neglect. One minute of stillness won’t spoil anything; on the contrary, it often saves you a whole week of clearing up.

Implementation: set yourself a concrete rule — when you hit a problem, pray silently for sixty seconds before you pick up your phone. You could stick a small note on your phone case: “Ask the Lord first.”

Evaluation: review once a week. How many times did you manage it this week? How many times did you forget?

Correction: if you often forget, lower the bar. It doesn’t have to be sixty seconds; start with ten. A practice you can sustain matters more than a high standard.

Repetition: let it become muscle memory. Research published in 2002 by the psychologist Wendy Wood, then of Texas A&M University, and her colleagues found that a considerable proportion of people’s daily behaviour consists of habits repeated in the same settings. Habits aren’t sustained by sheer willpower; they rest on stable cues and repetition.

Multiplication: share once in your small group a real experience of “praying first, then asking”. Your one small testimony may rewrite someone else’s whole year.

Practice 3: Before any church ministry, quietly seek the heart of Jesus

Whether you are leading worship, preaching, holding a meeting, teaching Sunday school or making pastoral visits, cultivate this habit: before you begin, ask Jesus, “Lord, how do you see this? What do you want to do?”

Even if you have done this a hundred times, keep learning not to rely on experience, but to connect with Christ afresh.

Brothers and sisters, proficiency is a grace, and it is also a temptation. What is frightening about proficiency is that it lets us “keep going without needing to rely on God.” The day the Gibeonites came, the Israelites were simply too proficient — they looked at the clothes, felt the dry bread, it all seemed reasonable, and so they “didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth” (Joshua 9:14).

Information: read Acts 13:1–3 until you know it well. Before the church in Antioch sent out Paul and Barnabas, it was “as they served the Lord and fasted” that the Holy Spirit spoke. The order is: first serve the Lord, then serve people.

Revelation: in the stillness before you serve, ask the Lord to show you the real motive of your heart. Is it to bring people before Jesus, or to put your own gifts on display?

Conviction: believe that “the Lord’s heart” matters more than “my preparation”. Preparation is necessary, but preparation must submit to his heart; his heart is not there to fit in with our preparation.

Implementation: before every time of service, be still for five minutes. When a team serves together, be still for three minutes at the start of the meeting before anyone begins the discussion.

Evaluation: after serving, ask three questions. Was Jesus lifted up? Were the brothers and sisters built up? Did I grab the Lord’s place?

Correction: if you find you have drifted, confess it on the spot. Don’t put it off. Every day you delay, the heart hardens a little more.

Repetition: let “first be still, then speak” become the culture of the team, not just one person’s private habit.

Multiplication: bring one co-worker into this practice, and let them bring another. This is the “3” of 235 relationships — spiritual parents and spiritual children. What is passed on is not a technique but a life that relies on Jesus.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Have Jesus, and You Have Everything
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, every person, every thing and every circumstance in this world may change, but Jesus never fails.

He is your ever-present help — “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1).

He is the Commander who leads you to victory — “I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army” (Joshua 5:14).

He is the anchor of your soul — “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil” (Hebrews 6:19).

Let me make the meaning of the anchor clear. A ship’s anchor isn’t dropped onto the ship; it is thrown overboard. An anchor hanging on its own deck is useless, however heavy it is. Hebrews says this anchor enters “within the veil” — within the veil is the Most Holy Place, where Jesus, by his own blood, opened for us a new and living way in. Brothers and sisters, if your anchor is cast onto your own abilities, onto some person or onto an insurance policy, it is still on the ship. The anchor that truly holds is fastened within the veil — fastened to Jesus.

So let us practise every day laying down our dependence on people, refusing to rely on power, on people or on ourselves, and relying on Jesus alone.

Let Jesus come in from outside the door, move from the side to the centre, change from consultant to Commander, from the last resort to the first one we turn to.

When we live like this, revival will no longer be only a longing; it will truly happen in our lives and in our churches.

Because revival has never been an event. Revival is Jesus reigning once again as King among his people.

Brothers and sisters, let us declare together: Lord Jesus, I do not rely on people; I rely on you alone!

May all the glory go to the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the same yesterday, today and forever.

keyVerses: “Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.’” (Jeremiah 17:5–8)
“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust in the name of Yahweh our God.” (Psalm 20:7)
“Jesus said to him, ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.’” (John 14:6)
practices: Declare it every morning
When you need help, pray first, then ask
Before church ministry, quietly seek the heart of Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We come before you confessing that we so often lean on mountains, on people, on ourselves. We wear ourselves out cutting our own cisterns, and we have forsaken you, the spring of living water. Lord, forgive us.

Lord, we see that you have not come to join our side; you have come to take command. This morning, like Joshua, we fall face down before you and hand the commander’s place back to you, saying: What does my Lord say to his servant?

Teach us to make our declaration to you first thing each morning; teach us to turn to you first when we meet difficulties; teach us to wait quietly on you before we serve. Remove from our hearts every dependence that has become an idol, and make us like a tree planted by the waters, spreading out its roots by the river; not afraid when heat comes; not anxious in the year of drought; never ceasing to bear fruit.
Reign as King in our families, reign as King in our small groups, reign as King in our churches. May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh’” (Jeremiah 17:5). Looking back over the past month, in which matter are you most prone to “go to people first and the Lord later”? Behind that matter, what are you really afraid of losing?

“He said, ‘No; but I have come now as commander of Yahweh’s army’” (Joshua 5:14). In your present life or service, is there a “commander’s place” you are still holding in your own hands and have not yet handed over? What concrete step will you take this week to hand it back to Jesus?
l014.title: Rely on No One but Jesus
l014.subtitle: Lean on a Mountain and It May Fall, Lean on People and They May Run — Lean on the Lord Jesus
l014.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Hardest Face to Let Go Of
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today let’s begin with a very ordinary scene.

A group of people have just taken a group photo, and someone posts it to the group chat. The moment each person opens the picture, where do their eyes land first? Not on the mountain in the background, not on the flowers to one side, not on the guest of honour standing in the middle — but on “my face”. Were my eyes shut? Was my hair a mess? Did I stand somewhere flattering? If I came out badly, then even if everyone else is beaming, a voice inside me will still say: don’t post this one.

It is a tiny reflex, yet it gives away a very deep secret: in the whole world we see, there is one image that always stands at the very front — and that is “self”.

Social media has magnified this secret. The invention of the front-facing phone camera allowed human beings, for the first time, to see themselves anytime and anywhere. How many times a day do we look at ourselves? In the mirror, in photos, in our stories, checking under our posts for likes. We live in an unprecedented age of “looking at ourselves without end”.

And two thousand years ago, the Bible had already set exactly the opposite picture before us. Matthew 17:8 says: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

This sentence comes right after the Transfiguration. The disciples lift their heads from the ground. The mountain is still the same mountain, the cloud still the same cloud, but in their eyes only one remains — Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, the “one” in this sentence that is hardest to let go of is not really Moses, nor Elijah, nor Peter, James or John. The “one” that is hardest to let go of is ourselves.

On the road of pursuing spiritual life, our greatest obstacle is often not our circumstances, nor other people, but “self”. However hard our circumstances, God can change them; however hard other people are, God can soften them. But the “self” standing right before my eyes and blocking my view of Jesus — only when I myself am willing to step aside can God be seen.

When we fix our eyes on ourselves and make much of ourselves; when “I” becomes the centre of our words, the motive of our service, the core of our faith, our gaze shifts away from Jesus. Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: this is not simply a matter of pride; it is a misaligned focus of faith. When the focus shifts, the direction shifts; when the direction shifts, a whole life shifts.

And this is exactly Satan’s favourite move. He doesn’t need to get you to commit adultery, commit murder or worship idols. All he has to do is gently turn your camera a few degrees — away from Jesus and towards yourself — so that you start looking at yourself, emphasising yourself, satisfying yourself. After that, he doesn’t need to do anything more, because the fall will happen on its own.

Let me use an astronomical phenomenon to show how frightening this is. The diameter of the sun is about 1.39 million kilometres, roughly four hundred times the diameter of the moon; yet the sun is also roughly four hundred times farther from us than the moon is. So, seen from the earth, the sun and the moon look almost exactly the same size. And that produces an astonishing phenomenon: that small moon, which gives off no light of its own, need only move into the right position to cover the entire sun completely — a total solar eclipse.

Brothers and sisters, “self” is like that moon. In itself it isn’t large at all, and it gives no light whatsoever. But when it comes too close to our eyes and happens to stand right in front of Jesus, it can blot out the glorious Christ entirely and plunge our world into darkness in an instant.

The darkness of a total eclipse lasts only a few minutes. But if a Christian lets “self” stand in front of Jesus year after year, that darkness can last a lifetime.

The title of this lesson is “Seeing Self Brings the Fall”. Together we will look at four things: first, our greatest enemy is often “self”; second, Satan’s first scheme is to get people to look at themselves; third, looking at ourselves means walking in Satan’s footsteps; fourth, Jesus’ example is to see not himself but only the Father. Finally we will practise together turning from “looking at ourselves” to “seeing Jesus alone”.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Transfiguration and the Words “Jesus Alone”
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of the words “they saw no one, except Jesus alone”, we must go back to their context.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, the tax collector whom Jesus called as he sat at the tax office (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish believers. That is why the whole book quotes the Old Testament again and again and sets out to prove one thing over and over: Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the offspring of Abraham.

The Transfiguration is recorded in Matthew 17:1–8, with parallel accounts in Mark 9:2–8 and Luke 9:28–36. It happened at a crucial turning point.

Just six days earlier, on the road at Caesarea Philippi, Jesus had asked his disciples, “Who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). That was a high point. But immediately afterwards, Jesus said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem to suffer, be killed and rise on the third day. Peter at once took him aside and rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” Jesus turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Brothers and sisters, notice the sequence. Peter had only just been praised, and the next moment he was called Satan. Why? Because he had turned from “setting his mind on the things of God” to “setting his mind on the things of men”. The moment the focus shifted, his spiritual standing changed. That is precisely the theme of this lesson: seeing self brings the fall.

Then Jesus spoke words that set the tone for the whole passage: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James and John and brought them up a high mountain by themselves. The text says: “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with Jesus. Moses represents the Law, Elijah the Prophets; the whole Old Testament stood there, speaking with this One.

Peter’s reaction is fascinating. He said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4). Luke 9:33 honestly adds a comment: “not knowing what he said.”

Three tents — this is a “seeing self” proposal. Peter wanted to hold on to the experience, to arrange the scene, to play a part in it. He put Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah: one tent each. And he would be the one putting up the tents.

How did God respond? “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him’” (Matthew 17:5).

God didn’t answer Peter’s question. God corrected Peter’s focus directly. Not three tents, but one beloved Son. Not three men, but one voice — “Listen to him.”

When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces and were very afraid. “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’ Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:7–8).

The action of “lifting up their eyes” is in the original ἐπαίρω τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς, literally “to raise the eyes”. They had been lying face down, heads bowed, seeing nothing but the ground and themselves. Only when Jesus came, touched them and told them to get up did they raise their eyes.

And “Jesus alone” in Greek is εἰ μὴ αὐτὸν Ἰησοῦν μόνον, literally “no one except Jesus himself only”. The word μόνον means “only, solely, alone”. This is not to say that Moses and Elijah are unimportant. It is to say that when the glory is revealed, every supporting actor must leave the stage, and only One may remain on it.

Brothers and sisters, this is the rule of heaven. Revelation chapter 5 describes worship in heaven: myriads upon myriads of angels, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders cry out with a loud voice, “Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12). Heaven has countless worshippers, yet only one focus of worship.

If we hope one day to join the worship team of heaven, then today, here on earth, we must begin learning the same thing: to see not ourselves, but Jesus alone.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Our Greatest Enemy Is Often “Self”
sections.html:
We often think that what holds back our spiritual growth is something outside us. Work is too busy; our family doesn’t believe; someone at church is hard to get along with; our health is poor; money is tight. These are all real difficulties, but they are usually not the greatest enemy.

The Bible speaks very directly about this. Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Notice the order: first deny yourself, then take up the cross, and only then follow. Denying of self is the first step. If the first step is never taken, the next two are only religious motions.

“Deny himself” in Greek is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown utterly, to refuse to acknowledge, to cut all ties with”. In Matthew’s Gospel this word appears on another famous occasion as well: when Jesus foretold that Peter would deny him three times, he used exactly the same word (Matthew 26:34, 75).

Brothers and sisters, do you hear the contrast? When Peter applied that “denial” to Jesus, it was the greatest failure of his life; yet when Jesus asks us to apply the very same “denial” to ourselves, it becomes the greatest success of ours. Denying of self means that when “self” walks up and demands sovereignty, we point at him and say: I do not know this man.

Paul puts it even more searchingly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

In this verse there is a death, and there is a life. “It is no longer I” is the death; “Christ lives in me” is the life. The 321 vision puts it very clearly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness does not mean annihilating ourselves into nothing; selflessness means letting the infinite Lord fill all my space. We are emptied in order to be filled; we step aside so that the Lord may be revealed.

Modern psychology has in fact brushed against the edges of this phenomenon. In 1972 the psychologists Shelley Duval and Robert Wicklund proposed Objective Self-Awareness Theory. They found that when a person is placed in front of a mirror or a camera, their attention turns from the outside world to themselves; and once attention turns to the self, people immediately compare themselves with the standards in their minds, and what follows is often unease, anxiety and self-criticism.

In other words, scientific experiments observed something the Bible had long since spelled out: when people keep staring at themselves, what comes is not peace but unrest.

In 1970 the psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr. published his famous “mirror self-recognition test” in the journal Science, showing that chimpanzees can recognise themselves in a mirror. Human infants gain this ability at around eighteen to twenty-four months. Interestingly, as soon as self-awareness appears, emotions such as shame, jealousy and showing off appear along with it. Seeing ourselves has never come cheap.

I want to point out one thing in particular. In 2003 the psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues (Jennifer Campbell, Joachim Krueger and Kathleen Vohs) published a large-scale review of the research in the journal Psychological Science in the Public Interest, and its conclusion shook the education world of the day: raising self-esteem does not cause better academic results or job performance; rather, good performance raises self-esteem. In other words, the decades-old assumption that “the more you look at yourself and affirm yourself, the better you’ll do” could not stand up to rigorous testing.

Brothers and sisters, the world spent decades and untold sums of money only to arrive, barely, at the Bible’s front door. And the Bible said from the outset: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” (Romans 12:3).

Let me give an example from everyday life. A sister sings beautifully and is invited to sing a solo at church. The first time she stands up, there is only one prayer in her heart: Lord, please use this song to comfort the people out there. When she finishes, she is in tears herself, and many in the congregation are touched by the Lord. The second time, someone praises her voice as truly anointed. The third time, she starts paying attention to whether the pianist is drowning her out, starts noticing the camera angle, and after singing, starts checking online whether anyone has shared the video.

The song hasn’t changed; the voice hasn’t changed; even the spot where she stands hasn’t changed. What has changed is the focus. The first time she was looking at Jesus; later she was looking at herself. From the outside, nothing is different; from heaven, these are two completely different things.

That is why we say our greatest enemy is often ourselves. This enemy doesn’t attack you from outside; he adjusts your camera from within. He doesn’t change what you do; he only changes why you do it.

The 321 vision reminds us: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is on myself, I live in comparison; when the focus is on others, I live in my emotions; when the focus is on my circumstances, I live in fear. Only when the focus is on Jesus do I live in faith.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Satan’s First Scheme — Getting People to Look at Themselves
sections.html:
The first spiritual battle in human history was not fought on a battlefield. It took place in a conversation in front of a tree.

In the Garden of Eden, the serpent said to the woman: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5).

Brothers and sisters, notice how clever Satan’s words are. He didn’t tell Eve to hate God; he didn’t tell her to worship another god; he didn’t say a single vulgar word. What he said was a word of “advancement”: you will be like God. It sounds like helping people move upwards, but in reality it pulls them away from God’s presence.

The heart of this move was to shift Eve’s attention from “what God has said” to “what I could become”. The moment the focus shifted, the result followed: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6).

“Good for food” is the need of the flesh; “a delight to the eyes” is the lust of the eyes; “to be desired to make one wise” is the pride of life. The apostle John later summed up these three in exactly the same way: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16).

From that moment on, human eyes have been fixed on ourselves. Look at their first reaction after they sinned: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves” (Genesis 3:7). Their eyes were opened, yet what they saw was not God but themselves; not glory but shame. Satan promised “like God”; what he actually delivered was “naked”.

When people see themselves, they want to satisfy themselves; when people set their minds on the flesh, they drift away from God’s will. Paul puts it with absolute finality: “because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God; for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be” (Romans 8:7).

The word “mind” here is the Greek φρόνημα (phronēma). It refers not to a passing thought, but to “the bent of the mind, a pattern of thinking, the direction the whole heart is facing”. So Paul is not talking about an occasional moment of weakness, but about which way your heart is heading as a whole. Romans 8:6 says: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.”

Brothers and sisters, there is a question here we must face honestly: why is it so easy for people to look at themselves?

Modern neuroscience offers an interesting piece of corroboration. In 2001 Marcus Raichle and his colleagues at Washington University in St. Louis published research in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that the human brain has a set of regions that are actually most active when we are “doing nothing”. They called it the Default Mode Network. A great deal of later research found that the activity of this network is closely tied to self-referential thinking — in other words, the moment a person is idle, the brain’s default channel switches automatically to “thinking about me”.

Brothers and sisters, this shows exactly why looking at Jesus takes practice, while looking at ourselves doesn’t. Looking at ourselves is the default setting; looking at Jesus is a choice. Drifting downstream takes no effort; only going against the current needs the oars.

So what can truly satisfy us? Not self-fulfilment, but God himself. Psalm 37:4 says: “Also delight yourself in Yahweh, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4).

Notice the order in this verse: first delight in Yahweh, and only then are the desires of your heart given. Many people reverse the order: let me first get what I want, and then I’ll be happy. The result? They get it, and the happiness lasts three days. So they want something bigger — and the happiness still lasts only three days. That is the mathematics of self-satisfaction: the denominator always runs faster than the numerator.

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a prayer that has been repeated down the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Those words sum up the whole human condition: the hole in our hearts was dug in the shape of God, and anything else we pour into it leaks away.

I often use an illustration. A small child stands in front of a waterfall holding a plastic cup. He keeps checking how full his cup is, but he never once looks up at the water pouring down. His cup can only ever hold so much, yet the waterfall has never stopped. Looking at ourselves is staring at the cup; looking at Jesus is lifting our eyes to the living water that never stops flowing.

This is what 321 calls the shift in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly system to God’s. Satan’s first scheme is to stop you making that shift; all he wants is for you to keep your head down, looking at your own cup.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Looking at Ourselves Means Walking in Satan’s Footsteps
sections.html:
Why did Satan fall from heaven? We tend to assume it was because he did something horribly evil. In fact, the reason the Bible records for his fall comes down to two words, said five times over: I will, I will, I will, I will, I will.

Isaiah 14:12–15 says: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’ Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit” (Isaiah 14:12–15).

Five times “I will”, and in return one “you shall be brought down”. Brothers and sisters, this is the shortest and most terrifying chain of cause and effect in the whole Bible.

Ezekiel 28:17 adds another angle: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” Notice: the reason for his fall was not that he was ugly but that he was beautiful; not that he lacked splendour but that he had splendour and looked at his own splendour. The root of Satan’s fall was not that he lacked power, but that he “looked at himself and wanted for himself” far too much.

The Hebrew root for “pride”, גָּאָה (ga’ah), originally means “to rise, to swell up”, like water rising. Pride is not a sudden movement; it is a slowly rising water level. By the time you notice, the water is already over the roof. That is why Proverbs 16:18 says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).

The 321 vision puts this very plainly: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Satan refused to be a creature; he wanted to be the Creator. He left his originally intended position, and he lost everything.

And this spirit of “I will” was not locked away in Sheol along with Satan. It has seeped into today’s society, and into today’s church as well:

I want to be seen. I want to be famous. I want to succeed. I want people’s approval.

Brothers and sisters, is any one of these an obvious sin? No. They even sound perfectly normal, ambitious, healthy. That is exactly what makes them dangerous.

Even if what we are doing is “spiritual work”, if the motive is “I want”, the end is still hostility towards God. That is a strong statement, but Jesus himself said something stronger still: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:21–23).

Notice what these people are holding in their hands: prophesying, casting out demons, doing mighty works. What a dazzling ministry CV! Yet the Lord’s reply is: “I never knew you.”

Why? Listen closely to their words: “Didn’t we prophesy in your name?” The subject of the sentence is “we”. All through their speech, “we” comes up again and again, while Jesus is used merely as a name to invoke. They used the Lord’s name to do their own work and make their own name.

In Matthew chapter 6 Jesus had already warned against this pattern: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1). Three times he speaks of giving, praying and fasting, and three times he closes with the same sentence: “Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16).

“Have received” in Greek is ἀπέχω (apechō), a technical term from the business documents of the day meaning “payment received in full; account settled”. In other words, the moment human applause breaks out, the account in heaven is settled; there is no balance left.

Brothers and sisters, if we make a name on earth but have our name struck off in heaven, how tragic that would be!

Let me give an everyday example. There is a way of spending called “buy now, pay in instalments”: easy right now, with the cost pushed into the future. Chasing human praise is spiritual buy-now-pay-later: it feels great now, and the bill comes afterwards. Denying of self is like paying in cash: it hurts a little at the time, but you owe nobody anything.

Here I also want to mention a fascinating finding from psychology. In 2000 the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky published a series of experiments on the “Spotlight Effect” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They had participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walk into a room, then asked them to estimate how many people had noticed. On average the participants estimated that about half the people had noticed; in fact only about a quarter remembered.

Brothers and sisters, this research shows a fact that is both funny and freeing: the spotlight you thought was always shining on you doesn’t actually exist. We spend most of our lives managing an image that hardly anyone is looking at.

So the pursuit of “I want to be seen” is, at heart, performing in front of empty seats. Meanwhile, the One who truly is watching is looking not at your performance but at your heart. First Samuel 16:7 says: “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

The 321 vision says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When one “I want” meets another “I want”, tension arises in the church; when two “I want”s refuse to give way, ministry grinds to a halt, relationships break down, and in the end both sides lose. But when one person steps aside first, humility starts to spread. Brothers and sisters, will you be the one who steps aside first?

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: Jesus’ Example — Seeing Not Himself but Only the Father
sections.html:
Having spent three key points on the problem, we now turn to the perfect answer.

The first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model”. And Jesus’ ministry on earth is the clearest demonstration of “seeing not himself but only the Father”.

Jesus said: “I can of myself do nothing. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is righteous; because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30).

In this verse there are two negatives and two positives. “Can … do nothing” and “don’t seek my own will” are the negatives; “as I hear, I judge” and “but the will of my Father who sent me” are the positives. This is the Son of God, who has all power, and yet he says, “I can of myself do nothing.”

Verse 19 of the same chapter says it more fully: “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19).

Brothers and sisters, notice the spiritual order here: first see, then do. Jesus’ actions did not start from his own plans; they started from what he saw the Father doing.

Nor did he ever contend for his own glory. John 8:50 records him saying: “But I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). And in his final prayer, he said to the Father: “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4).

Jesus did not perform miracles to make a name for himself, nor teach the truth to build a reputation. His focus was always “the Father’s will”; his actions were “doing only what he saw the Father doing”; his joy was “letting the Father be glorified”.

Paul turned this example into the greatest hymn in the history of the church: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” in Greek is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty, to make void”. Brothers and sisters, set Philippians 2 side by side with Isaiah 14 and you will see two completely opposite paths in the universe:

Satan said, “I will ascend into heaven,” and ended up brought down to Sheol. Jesus said, “I don’t seek my own will,” and emptied himself, going down to the very lowest place — and God raised him to the very highest. Philippians 2:9 goes on: “Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

One path is wanting to be high, and ending up brought low; the other is going low, and being raised up by God. Brothers and sisters, which path will you take?

Today Jesus has been lifted up onto the throne. In heaven, all worship has only one focus — Jesus Christ. The scene in Revelation chapter 5 shows plainly that heaven allows only one focus: the Lamb of God. The apostle John says: “I heard every created thing which is in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea, and everything in them, saying, ‘To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb be the blessing, the honor, the glory, and the dominion, forever and ever! Amen!’” (Revelation 5:13).

Heaven has no second pulpit, no second spotlight, no second name being cheered.

John the Baptist is another beautiful example in the New Testament. His disciples came running to tell him: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him” (John 3:26). This was an obvious attempt to stir him up: your people are being stolen. John’s reply became the motto of everyone who serves: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

“Increase” and “decrease” in the original are αὐξάνω and ἐλαττόω, a pair of contrasting verbs: one growing, one diminishing. John was not forced off the stage; he gladly turned the spotlight away from himself. He said he was only the friend of the bridegroom, who rejoices greatly at hearing the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29).

Brothers and sisters, our greatest temptation in serving is to mistake the friend of the bridegroom for the bridegroom.

Let me use an illustration. The moon at night is beautiful, but the moon has not a glimmer of light of its own. It shines only because it reflects the light of the sun. The best moon is the one that blocks the least light and reflects the most. Yet, as we said earlier, that same moon, if it moves into the wrong position, can cover the entire sun.

The same moon, in the right position, reflects glory; in the wrong position, it hides glory. Brothers and sisters, what decides it is not your size but your position.

Paul uses another lovely image: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

When psychologists put a mirror in front of people, they see themselves, and the result is anxiety. Paul says that when we behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we ourselves become that mirror, reflecting the Lord’s image, and the result is “from glory to glory”.

The same mirror: look at yourself and you are trapped in it; look at the Lord and you are transformed. This is what 321 calls the fivefold change, which begins with the mindset — change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. And the first step of all this is simply to lift your eyes off yourself.

If we long one day to join the worship team of heaven, then we must start learning now: to see not ourselves, but Jesus alone.

sections.heading: 7. An Important Reminder: Not Suppressing Ourselves, but Lifting Up Jesus
sections.html:
At this point some brothers and sisters may be struggling inside: Does that mean I’m not allowed any thoughts of my own? Is even looking after myself a sin? Do I have to keep putting myself down and disliking myself?

No. We need to be clear about this.

The trouble with looking at ourselves is not that self-knowledge is wrong. At the very opening of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, Calvin says that nearly all our wisdom consists of two parts: the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves — and the two are bound together. Knowing yourself is not wrong; on the contrary, it is part of godliness.

So where does the problem lie? It lies in the moment when “I” becomes the focus, becomes the motive, becomes the one in charge. That is when faith goes off course.

The difference here is a matter of position, not of existence. God has never wanted to erase you; God wants you to return to your originally intended position. 321 puts it superbly: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

In the Bible, the reactions of those who truly saw God are worth noticing. Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a high and lofty throne in the temple, and he said: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). After God questioned Job out of the whirlwind, Job said: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6).

Notice: they did not first loathe themselves and then see God. They first saw God, and only then came to a true assessment of themselves. The order matters enormously. If a person simply stares at themselves, digging out their faults, that is not humility; it is just another form of self-centredness — negative self-centredness, but self-centredness all the same. True humility is having your eyes so filled by a far greater Presence that there is simply no room left to keep fussing over yourself.

And look at what happened next. After Isaiah was cleansed by a live coal from the altar, God asked, “Whom shall I send?” Isaiah said: “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8). And Job? “Yahweh turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before” (Job 42:10).

Brothers and sisters, those who see God are not wiped out; instead they are sent, restored and given double.

God does not want you to suppress yourself or deny your worth. He wants you to find your true self in Jesus — and that “self” exists to glorify him.

Jesus himself once spoke words that hold both losing and finding: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 16:25).

The 321 vision says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — entering the limitless and living out the limitless; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Put a drop of water on the palm of your hand, and in less than half a day it has evaporated; pour the same drop into the ocean, and it will never dry up. Selflessness is not disappearing; it is entering the limitless.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Overcomes Satan
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the message of this lesson is in fact the very heart of the 321 vision.

Each of the Three Foundations moves the focus away from ourselves.

Jesus is my role model — he said, “I can of myself do nothing” (John 5:30). If even the Son of God did not act on his own, what grounds do I have for acting on my own?

The Bible is my standard — when “I want” rises up in my heart, I don’t ask what I want; I ask what the Bible says. If the standard lies within me, I have become my own god; only if the standard lies in the Bible is God God.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23).

The Two Core Values are the very conclusion of this lesson.

Let Jesus be King — a kingdom can have only one king. When I sit on the throne, Jesus can only be an adviser; and an adviser can be consulted — or ignored. Letting Jesus be King means handing that chair back to him.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — notice: “all”. Not ninety per cent to the Lord and ten per cent kept for myself. The person who keeps back ten per cent will sooner or later end up quarrelling with someone over that ten per cent.
