The Goal is to establish God’s system. A human system is a pyramid: the higher up you are, the more you are seen. God’s system is a body, in which each member does its own part, and there is only one Head — Christ (Ephesians 4:15–16).

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Satan fell because of “I will”; Adam and Eve fell because of “you will be like God”. The title of this lesson hits the mark exactly: seeing self brings the fall.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Brothers and sisters, remember this: you don’t need pride to defeat Satan’s pride. Just use humility, and he has nothing to push against. Satan can attack someone standing on a high place, but he cannot drag down someone who is already lying face down at the Lord’s feet.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. What this lesson must change first is the mindset — so the greatest enemy is not my circumstances but myself; so “I want” is not ambition but danger; so not seeing myself is not a loss but freedom. When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, the way I speak, the way I spend money and the way I set priorities all change; then the relationships at home change, and only last of all does ministry change.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people reverse the order and charge into ministry first, and the result is that the bigger their ministry grows, the emptier their life and the worse their relationships. Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The shift in perspective: from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly system to God’s. “Famous on earth, struck off in heaven” — that phrase is exactly the showdown between “temporary” and “eternal”. Earthly fame lasts at most for one generation’s memory; heaven’s remembrance endures forever and ever.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, we practise living a selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice this: not one of these nine graces is borne for ourselves. A fruit tree never eats its own fruit. If you are still looking at yourself, the fruit you bear will never get any further than you.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, spiritual companions to each other, reminding one another where the focus belongs; build the “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing “see not yourself, but Jesus alone” on to the next generation; become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, serving together with no one fighting for the place in the middle.

The Path of Serving is Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, I let him be King, and in the end all glory goes to him. On this path, with every step, there is a little less of “self” and a little more of Christ.

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: From “Looking at Myself” to “Looking at Jesus”
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We will keep all three, and use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: Every morning, say to the Lord: “Lord, today I don’t want to look at myself; I only want to look at you.”

After you get up, while you wash, or before you head out, close your eyes and say honestly to Jesus: “Lord, today I don’t want to fix my eyes on my own weaknesses, cravings, needs or performance. I only want to fix my eyes on you.”

This is a spiritual vaccination. A vaccine works by preparing the body’s defences before the virus invades in force. In the same way, if we set our focus right before the day’s pressures, comparisons and criticisms arrive, we won’t be dragged around by our emotions all day.

Brothers and sisters, notice the timing: after you get up, not before you go to sleep. The first thought of the day often sets the direction of the whole day. Psalm 5:3 says: “Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly” (Psalm 5:3).

Practice 2: Whenever you think “I want …”, stop at once and ask, “What does Jesus want?”

When thoughts like “I want to succeed”, “I want to be famous” or “I want to be in control” start up in your life or service, pause immediately and ask in your heart: “Lord Jesus, what do you want in this?”

It is a very short question, but it is a steering wheel. If a plane flying from Taipei to Tokyo is off course by a single degree, it will miss its destination by tens of kilometres. Life is the same. This small question will help you break out of self-centredness and turn towards God’s will.

The Lord Jesus himself modelled this turn in the Garden of Gethsemane: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). Brothers and sisters, if even the Lord had to say these words, how much more do we need to say them every day.

Practice 3: Every evening, reflect: “Where did I see myself today? Where did I see Jesus?”

At the end of the day, take a few quiet minutes and honestly ask yourself three questions:

First, at what moment today was I making myself stand out?

Second, was there anything I did to satisfy my own “I want”?

Third, at what moments today did I fix my eyes on Jesus, obey him and let him be glorified?

Brothers and sisters, don’t let this reflection turn into self-accusation. Psalm 139:23–24 gives us the right attitude: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Notice the last line: it doesn’t stop at “any wicked way”; it moves on to “lead me in the everlasting way”.

Deepening the three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

Stage 1, Information. Today’s lesson is the information. Now you know: seeing self brings the fall; see no one else but Jesus.

Stage 2, Revelation. If information stays only in the head, it is just knowledge. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn these words into your own seeing, so that in some specific situation you suddenly recognise: so that moment, I was looking at myself.

Stage 3, Conviction. True conviction is admitting that this applies to you, not just to other people. The sign of conviction is that you stop defending yourself.

Stage 4, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, do Practice 1. Don’t wait until you feel like it; do it first, and the feelings will catch up.

Stage 5, Evaluation. The evening reflection of Practice 3 is your evaluation. A few minutes each day — it needn’t be long, but it must be honest.

Stage 6, Correction. Evaluation without correction is only regret. If you find that in some matter today you looked at yourself, then tomorrow, in that same matter, deliberately step aside once.

Stage 7, Repetition. One time of practice won’t change a person; a year of practice will. Brothers and sisters, spiritual muscle is like physical muscle: it grows through the number of repetitions.

Stage 8, Multiplication. Find a brother or sister to be your “2”. Practise together, and once a week ask each other: “This week, where did you see yourself? Where did you see Jesus?” If the practice stops with you, it still circles back to self; only when it is passed on to others have you truly stepped out of yourself.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call: Unseen on Earth, Remembered in Heaven
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have come to the end of this lesson.

Jesus said: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

These words come from a banquet scene. Jesus noticed how the invited guests were jostling for the places of honour, and he told them a parable: don’t go and sit in the place of honour yourself, in case a guest more distinguished than you has been invited and the host comes and says to you, “Give this person your place,” and then, red-faced, you have to move down to the lowest place. Better to go and sit in the lowest place, so that when the host comes he says to you, “Friend, move up higher,” and then you will be honoured in front of everyone at the table.

Notice that Jesus did not say, “Don’t have any honour.” He said that honour should be received from the host’s hand, not grabbed for yourself.

“Exalt” and “humble” in Greek are ὑψόω (hypsoō) and ταπεινόω (tapeinoō), and both words appear together in Philippians 2 as well: Christ “humbled himself” (tapeinoō), and God “highly exalted him” (hyperypsoō). Brothers and sisters, this is not a motivational slogan. It is a law by which the universe runs — a law God himself demonstrated in his own Son.

First Peter 5:5–6 says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:5–6).

“In due time” — those three words are for every anxious heart. You don’t have to arrange the timetable yourself, fight for a position yourself, or argue your own innocence. God has his time.

When we are willing not to put ourselves forward or exalt ourselves on earth, the Father himself will remember us and lift us up into the right place.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let us make three decisions together.

First, step aside. Move the shadow that stands in front of Jesus out of the way. You don’t have to destroy it; you only have to step aside.

Second, look up. Like the disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration, lift your eyes from where you lie face down. Jesus will touch you and say to you: “Get up, and don’t be afraid” (Matthew 17:7).

Third, let him be King. Hand the chair on the throne back to him; let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Let us learn to be like Jesus, living not for ourselves but only for the glory of God. Let us practise every day seeing not ourselves but Jesus alone, until the day we stand with him in glory.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Every morning, say to the Lord
Whenever you think “I want …”, stop at once and ask
Reflect every evening
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you for setting this mirror before us this morning. We confess that for years, what has stood between us and you has often been not our circumstances, not other people, but ourselves.

Lord, forgive the “I want” in our hearts. Forgive us for doing things in your name while quietly building our own name. Forgive us for fussing over position in our service, over who is right in our relationships, and over our image in front of others.
Touch us, as you once touched those three disciples lying face down on the ground, and say to us: “Get up, and don’t be afraid.” When we lift up our eyes, let us see no one, except you alone.

Lord, we are willing to step aside, willing to look up, willing to let you be King. May the Holy Spirit remind us every day that whenever an “I want” rises in our hearts, we turn to you at once and ask: Lord, what do you want?
May we be unseen on earth and remembered by you in heaven. To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, be the blessing, the honour, the glory and the dominion, forever and ever.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8). In your life or service over the past week, was there a moment when you realised you were actually “looking at yourself”? What was the situation? What do you think Jesus wanted from you in that moment?

“He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). When his disciples were all turning to follow Jesus, John the Baptist still gladly stepped aside. In your family, workplace or ministry right now, what is one matter in which the Holy Spirit is reminding you to “step aside first”? What concrete step are you willing to take on it this week?
l015.title: Seeing Self Brings the Fall
l015.subtitle: From “Looking at Myself” to “Seeing Only Jesus”
l015.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: What Brings Us Down Is Often Not the Storm but a Glance
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin with a very simple question, but one that cuts deep: over this past week, what picture has filled your heart most often — Jesus, or yourself?

In April 1912, the Titanic struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. What the inquiries found afterwards was shocking: the part of that iceberg showing above the water was not especially large. What actually tore open the hull was the great mass below the surface that no one could see. Oceanographers often quote a proportion: only about one-ninth of an iceberg’s volume floats above the water; the rest lies hidden beneath. That proportion comes from a simple physical fact — sea ice has a density of about 920 kilograms per cubic metre, seawater about 1,025, and from those two numbers the share above the surface can be calculated.

Our life of faith is just the same. What really sinks a Christian is seldom the great wind and waves everyone can see. It is the mass beneath the surface that we don’t want to face — our gaze fixed on ourselves. The circumstances outside are only the impact; the “looking at self” inside is the breach.

On the road of faith, the greatest danger is not only the storms outside. It is this: if our eyes leave Jesus and turn towards ourselves, fear will quietly come in. It doesn’t knock at the door; it seeps in under it. You won’t hear a sound. You’ll simply find, one day, that prayer has grown heavy, that going to fellowship has become a chore, that you rehearse every sentence three times in your head before you say it, and that when the brothers and sisters are chatting warmly in the group chat, you quietly switch off your phone.

How does it start? Very often with a glance. A glance at your own weakness, a glance at your own failure, a glance at the gap between you and others.

The first time the Bible records a human being feeling afraid, it comes right after just such a glance. When Adam and Eve had sinned, the first thing they felt was not repentance but fear. They saw that they were naked, so they hid from God and covered themselves with fig leaves. Why were they afraid? Because they saw themselves — their own shame, their own failure, their own unworthiness. They dared not face God, because their focus was no longer on God; it had turned to themselves.

That is what “seeing self” brings: fear, shame, flight and separation.

And the Bible’s answer is compressed into one short line of our theme verse: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) Brothers and sisters, this is one of the quietest and yet most powerful sentences in the whole Bible. A moment before, the disciples were lying face down, terribly afraid. Then Jesus touched them, said “Get up, and don’t be afraid,” and when they raised their heads the world was suddenly clear — they saw no one but Jesus.

In this lesson we will walk four stretches of road together: from the Garden of Eden to the Sea of Galilee, from the wilderness of Kadesh to the Lord Jesus’ prayer for his disciples’ unity. We will see one thing: where your focus is, there your life is. If the focus is on self, fear reigns as king; if the focus is on Jesus, faith overcomes.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Transfiguration and That One Phrase, “No One”
sections.html:
Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8. The author of Matthew’s Gospel was Matthew the tax collector, also called Levi, one of the Lord Jesus’ twelve apostles. The early church fathers Papias (c. AD 60–130) and Eusebius (c. AD 260–340) both testify that Matthew was the first to compile the Lord’s words and deeds in a Hebrew style. The book is generally thought to have been written around AD 60–70, mainly for communities of Jewish believers. That is why Matthew loves to quote the Old Testament, and especially loves phrases like “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet”: he wants to prove to his own people that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the descendant of Abraham.

Church history calls this passage in chapter 17 “the Transfiguration”. Where it falls is crucial. Just six days earlier, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, Peter had made his great confession: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16) Straight afterwards the Lord told his disciples plainly, for the first time, that he must go up to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed and rise on the third day. Peter took him aside on the spot and rebuked him: “Far be it from you, Lord! This will never be done to you.” (Matthew 16:22) The Lord Jesus’ reply came down like thunder: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order here. The disciples have just been told that their minds are set “on the things of men” — that their gaze is fixed entirely on the human, the earthly, the temporary. Six days later the Lord takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain and lets them see his glory with their own eyes. “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:2) This was a lesson in training the eyes. The Lord was adjusting their focus from the things of men to the things of God.

What happens next is fascinating. “Behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them talking with him.” (Matthew 17:3) Moses stands for the Law, Elijah for the Prophets; these are the two weightiest figures in Old Testament history. The moment Peter sees them, he says, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4) Peter’s problem was not a lack of zeal. It was that he put Jesus on the same level as Moses and Elijah — three tents, all the same size.

God’s answer came at once: “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5) This bright cloud is the Shekinah glory of God’s presence in the Old Testament, the very cloud that once filled the tabernacle and the temple. The Father’s declaration amounts to this: Moses may step back, Elijah may step back; there is only one focus — my beloved Son.

And so we come to verses 6 to 8: “When the disciples heard it, they fell on their faces, and were very afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’ Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:6–8)

There are three actions here, and their order cannot be reversed: he takes the initiative to come near, he touches them with his own hand, and only then comes “don’t be afraid.” Brothers and sisters, the Lord never stands at a distance shouting, “Don’t be scared!” He comes over, he touches you, and then he says: don’t be afraid. In the original, “no one” is οὐδένα (oudena), and “except Jesus alone” is εἰ μὴ αὐτὸν Ἰησοῦν μόνον; that μόνον (monon) means “only, solely.” The meaning of the whole scene is this: all the noise in their field of vision has been cleared away, and only one remains.

And that is exactly what this lesson wants to say to us. When the picture in our heart holds only Jesus, fear has no ground to stand on; when the picture is crammed full of ourselves, faith is devoured bit by bit.

sections.heading: 1. When the Focus Turns to Self, Fear Devours Faith
sections.html:
“Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden. Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’ The man said, ‘I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.’” (Genesis 3:7–10)

Brothers and sisters, notice that this is the first time the word “afraid” appears in the whole Bible. It doesn’t appear at the Flood, or on a battlefield, or in the face of death. It appears the first time a human being truly and carefully looks at himself.

The Hebrew hides a profound play on words here. Genesis 2:25 says, “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.” That word “naked” is עֲרוּמִּים (arummim). Immediately afterwards, 3:1 says, “Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made.” That word “subtle” — crafty — is עָרוּם (arum). The two words sound almost exactly alike. The writer of Scripture is reminding us that human nakedness was originally unafraid: the freedom of standing before God with nothing hidden and nothing to defend. But once the serpent’s craftiness came in, the very same nakedness turned into shame. Nothing about the thing itself changed; what changed was the way of seeing.

That is why verse 7 says, “Their eyes were opened.” The serpent’s original promise was that “in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Their eyes were indeed opened — but the first thing they saw was not God; it was themselves. This is the truest picture of the human fall: not a loss of sight, but a change to the wrong focus.

The word “afraid” in verse 10 is the Hebrew יָרֵא (yare’). It’s a remarkable word, because it can be translated “to be afraid” and also “to fear” in the sense of reverence. The same word, directed to God, becomes holy reverence: “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). Directed to ourselves, it becomes a fear that binds us. Brothers and sisters, this tells us something: fear is not some surplus emotion; fear is reverence pointed at the wrong object. The very energy you were meant to spend looking up to God, once it is turned on yourself, becomes the dread that torments you.

Under fear, people do three things, and Adam did all three: cover, hide and shift the blame. First he covered himself with fig leaves; then he hid among the trees, away from God’s presence; finally, when God pressed him, he said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” (Genesis 3:12) Cover, hide, shift the blame — these three are still our instincts today. We cover ourselves with qualifications, with job titles, with busyness, even with ministry. We hide in our phones, in our work, in our silence. Then we push the responsibility onto our family of origin, onto the church, onto our spouse, onto our circumstances. This whole routine has one single starting point: I saw myself.

Psychology offers clear corroboration here. The Yale psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema (1959–2013) pioneered research on “rumination”. Her series of experiments and longitudinal studies showed that when people repeatedly and passively fix their attention on their own feelings and shortcomings — asking over and over, “What’s wrong with me?” “Why am I so awful?” — their low mood is not resolved; it is prolonged and deepened. Her research showed again and again that rumination is a significant predictor of how long depression lasts. In other words, science is telling us too: staring at yourself does not make you better; it only makes things darker.

This is precisely the root problem the 321 vision addresses from the very start: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. We often imagine the proud person as the one who struts with his chin in the air, looking down on everyone. But the person hiding in the corner, endlessly blaming himself, is also proud — because the one sitting on the throne of his heart is still himself. Boasting is making yourself big; self-loathing is making yourself big and then slapping yourself in the face. In both cases the focus is on the same person.

What is pride? It is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take the place of God. When Adam ate that fruit, it was to be “like God”, to decide good and evil for himself. What is humility? It is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. The real issue in Eden was never a piece of fruit; it was a position.

So listen carefully: when God called out in the garden, “Where are you?”, it was not because he couldn’t find Adam. God knows all things; of course he knew which tree Adam was hiding behind. What God was asking was this: Adam, what position are you living in now? Are you standing in your place as a creature, or are you hiding in a false position you have made for yourself? Brothers and sisters, this morning God asks you and me the same thing: Where are you?

sections.heading: 2. When We See Ourselves, We Cannot See Jesus
sections.html:
“Peter answered him and said, ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the waters.’ He said, ‘Come!’ Peter stepped down from the boat, and walked on the waters to come to Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:28–30)

Brothers and sisters, the lesson text puts it beautifully. Let’s read it slowly together:

When we see our own lack, we cannot believe in Jesus’ abundance;

When we see our own smallness, we cannot rely on Jesus’ greatness;

When we see our own weakness, we can hardly experience Jesus’ almighty power.

If our focus is on ourselves, we sink into self-pity, self-blame, anxiety and fear; but if our focus turns to Jesus, even in the middle of the storm we can still walk on the water. Peter’s experience is the best reminder of all.

We often say Peter “failed”. But brothers and sisters, let’s be fair: of the twelve disciples, only one got out of the boat. The other eleven stayed in it from start to finish, watching. Peter stepped out, and he really did walk on the water — that was no illusion; it was a miracle. So where did it go wrong? The text could not be clearer: “When he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid.”

The word “saw” is the Greek βλέπων (blepōn), a present participle of “to see, to look at”, describing a continuing action. Peter didn’t just catch a glimpse of the wind; he let his gaze rest on the wind and kept staring at it. And notice a small detail: the wind had been there the whole time. It was already strong when he got out of the boat; the disciples had been straining at the oars all night precisely because of the wind and the waves. The wind didn’t get stronger; Peter’s eyes changed. The circumstances didn’t change; his attention did.

This is the exact opposite of what Hebrews describes: “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2). That word “looking” is the Greek ἀφορῶντες (aphorōntes), formed from “away from” (apo) and “to look” (horaō). Its literal sense is to take your eyes off everything else and fix them on one object alone. Brothers and sisters, looking to Jesus isn’t “taking one more look at Jesus”; it is “taking your eyes away from everything else.” You cannot stare at the wind and look to the Lord at the same time.

In 1999 the Harvard psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris carried out an experiment that later became very famous, published in the journal Perception. They asked participants to watch a video and count how many times the team in white passed the ball. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walked into the frame, beat his chest right in the centre of the screen, and stayed there for about nine seconds. Around half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all. The phenomenon is called “inattentional blindness”.

Brothers and sisters, what a sobering reminder this experiment is for us: human attention is limited. When your attention is filled with one thing, you become blind to the most obvious thing right in front of you. When we spend all day counting up our own weaknesses, failures and inadequacies, we become completely blind to the One standing right in front of us — the true and living Jesus, full of grace and power. It isn’t that Jesus isn’t there; it’s that we aren’t looking.

But the tenderest part of this passage comes next: “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31) The Lord didn’t wait for Peter to swim back on his own first; the Lord “immediately stretched out his hand”. This Lord’s hand is faster than our failure.

The nineteenth-century Scottish minister Robert Murray M’Cheyne (1813–1843) is generally credited with saying: “For every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.” That ratio is worth remembering for a lifetime. It isn’t that we never look at ourselves — the Bible also teaches us to examine ourselves — but the proportion must be right. One to ten. If you turn the ratio upside down, looking at yourself ten times for every one look at Christ, you will live in fear.

In terms of the 321 vision, this is what we mean by “Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.” Peter’s three possible focal points on the water are exactly the three temptations of our whole lives: look at yourself, and you feel inferior; look at others, and you envy or judge; look at your circumstances, and you are afraid. Only by looking at Jesus can we walk on the water. That is also why we say: “selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, living out the limitless.” When Peter let go of himself and stepped out of the boat, he entered a realm no human being could possibly enter; the moment he picked himself back up again, he began to sink. The apostle Paul put this mystery most clearly of all: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: 3. Faith and Fear: You Can Walk by Only One
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, fear is faith’s number-one enemy. It does three things: it makes us forget God’s promises, deny God’s power and misread God’s heart. And the most painful example of it in the whole Bible took place in the wilderness of Kadesh Barnea.

After the Israelites came out of Egypt, they arrived at the doorstep of the Promised Land. God told Moses to send twelve spies to explore Canaan. Forty days later they came back, carrying a single cluster of grapes so heavy it took two men with a pole to bear it. Their opening report was actually accurate: “We came to the land where you sent us. Surely it flows with milk and honey.” (Numbers 13:27) But the very next sentence turned: “However, the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are fortified and very large.” (Numbers 13:28)

Caleb stood up at once: “Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, ‘Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!’” (Numbers 13:30) But the conclusion of the other ten spies was this: “We aren’t able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we.” (Numbers 13:31)

Then came those heartbreaking words: “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.” (Numbers 13:33)

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to the second half of that verse. “And so we were in their sight” — tell me, had these ten spies interviewed a single one of the sons of Anak? Not one. They had no idea at all how the enemy saw them. In fact, forty years later the prostitute Rahab told the spies Joshua sent, in her own words: “As soon as we had heard it, our hearts melted, and there wasn’t any more spirit in any man, because of you.” (Joshua 2:11) The other side had been scared to death all along!

This is fear’s greatest lie: first it makes you look down on yourself, and then it makes you “decide for the enemy how he sees you.” “In our own sight” was a misjudgement of the facts; “in their sight” was a projection out of thin air. Brothers and sisters, how many nights when you didn’t dare to speak, how many steps you didn’t dare to take, have been built on an “other people will surely see me this way” that you never once checked?

The Hebrew word for “grasshopper” is חָגָב (chagav), the kind of little insect that crushes underfoot and scatters at a wave of the hand. It wasn’t that they didn’t know God; it was that they no longer kept their eyes on God. They wrongly put themselves at the centre of focus, and so they missed the Promised Land. A whole generation, forty years, wandering around the Sinai Peninsula until they died — not because the enemy was too strong, but because their focus was in the wrong place.

Set that beside the words of Caleb and Joshua and it becomes clearer still: “Only don’t rebel against Yahweh, neither fear the people of the land; for they are bread for us. Their defense is removed from over them, and Yahweh is with us. Don’t fear them.” (Numbers 14:9) The same walls, the same sons of Anak — two completely opposite reports. The difference wasn’t in the intelligence; it was in the focus. The ten spies looked first at the giants and then at themselves, and God disappeared from view. Caleb and Joshua looked first at God and then at the giants, and the giants became bread.

That is why what God said to Joshua as he took up the leadership matters so much: “Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.” (Joshua 1:9) Notice that God’s assurance to Joshua was not “your enemies have grown weaker” but “I am with you.” True faith is not looking at how strong you are; it is believing that Jesus is with me, and so I have nothing to fear.

In 1979 the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky published their famous “Prospect Theory” in the journal Econometrica. Their research found that the pain people feel at a loss is roughly twice the pleasure they feel at an equal gain. This is called “loss aversion”. Kahneman was later awarded the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics for this body of work.

Brothers and sisters, that explains something: why did the ten spies bring back bad news? Because in human nature, “what I might lose” always sounds twice as loud as “what I might gain.” Milk and honey were right before their eyes, yet all they could hear was the echo of the city walls. This is why we need faith. Faith is not blind optimism; faith recalibrates the scales and puts God’s presence on them to be weighed. “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen.” (Hebrews 11:1)

Corrie ten Boom of the Netherlands (1892–1983) is generally credited with saying: “Worry does not empty tomorrow of its sorrow; it empties today of its strength.” This sister, who lost her sister and her father in the Nazi camps and later travelled the world preaching forgiveness, had every right to say it.

Seen through the 321 vision, the battle between faith and fear is at heart a battle of perspectives. The ten spies used a human, earthly, temporary, worldly perspective: how high the walls are, how short we are, whether there is enough food. Caleb and Joshua used God’s perspective — heavenly, eternal, godly: does what God said count or not? The fivefold change of 321 begins right here — change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes. Israel failed at the very first hurdle: their mindset never changed.

sections.heading: 4. “Separation” Makes Us See Too Much of “Self”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let me ask you an intriguing question: when do you notice a single drop of water?

Standing on the beach, looking out over the whole Pacific Ocean, you don’t notice any single drop of water. When you drink a glass of water, you don’t notice any single drop either. So when do you notice one? When it is on its own, separated, cut off from the other drops — a drop hanging on the tip of a leaf, a drop landing on the back of your hand, a drop falling from the eaves.

In the same way, when people lose their unity with one another, we easily “see one person” — and that person is ourselves.

There is a real scientific fact here. Whether water evaporates quickly or slowly depends above all on the “ratio of surface area to volume”. The smaller a drop of water, the larger its surface area relative to its volume, and the faster it evaporates. Spread a quantity of water into a thin mist, and in a few minutes it’s gone; gather the same quantity into a reservoir, and it can supply a whole city. Brothers and sisters, this is no mere coincidence of metaphor; it is a spiritual sign the Creator placed in the material world: isolation exposes us; gathering preserves us.

Often we are not isolated by others; we choose to separate ourselves from them. We protect ourselves, we refuse to trust, we won’t connect, and as time goes on we become lonelier, more fragile and more afraid. Notice which way this vicious circle runs: it isn’t that we are afraid because we are lonely; it’s that we hide because we are looking at ourselves, and once we are hidden we see ourselves even more, and so we grow more afraid. That is exactly how Adam ended up hiding among the trees.

In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad, a professor of psychology at Brigham Young University in the United States, and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine, pooling data from 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand participants. The conclusion: people with stronger social connections had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival. In later research she went further, showing that the harm of social isolation and loneliness to health is comparable to well-known health risk factors. Brothers and sisters, even our bodies protest: human beings were not designed to survive alone.

And God said this before human beings had ever sinned: “Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’” (Genesis 2:18) Notice that this was said before the Fall. It is not good to be alone — not because of sin, but because of God’s design. The triune God is, within his very being, fellowship; human beings, created in his image, exist by nature for relationship.

Solomon put this truth beautifully: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10) And again: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12)

A solitary drop of water soon evaporates. But if that drop is willing to become one with other drops, it can become a stream, a river, even a great river that brings life. The Lord Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38) A river has never been the work of one drop.

In the same way, when we are willing to lay ourselves down, enter into unity and connect with one another, we will “no longer see ourselves, but see only Jesus.” The Lord’s prayer on the eve of his Passion takes this to its height: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me. The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one.” (John 17:21–22) The psalmist says too: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) And the psalm ends: “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

Jesus displays his glory in unity; Jesus brings revival to pass in fellowship.

This is the 321 “235 relationship”: become a “2” with someone who is selfless, spiritual companions who support each other; establish a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children who pass life on from generation to generation; and go on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades in which apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers work hand in hand. Paul says, “so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.” (Romans 12:5) Brothers and sisters, a body part taken off on its own is only a piece of flesh; joined back to the body, it has life, function and glory.

So remember: you are not a lonely drop of water; you are part of a river of living water.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Fear to Faith
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set today’s four key points within the 321 framework, we see them even more clearly.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model: in the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus was deeply distressed, his sweat falling to the ground like great drops of blood, and yet he said, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). This is the perfect example of facing fear — not denying the emotion, but handing over sovereignty. The Bible is my standard: when feelings say “You’re finished,” the Bible says “I am with you”; we must let the standard speak, not our feelings. The Holy Spirit is my guide: the Lord promised, “he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). When we are afraid, what we need most is not more analysis but a return to the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: the root of fear is that we are still sitting on our own throne, still feeling that we have to hold everything up by ourselves. When Jesus truly reigns as King, the responsibility is no longer on me; I only have to follow. Let Jesus receive all the glory: in the ten spies’ report there was no glory of God, only their own size; when our focus is that the glory goes to Jesus, our own size no longer matters.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God never wanted merely to save one person out of Egypt; he wanted to establish a nation and bring it into Canaan. He doesn’t want just one drop of water saved; he wants a river.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. From beginning to end, this lesson is really about one thing only: focus. The self-centred person’s focus is on himself, so he covers, hides, shifts the blame, sinks, sees himself as a grasshopper and isolates himself. The selfless person’s focus is on Jesus, so lifting up his eyes he sees no one except Jesus alone. Andrew Murray (1828–1917) put it superbly in his book Humility; in substance he says that true humility is nothing but the disappearance of self in the vision that God is all. Brothers and sisters, this is not self-destruction; it is self stepping aside.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. When Satan tempted the Lord Jesus in the wilderness, all three times he used the same formula: “If you are the Son of God…” — he wanted to shift the Lord’s focus from “what the Father says” to “who you are and what you can do.” All three times the Lord answered, “It is written,” and his focus did not move even once. Brothers and sisters, Satan uses the same trick on us: he won’t tell you not to believe in God; he will just keep you looking at yourself. And the kind of person he fears most is the one who “sees no one except Jesus alone”, because such a person gives him nothing to grab hold of.

Pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The fear of the ten spies spread to the whole congregation overnight: “All the congregation lifted up their voice, and cried; and the people wept that night” (Numbers 14:1). Fear is contagious — and so is faith. If you choose this morning to look to Jesus, the people around you gain one more companion who can lift them up.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many brothers and sisters grow weary, fearful and ready to run in their service, and often the reason is that the order has been turned upside down: ministry comes first, while relationships haven’t been built and life hasn’t been received. So remember the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If you are not yet aligned with God, you will use ministry to prove yourself; if you are not yet at peace with yourself, you will let other people’s eyes grade you.

A shift of perspective: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The very same city walls of Canaan are a dead end from the human perspective and a promise from God’s. The very same storm on the Sea of Galilee is danger from the earthly perspective and a training ground from the heavenly one. Brothers and sisters, the circumstances don’t need to change first; change the perspective, and the meaning of the circumstances changes.

The 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When we live out the “0” before them — a selfless life — the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in that relationship: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice that not one of the nine is a “power”; every one is a matter of character, and every one shows itself only within relationships. A person living alone cannot practise patience; an isolated person cannot live out kindness. So unity is not a luxury; unity is the soil in which fruit grows.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Training a Rhythm of Life That Moves from Fear into Faith
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the eight stages of changing our mindset are Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. Today we have received the “Information”; let us ask the Lord to grant “Revelation”, so that it becomes “Conviction” in our hearts. Next we must move into “Implementation”. The lesson gives us three practices; let’s take them one at a time.

Practice 1: Notice when you start “looking at yourself”

Pay attention to your inner conversation every day. When you find yourself saying any of these sentences, the alarm bell should ring:

sections.heading: 1. “I’m so weak; I just can’t.”
2. “What if it doesn’t work out?”
3. “What will people think of me?”
sections.html:
These are all the language of “looking at self”. The first looks at my own ability, the second at my own results, the third at my own image. When you notice them surfacing, say one sentence to yourself straight away: “Lord Jesus, I turn to you.”

This is “Evaluation” among the eight stages — not self-blame, but awareness. Brothers and sisters, self-blame is looking at yourself one more time; awareness is lifting your eyes. The Reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546) is generally credited with saying that you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair. Thoughts will come, and that is not sin; it is letting them nest that turns them into bondage.

A suggestion: set three reminders on your phone — morning, midday and bedtime — and spend one minute each time looking back: how many times today did I put the focus back on myself? Don’t record how many times you failed; record only how many times you turned to the Lord.

Practice 2: Replace the language of fear with the language of faith

Learn to counter fear with declarations of faith:

sections.heading: 1. Though I am weak, the Lord is my strength.
2. Though the storm rages, the Lord is still with me.
3. What is impossible for me is possible for God.
sections.html:
Each of these three declarations has a verse of Scripture standing behind it. “Though I am weak, the Lord is my strength” — the Lord said to Paul, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) “Though the storm rages, the Lord is still with me” — “Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness.” (Isaiah 41:10) “What is impossible for me is possible for God” — “Looking at them, Jesus said, ‘With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’” (Matthew 19:26)

You can write these words in a note on your phone or on a small card, meditate on them and read them aloud every day, and let faith overcome fear. For “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Your ears need to hear your own mouth speaking God’s words.

This is “Repetition” among the eight stages. Brothers and sisters, fear has power because it repeats itself; faith has power because it repeats itself too. Whichever voice repeats more often in your heart is the one that will reign as king.

Practice 3: Reach out and connect with others; refuse “isolation”

This week, please deliberately do at least one of these things:

sections.heading: 1. Take the initiative to greet a member of the church body.
2. Share your struggle with a brother or sister you trust.
3. Join a small group or a ministry team.
sections.html:
Refuse to fight alone; choose to connect with the body. This is exactly the 321 “2” — finding a spiritual companion. James says, “Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed.” (James 5:16) Notice that the condition for healing is “to one another” and “for one another”. Of course God hears a confession made alone behind a closed door; but the kind of healing the Bible promises here happens in relationship.

This is “Multiplication” among the eight stages. When you reach out and connect with someone, you are not only helped yourself; you walk this road from fear to faith in front of someone else, so they can see it.

A Gentle Reminder: Don’t exalt your feelings; exalt the truth of Jesus

Our feelings change, but God’s word does not. Feeling like a failure doesn’t mean you can’t overcome; feeling small doesn’t mean God can’t use you.

Feelings are excellent servants but terrible masters. A feeling is like a warning light on the dashboard — it tells you “something is happening”, but it cannot tell you “what the truth is”, still less “what to do about it”. You don’t scrap the whole car because the fuel light comes on; you follow the owner’s manual and fill up. God’s word is our owner’s manual. “Yahweh’s words are flawless words, as silver refined in a clay furnace, purified seven times.” (Psalm 12:6)

Let truth be greater than feelings; let Jesus be greater than self. This is “Correction” among the eight stages — every time a feeling tries to take the driver’s seat, we hand the steering wheel back to the truth.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Lift Your Head Out of Fear and See Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the conclusion of the lesson. It says that God has not given us a timid heart, but a heart of power and love. These words come from Paul’s letter to Timothy, and the full verse reads: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

The word for “fear” here is the Greek δειλία (deilia), the kind of timidity that shrinks back, retreats and dares not go forward. And the three things God gives correspond exactly to the three breaches fear makes. Fear paralyses us, so God gives “power” (δύναμις, dunamis, that is, strength and ability); fear makes us shrink back and look out only for ourselves, so God gives “love” (ἀγάπη, agapē); fear throws our thoughts into confusion and sends our imagination running wild, so God gives “self-control” (σωφρονισμός, sōphronismos), a clear, sound and disciplined mind. Brothers and sisters, these three are not things we must strive to manufacture; God has already given them. When Paul wrote this letter he was in prison in Rome, soon to be martyred for the Lord; in the place where he had every reason to be afraid, he wrote the least fearful sentence of all.

Fear should not become our habit; faith is our calling.

Let us turn our focus from ourselves to Jesus, from separation to unity, from fear to faith. When we no longer see ourselves but see only Jesus, we will be strong and courageous, and step boldly into the future God has promised.

Look once more at the scene in our theme verse. The disciples lay face down, terribly afraid. And then? “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid.’” (Matthew 17:7) Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord is coming to you too, and touching you. You don’t have to become strong first before you can lift your head; you lift your head first, and then you become strong.

Lift up your eyes. See no one, except Jesus alone. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Replace the language of fear with the language of faith
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

This morning you have shone the light of your word on us. We confess that we are so often like Adam, hiding the moment we see our own nakedness; so often like Peter, sinking the moment we see the wind and the waves; so often like those ten spies, seeing ourselves as grasshoppers and not daring to step into the promise you have long since given.

Lord, forgive us for putting our focus in the wrong place. We will no longer exalt our own feelings; we will exalt your truth. Reach out and touch us, as you once touched those three disciples lying face down on the ground, and say to us: “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”

Holy Spirit, help us to begin practising today: the moment the language of fear appears, we will turn to you; whenever we want to hide, we will reach out and connect with our brothers and sisters. Take us from being a lonely drop of water and gather us into your river of living water, so that in unity we may see your glory.
Lord, when we lift up our eyes, may we see no one, except you alone. Reign as King within us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “The man said, ‘I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.’” (Genesis 3:10) Think back to the last time fear welled up in your heart. What were you looking at then — your circumstances, other people, or yourself? How did you “cover” or “hide”? Please share one specific example.

Question 2: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12) Who is the “2” in your life right now — the spiritual companion you are willing to be honest with about your struggles? If you don’t have one yet, whom could you reach out to this week? Pray for one another, and agree to follow up with each other next time you meet.
l016.title: Seeing Self Brings Fear
l016.subtitle: When Our Focus Turns to Ourselves, Fear Swallows Up Faith
l016.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Greatest Distance Is the Silence Under One Roof
sections.html:
A couple who had been married for more than twenty years came to see their pastor. They hadn’t been fighting or throwing things; they sat at either end of the sofa with an empty seat between them. The wife said, “We haven’t had a proper conversation in three months.” The husband, head bowed, added, “Actually, we see each other every day. It’s just that we stopped living in the same house a long time ago.”

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that the greatest distance between two people is not high mountains and long rivers, not the ends of the earth, but two people sitting right next to each other while their hearts draw back, inch by inch?

The Bible has a name for this drawing back. It is called “separation”.

Separation makes no sound. It isn’t fierce like an argument or glaring like a betrayal. It is quiet, slow and perfectly polite. It simply makes you reply to one message fewer, go to one meeting fewer, speak one honest word fewer, take one step fewer towards someone. But by the time you come to your senses, that invisible wall has already been built high and thick.

Today we are going to face a very important question together: why does separation happen?

Right at the start, the lesson uncovers the first layer of the answer — separation is not neutral; it is Satan’s weapon. Then the lesson helps us see Jesus: he came to restore relationships. And then the lesson names the first cause of separation in a single word: comparison.

The theme verse for this lesson is just one short sentence, yet it is the key to the whole lesson: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order in this sentence. First “no one”, then “Jesus alone”. When our eyes move off people and our focus turns to Christ, comparison stops; when comparison stops, fear fades; when fear fades, the wall of separation comes down.

This is the core practice of Kingdom 321: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

This morning, let’s lift up our eyes together. May the Holy Spirit help us take down, one by one, the walls that have long fallen into disrepair yet still stand between us and other people.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: “Jesus Alone” on the Mount of Transfiguration
sections.html:
Our theme verse is Matthew 17:8. To really grasp the weight of this sentence, we have to go back up that mountain.

(1) Author, date and audience

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, also called Levi, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9). A man his own people regarded as a traitor and the religious world regarded as a sinner was called by Jesus to be a disciple. That fact is itself a footnote to this lesson: from the very beginning, Jesus was tearing down the walls between people.

Evangelical scholars generally hold that Matthew’s Gospel was written around AD 60–70, mainly for Jewish Christians. The book quotes the Old Testament more than sixty times, and everywhere it sets out to prove one thing: Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the son of David, the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1).

But Matthew is also the only one of the four Gospels to use the word “church” explicitly (Matthew 16:18; 18:17). In other words, Matthew wants people not only to know the King, but to enter the King’s community. Knowing Jesus is life; entering the community is relationships — this is exactly what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.”

(2) The context

The Transfiguration in chapter 17 follows straight on from chapter 16. In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:15–16) Immediately afterwards, the Lord said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed and rise on the third day. But Peter took him aside and tried to talk him out of it, and the Lord turned and rebuked him: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men.” (Matthew 16:23)

Brothers and sisters, notice: it was just when the disciples were at their most confused, most prone to comparing themselves with each other, most eager to argue about who was the greatest, that Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain.

“After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:1–2)

Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Jesus. The moment Peter saw them, he said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” (Matthew 17:4)

Brothers and sisters, what lies hidden in Peter’s words? The most natural and the most deadly of human habits — ranking, comparing, grading. Three tents means three positions; three positions means a league table. Once people start a league table, their eyes fill with “who is greater than whom”, and cracks begin to appear in relationships.

How did God respond? “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5) The disciples fell on their faces, terribly afraid. Jesus came and touched them and said, “Get up, and don’t be afraid.”

And then comes our theme verse for today: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

(3) The threefold message of this verse

First, the three tents were never built. The league table people wanted, God blew away with a single sentence.

Second, Moses stood for the Law and Elijah for the Prophets; both Old Testament giants withdrew, and only Jesus remained. Hebrews says, “God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son.” (Hebrews 1:1–2) There is only one focus.

Third, the tone of “no one” in the original is that they raised their eyes and looked all around, and apart from Jesus they could see no one else. It doesn’t mean that people vanished; it means that when Christ is lifted up, other people are no longer the ruler we measure ourselves by.

Brothers and sisters, this is the key to the lesson. Comparison is “lifting up our eyes and seeing only people”; faith is “lifting up our eyes and seeing only Jesus”. Today’s lesson is learning to move our eyes off people and back onto the Lord.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Separation Is Not Neutral — It Is Satan’s Weapon
sections.html:
The lesson comes straight to the point: Satan doesn’t only want people to drift away from God; he wants them separated from one another.

(1) The first scene of separation: the Garden of Eden

The first human separation happened at the moment of the Fall. “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8)

Notice the order: the moment humans sinned, their first reaction was to hide from God. That is separation from God. Then God came and questioned him, and Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” (Genesis 3:12) In one sentence he shifted the blame onto his wife — and onto God. That is separation from people.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? When sin comes in, separation follows right behind. Satan has never changed his methods: first he cuts you off from God, then he cuts you off from people, and finally he sets you at odds even with yourself.

This is exactly what 321 says: the root sickness of the old self is the self-centred life. Self-centred people make themselves the centre of everything, and people who make themselves the centre inevitably push others away. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; and every time we leave our originally intended position, it leaves a crack in our relationships.

(2) The thief comes to steal, kill and destroy

The lesson quotes the words of the Lord Jesus. In full they read: “The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

This verse sets out two very clear lines. Satan’s line is stealing, killing and destroying; Jesus’ line is life, and life more abundant.

What does Satan steal? Our unity. What does Satan kill? Our relationships. What does Satan destroy? God’s purpose that we should “all be one”.

In his high-priestly prayer before his Passion, the Lord Jesus said: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the last phrase — “that the world may believe”. Unity isn’t just a slightly nicer atmosphere; unity is the evidence for the gospel. And so that evidence is precisely what Satan attacks.

In Life Together, Bonhoeffer gives a weighty warning: the person who loves his dream of community more than the actual community becomes a destroyer of community. Brothers and sisters, we seldom leave a group because we hate it; we usually leave because that group “doesn’t quite match the picture in my head”. This is the most respectable kind of separation, and Satan’s favourite.

(3) Once a member is cut off, the result is death

The lesson uses a very powerful image: we are members of the body of Christ. Paul says, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” (1 Corinthians 12:27) And again: “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

A finger separated from the hand doesn’t become freer; within minutes it begins to die. Because life isn’t in the finger; life is in the body.

This is not just an image; it is a measurable fact. In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad, a psychologist at Brigham Young University in the United States, and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine combining 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand participants. The results showed that people with strong social connections had about a 50 per cent higher likelihood of survival than those who lacked them. In further research in 2015 she found that loneliness raises the risk of death by about 26 per cent, and social isolation by about 29 per cent. In 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, issued an advisory on “Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation”, stating that the harm of social disconnection to health is comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes a day.

Brothers and sisters, science is only saying again, with data, what the Bible said long ago: a member cut off from the body dies.

So the lesson draws a conclusion, and I ask you to keep it in your heart: the final result of separation is not independence; it is death.

People who leave the church slowly dry up spiritually; people who cut themselves off from others grow harder and lonelier at heart; couples who choose a cold war at home lose the warmth of their relationship drop by drop. A cold war sheds no blood, but it lets love slowly lose its heat — and losing heat is also a way to die.

(4) Applying 321

321 says the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Satan attacks every single link in that chain. So we must be very clear-headed: when you notice yourself starting to want to avoid people, to leave the group chat, to be “fine on my own”, most of the time that is not maturity; that is a battlefield.

Lord, give us eyes to discern: separation is not neutral. It is never simply a matter of personality, or simply of being busy. It is a weapon, and the one holding it is the evil one.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Jesus Came to Restore Relationships
sections.html:
How warmly the lesson puts it: thank the Lord, Jesus didn’t come to rebuke us, but to restore our relationship with God and with others.

(1) He came to break down the dividing wall

Paul says of Christ: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation,” (Ephesians 2:14)

In those days “the middle wall of separation” was a physical thing. Between the outer and inner courts of the Second Temple stood a stone barrier, engraved with warnings in Greek and Latin: any Gentile who crosses this boundary does so at his own risk, and the penalty is death. One wall divided people into two kinds: those who may come near, and those who may not.

Paul says that Christ tore down this wall on the cross. He goes on: “and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it.” (Ephesians 2:16)

Brothers and sisters, the cross has a vertical beam and a horizontal one. The vertical beam restores our relationship with God; the horizontal beam restores our relationship with others. Take away either one, and it is no longer a cross.

(2) He chose not a palace but a manger

The lesson reminds us: he could have chosen to be born in a palace, but he chose a manger, because he would not be separated from people.

“She gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in bands of cloth, and laid him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them in the inn.” (Luke 2:7)

A palace has guards, gates and ranks; a manger has no door. So that night the wise men from the east could come, and the shepherds keeping watch over their flocks in the fields could come too. Scholars and shepherds, rich and poor, knelt for the first time before the same baby. Brothers and sisters, the very first scene of salvation is a scene without walls.

The place where he grew up was the same. The people of Nazareth said, “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” (Matthew 13:55) He chose to grow up in a carpenter’s family, planing wood day after day, mending roofs, paying the rent, because he wanted to live among people. The Word became flesh and lived among us (John 1:14) — and the word “lived” in the original carries the sense of “pitching a tent”. He doesn’t shout to us from behind the clouds; he pitches his tent right next door to ours.

(3) He drew near to sinners, embraced children and touched the sick

The lesson says: in Jesus’ ministry we see him drawing near to sinners, embracing children and touching the sick, paying no attention to the world’s opinion, all to close the distance between himself and people.

He drew near to sinners. “The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, ‘This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them.’” (Luke 15:2) In that culture, eating at the same table meant identifying with someone, accepting them. They meant this as an accusation, without realising that it is the very definition of the gospel.

He embraced children. The disciples rebuked those who brought children to him, but the Lord was indignant and said, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.” “He took them in his arms, and blessed them, laying his hands on them.” (Mark 10:14, 16)

He touched the sick. A man with leprosy came and pleaded with him. Under the law of Moses, this man was not to be touched, and Jesus could perfectly well have healed him with a single word. But the Bible says: “Jesus stretched out his hand, and touched him, saying, ‘I want to. Be made clean.’ Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.” (Matthew 8:3) Brothers and sisters, that man may not have been touched by anyone for years. The Lord knew that sickness can be healed with a word, but loneliness has to be healed with a touch.

(4) An example from life, and a piece of research

A brother once told me that while he was in hospital, the messages he received most were “Hang in there!” But what really made him cry was a pastor’s wife who said nothing at all — she just sat by his bed and held his hand for fifteen minutes.

In 2003 the social neuroscientist Naomi Eisenberger of the University of California, Los Angeles, and her colleagues published a study in the journal Science. They found that when people were excluded by a group in an experiment, the brain region activated (the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) overlapped heavily with the region activated by physical pain. In plain words: being left out really does hurt — and the brain counts it as that kind of pain.

Brothers and sisters, this is why Jesus “touched”. He wasn’t only dealing with disease; he was dealing with the pain of being shut out.

(5) Applying 321

321 says: Jesus is my role model. So when it comes to “relationships”, what is Jesus’ role model for us? Taking the initiative, humbling himself, drawing near, setting no threshold.

321 also says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Notice that “relationships” comes before “ministry”. We often work very hard while our relationships run up debt all the way. That is not the Lord’s order. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The lesson concludes: unity is his mission; separation is Satan’s scheme. If you and I want to live in the likeness of Jesus, we must break free from the snare of separation and learn to connect with people and be one with God.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Why Does Separation Happen? The First Cause — Comparison
sections.html:
The lesson goes to the heart of it: why does separation happen? The first cause is comparison.

(1) Comparison defined, and the Scripture

Paul puts it very strongly: “For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

“Without understanding” in the original means having no insight, being unwise. Paul’s point is that using people as a ruler is foolish in itself, because the ruler keeps changing. Today you beat this person; tomorrow you meet that one. You come out ahead in this, and fall behind in something else. Measure yourself with a moving ruler, and you can measure for a lifetime without ever arriving at peace.

Ecclesiastes saw through this long ago: “Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.” (Ecclesiastes 4:4) So the motive behind all our striving, much of the time, isn’t love; it’s not wanting to lose.

Proverbs says, “The life of the body is a heart at peace, but envy rots the bones.” (Proverbs 14:30) Rot starts from the inside: the outside still looks fine while the bones are already hollow. Comparison is that kind of disease: it doesn’t shout or make a scene; it just slowly eats away the joy inside you.

(2) Comparison → fear → separation: Satan’s favourite strategy

The lesson gives us a very clear chain: comparison makes us anxious, envious and afraid, and in the end it makes us separate. Comparison → fear → separation.

Why does comparison breed fear? Because the moment I compare, my worth is placed somewhere others can overtake it at any time. Since I could be overtaken at any time, I have to be on my guard; since I have to be on my guard, I can’t get too close; since I can’t get too close, separation is born.

The apostle John gives us the antidote: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment. He who fears is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: what deals with fear is not trying harder to win, but experiencing love more deeply. You don’t have to beat anyone to deserve to be loved; in Christ you are already loved.

(3) Confirmation from psychology

In 1954 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward “social comparison theory” in the journal Human Relations. He argued that people have a basic drive to evaluate their abilities and worth by comparing themselves with others. When an objective standard is lacking, people automatically take those around them as the standard.

Festinger was describing, not promising. He described a human tendency; the Bible sets out to change that tendency. Paul says, “But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.” (Galatians 6:4) God gives each person a different measure; he asks only whether you have been faithful, not whether you have won.

Today this tendency has been magnified countless times over. In 2012 Hui-Tzu Grace Chou and Nicholas Edge published a study in the journal Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking whose very title was “They Are Happier and Having Better Lives than I Am”. They found that the more often people browsed social media, the more likely they were to believe that other people’s lives were happier than their own. Brothers and sisters, what we scroll past on our phones every day is usually other people’s carefully chosen highlights, and what we compare them with is our own unedited everyday life. That contest is unfair from the very start.

(4) A parable

A piano teacher once said something very wise: if a student keeps his attention on the practice room next door, his fingers will never play well, because his ears aren’t on his own piano.

Comparison is putting your ears in someone else’s practice room. Your hands are still on your own keys, but your heart left long ago. No wonder there’s no music.

In Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis says that pride is essentially competitive — people are proud not of having something, but of having more of it than others. That goes straight to the heart of it: the root of comparison is pride.

(5) Applying 321

321 says: pride is the root of the problem; humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Comparison is the classic symptom of the self-centred life. Self-centred people have to keep confirming where they stand, so they have to keep measuring and comparing. Selfless people don’t. Because selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

In The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness, Pastor Timothy Keller wrote a line that is often quoted: gospel humility is not thinking more of myself or thinking less of myself; it is thinking of myself less. Brothers and sisters, that is “selflessness” — not putting yourself down, but no longer needing to think about yourself all the time.

That is why our theme verse is so precious: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8) Comparison looks at people; faith looks at Jesus.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: An Example from Scripture — Saul and David
sections.html:
The lesson gives a heartbreaking example, one that acts out every step of “comparison → fear → separation” before our eyes.

(1) It began with affection
