King Saul was fond of David at first. Because David was skilled at playing the lyre, he was summoned to serve at the palace. The Bible says, “David came to Saul, and stood before him. He loved him greatly; and he became his armor bearer.” (1 Samuel 16:21)

Brothers and sisters, remember this verse. Their relationship wasn’t bad from the start. Many broken relationships were beautiful at the beginning. The problem isn’t how they began, but what happened along the way.

(2) A song that stirred up comparison

After David killed Goliath, the Israelites came home victorious. “The women sang to one another as they played, and said, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.’” (1 Samuel 18:7)

To be fair, this song was praising Saul. “Saul has slain his thousands” was very high praise. But Saul didn’t take in a word of it. He heard only one thing: David’s number is bigger than mine.

“Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, ‘They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?’ Saul watched David from that day and forward.” (1 Samuel 18:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, this is how terrible comparison is. Comparison makes you hear a compliment as a threat. Comparison makes you hear your own death knell in someone else’s good news. The original says Saul “watched” David — eyed him — and the word carries the sense of a continual, unrelenting stare. From that day on, Saul could never take his eyes off David. His focus had changed — no longer God, no longer the nation, but that man.

(3) Comparison breeds fear

The Bible goes on: “Saul was afraid of David, because Yahweh was with him, and had departed from Saul.” (1 Samuel 18:12)

Notice the order: first anger, then the hostile stare, then fear. On the surface it was anger; underneath it was all fear. The voice in Saul’s heart was just what the lesson describes: “Will he replace me? Will he take my place?”

Brothers and sisters, let me be honest: nine times out of ten, when we lose our temper it isn’t because we are strong, but because we are afraid. Afraid of being replaced, afraid of being looked down on, afraid of being outshone.

(4) Fear breeds separation

And then separation came. “Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.” (1 Samuel 18:13)

See how cleverly this was done. Saul didn’t drive David away; he promoted him. On the surface it was a vote of confidence; in reality it was a transfer. The title “captain over a thousand” bought the words “removed him from his presence”.

Brothers and sisters, in the church, at work, in the family, how much separation is accomplished in this respectable way? I haven’t fallen out with you; I just don’t consult you any more. I haven’t kicked you out; I’ve just moved you to another group. I haven’t said I don’t want you; I’m just “giving you more room to grow”.

The words of separation are often very polite, but the results of separation never are.

(5) How separation ends

The lesson is right: separation doesn’t solve the problem; it ends in broken relationships, a divided kingdom and one’s own ruin.

From then on Saul threw his spear at David, sent men to lie in wait for him, hunted him into the wilderness, slaughtered eighty-five priests of the city of Nob (1 Samuel 22:18), and finally died by his own hand on Mount Gilboa (1 Samuel 31:4). And the very thing he feared — David taking the throne — was not delayed by a single day because of his separation.

This is exactly what 321 says: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose. Saul wanted to hold on to his throne, and he lost it; he wanted to get rid of a threat, and he got rid of his most loyal servant.

By contrast, how different David’s response was. When Saul was asleep in the cave, David’s men said his chance had come, but David only cut off the corner of his robe, and afterwards his heart struck him, and he said: “Yahweh forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, Yahweh’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is Yahweh’s anointed.” (1 Samuel 24:6)

Brothers and sisters, why was David able not to take revenge? Because David’s focus wasn’t on Saul; it was on God. He didn’t need to knock someone else down to keep himself safe, because the one who had set him up was God, not himself.

This is humility drawing out humility, so that both sides win. Saul lifted his eyes and saw only David, and so he lost everything; David lifted his eyes and saw only Yahweh, and so he gained everything.

(6) A reminder

Saul’s tragedy didn’t begin with killing; it began with listening to a song. A song, a remark, a number, a post — the seeds of comparison are often too small to mention. But if a seed isn’t dealt with, it grows into a tree, the tree bears the fruit of fear, and when the fruit falls, it is separation.

So we have to deal with it at the seed stage. And that is exactly what the lesson’s first practice asks us to do.

sections.heading: 7. Key Point 5: Today’s Church Often Falls into the Trap of Comparison Too
sections.html:
The lesson very honestly turns the mirror on us. It lists three common situations.

(1) Small churches fear that big churches will steal their people

They worry that their members will be lured away by a big church’s programmes, venue and choir. So now and then things are said from the pulpit that sound like reminders but are really defence.

(2) Big churches fear that small churches will be a burden

They worry about too many needs, resources being divided, being tied down by responsibilities. So they politely keep their distance, and cooperation never gets past “let’s wait and see”.

(3) Denominations separate from one another

Over differences in speaking in tongues, worship style, views of the end times, church government and how often to take Communion, they separate from one another, refuse to cooperate, and even attack each other.

The lesson puts its finger right on it: behind these actions that look like “standing for pure faith” lies, in fact, the fear and insecurity brought on by “comparison” that has never been dealt with.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand me. Pure faith must be held fast, the boundaries of truth must be clear, and heresy must be discerned. For the truth of the gospel, the apostle Paul once opposed Cephas to his face (Galatians 2:11). But we must honestly ask ourselves one question: is my insistence this time really for the truth, or for saving face? Is it to guard God’s glory, or to guard my position?

Telling the difference isn’t actually hard. Someone who separates for the sake of truth feels sorrow in their heart; someone who separates because of comparison feels a thrill. When we hear that another church has run into trouble, if a flicker of relief crosses our heart, that is a warning sign.

Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.” (Romans 12:15) This verse is the best thermometer for testing separation. When others are honoured, can I be genuinely glad? When others fall, can my heart genuinely ache?

“When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26)

(4) An example from nature

California’s redwoods are the tallest trees on earth, growing to more than a hundred metres. You’d expect trees that tall to have very deep taproots, but the truth is quite the opposite: redwood roots are shallow, usually only two or three metres deep, yet they spread out sideways for tens of metres, tightly intertwined with the roots of the redwoods beside them. A redwood standing alone would fall in a strong wind; a redwood forest, holding hands, stands even against a hurricane.

Brothers and sisters, the church is a redwood forest. We can stand tall not because each of us has rooted deeply on our own, but because we are tightly bound to one another.

Geese are the same. In 1970, Lissaman and Shollenberger published an aerodynamic analysis in the journal Science showing that birds flying in V formation, by using the upwash from the wingtips of the companion ahead, can increase the flock’s range by as much as 71 per cent compared with flying alone. The lead goose works hardest, so they take turns; the geese behind keep honking to encourage those in front.

God has already written his purpose into his creatures: fly together, and you fly far.

(5) Applying 321

321 says the Goal is to establish God’s system. A system is not an institution; it is a network of relationships. Satan has his system too, and it runs on comparison, competition and fear; God’s system runs on humility, connection and love.

Every time we choose not to compare, choose to draw near, choose to bless, we are dismantling Satan’s system and establishing God’s system.

The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) The psalm goes on to say that it is like the precious oil on the head, like the dew of Hermon, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

Brothers and sisters, the place where the blessing is commanded is “there” — where brothers live together in unity. If you leave that place, the blessing won’t run after you.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Comparison to Unity
sections.html:
(1) The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model. In relationships, Jesus’ role model is to set up no walls, set no limits and take the initiative to draw near. He chose not the palace but the manger, not the throne but the cross.

The Bible is my standard. When the voice of comparison speaks up, we don’t take our feelings as the standard; we take God’s word as the standard: “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Unity isn’t something people squeeze out by effort. Paul says, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) Notice that it is the unity “of the Spirit” — given by the Spirit; our responsibility is not to manufacture unity but to “keep” it.

Let Jesus be King. Saul’s problem, in the end, was that he would not let God be King; he wanted to be king himself. Everyone who makes himself king sees other people as rivals.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. When all the glory goes to him, we don’t have to scramble for the few crumbs that could never go round anyway. If the glory goes to me, there’s never enough to share; if the glory goes to the Lord, there’s always enough.

Establish God’s system. God’s system is a system without separation, a family where people care for one another and build one another up.

(2) The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

Comparison is the self-centred life’s most honest confession. Someone who is still comparing is saying: my worth needs other people falling behind to prove it.

But the new self in Christ doesn’t have to live like that. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, if the “I” has already been crucified, who is left who needs to win?

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. When you no longer need to prove yourself, you are truly free for the first time.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Saul wanted to take God’s place in deciding who would be king, and so he destroyed himself; David let God be God, and so God lifted him up.

(3) The fivefold change

Change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes.

You can’t deal with comparison by starting with behaviour; you have to start with mindset. If deep down you still believe “my worth depends on my ranking”, however hard you suppress envy, it will still break out through some other crack. The mindset must change first: my worth has been set by Jesus with his precious blood, not by other people’s results.

(4) A shift of perspective

From the human perspective to God’s: what Saul heard was a league table; what God saw was a servant after his own heart.

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: on earth there is only one seat at the top; in heaven a seat is prepared for every overcomer.

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: thousands and tens of thousands of battle honours will be forgotten in thirty years; but the step you take today towards someone you feel distant from will remain in eternity.

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the world says you only have worth if you beat others; God says that in Christ you are already loved.

(5) The 920 practice and the 235 relationship

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. This week, whoever God places beside you is your “2”. And the way to practise is to live out the selfless “0” — laying yourself down and letting the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces grows in separation. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; peace needs someone to be at peace with. God has placed that person who makes you uncomfortable beside you not to torment you, but to bear fruit in you.

The 235 relationship: become a “2” with someone who is selfless, as spiritual companions; establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10)

Comparison turns us into one person on our own; connection makes us two, three, a fivefold team. Satan wants you on your own, because someone on their own is the easiest to deal with.

sections.heading: 9. Putting It into Practice: Training a Mindset That Removes Separation
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s work them through thoroughly using 321’s “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Notice the seeds of comparison

This week, watch whether you are comparing yourself with others without realising it: comparing work, gifts, service, achievements, families, churches.

Whenever you catch yourself thinking this way, say to the Lord: “Lord, I won’t look at people, and I won’t look at myself; I will see only you!”

Information: first accept a fact — comparison is a human instinct, not a sign that you are especially bad. Festinger’s 1954 social comparison theory has already shown that people naturally use those around them as a ruler.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light so you can see where you are most prone to compare. Usually that is the area where you feel least secure.

Conviction: believe God’s word over your feelings — “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12)

Implementation: this week, carry a small card or open a page in your phone’s notes; every time a comparing thought arises, make a mark and immediately say that declaration.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look at that page. What do you compare most — ability, appearance, achievement, or other people’s praise?

Correction: for the item that comes up most, find a verse of God’s word and memorise it; tomorrow morning, read that verse before you switch on your phone.

Repetition: not for a week, but for a lifetime. Lifting your eyes is a single movement, yet you have to keep doing it all your life.

Multiplication: tell a spiritual companion about this practice, and do it together, checking in with each other.

Practice 2: Stop spreading words of comparison

When we keep repeating things like “Such-and-such church is amazing,” “Look, he’s better than you,” or “Why can’t we measure up to others?”, these words not only trap us in comparison but also push others into fear and competition.

This week, practise turning words like these into: “God has a different plan and a different grace for every person and every church.”

Information: words have power. “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” (Proverbs 18:21)

Revelation: listen to your own mouth. When you praise one child, do you casually put down another? When you praise one church, do you casually take a swipe at your own?

Conviction: believe that one sentence from me can plant fear in someone’s heart — or plant a blessing there.

Implementation: this week, make a rule — never give praise that compares two people. If you praise, praise someone on their own; if you correct, correct someone on their own.

Evaluation: every night before bed, ask one question: did the words I spoke today draw people closer or push them away?

Correction: if you got it wrong, go back the next day and add a sincere word of blessing.

Repetition: keep it up for thirty days in a row, until the new way of speaking becomes a habit.

Multiplication: share it in your small group and invite everyone to make this commitment together.

Practice 3: Take the initiative to connect with someone you feel “distant” from

This week, choose someone you have drifted away from because of a misunderstanding, a difference of opinion or comparison, and take one step towards reconciliation: send a message to say hello, invite them for a coffee, or pray for them and bless them.

The lesson says: being one with others is the greatest weapon for defeating Satan’s scheme of separation.

Information: the Lord says, “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23–24) The Lord didn’t say to wait until you feel like it; he said go first.

Revelation: be still for three minutes and let the Holy Spirit place a name on your heart. The first name that comes to mind is usually the one.

Conviction: believe that the one who takes the initiative is not the loser but the overcomer.

Implementation: send that message today. Don’t explain the past; just say hello to the present. A simple “How are you doing these days? I thought of you and prayed for you” is enough.

Evaluation: the other person may respond warmly, or coolly, or not at all. Either way, you have taken down the wall on your side.

Correction: if the first step is too big, make it smaller; if the timing isn’t right, pray first and try again in a month.

Repetition: reach out to one person every month, and in a year twelve walls will have come down.

Multiplication: when you have tasted the joy of reconciliation, tell others about it, so they too find the courage to take that step.

A Gentle Reminder: Comparison looks at people; faith looks at Jesus

The lesson ends with this reminder: when we take our eyes off people and turn from competition to Christ, we discover that in Christ we have long since received grace, been loved and been accepted, and we don’t need comparison to prove ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this is our theme verse: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call: Choose Unity, and You Are Walking the Road of Revival
sections.html:
The lesson’s conclusion is weighty, and it is right: the church is not an arena; it is God’s family.

The rule of the arena is: if someone wins, someone has to lose. The rule of the family is: when one does well, the whole family does well.

If we separate because of comparison, we give Satan an opening and rob God’s family of its power. A divided army is defeated before the enemy lifts a finger.

So the lesson calls us: let us learn to be like Jesus, willing to take the initiative to draw near to anyone at all, regardless of status, setting up no barriers. Let us accept one another, build one another up, and become vessels of unity in God’s hands.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King. No longer let comparison be king, no longer let fear be king, no longer let “I have to win” be king. Hand the throne back to the Lord who alone is worthy of it.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When someone else is lifted up and you can say in your heart, “Amen, may the glory go to the Lord,” in that moment you have already overcome.

Third, lift up your eyes. Today, right now, take your eyes off the person who unsettles you and raise your head — see no one, except Jesus alone.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, running continuously since 1938, has followed several hundred men throughout their lives, tracking their health and happiness. Its director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled more than eighty years of findings into one sentence: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Not wealth, not fame, not rankings.

God wrote this truth into Genesis long ago: “Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone.’” (Genesis 2:18)

Brothers and sisters, it is not good to be alone. Unity is good.

Let us make the lesson’s declaration of faith together: Lord Jesus, I will not let comparison separate me; I choose unity, to bear witness to your love and your glory!

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Notice the seeds of comparison
Stop spreading words of comparison
Reach out to someone you feel “distant” from
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You came not to rebuke us, but to restore our relationship with God and with others. You broke down the dividing wall; you chose the manger rather than the palace; you reached out and touched the one no one else dared to touch. Lord, you are our role model.

Lord, we confess that there is comparison in us. We compare our work, our gifts, our service, our achievements, our families, our churches. Comparison makes us anxious, anxiety makes us afraid, and fear makes us draw back step by step, building one invisible wall after another. Please forgive us.
Take Saul’s eyes away from us and give us David’s heart — not looking at people, not looking at ourselves, but looking to you alone.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on us, and show us the name of the one we have drawn away from; and give us courage to take a step towards reconciliation today.

Lord, we hand the throne to you. Reign as King, and receive all the glory. Use us in our families, our churches and our workplaces as vessels of unity, as people who tear down walls, to establish God’s system.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: “For we are not bold to number or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding.” (2 Corinthians 10:12) Please share honestly: what was the most recent comparison that left you feeling uneasy? Underneath that unease, what was the real fear?

Question 2: “Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.” (1 Samuel 18:13) Saul accomplished separation by “promotion”. In your own life, is there a relationship where you are keeping your distance in some respectable way? What concrete action are you willing to take this week to make the first step towards reconciliation?
l017.title: Comparison Brings Separation
l017.subtitle: Why Separation Happens (Part 1)
l017.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: A Wall No One Built
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin by asking you to picture something.

Two co-workers in ministry, once as close as brothers. Same church, same small group, same table at mealtimes. Then one day, one of them passes the other in the corridor without saying hello. The other notices, and something inside him lurches: Is he angry with me? Has he heard something? Does he think what I said last time was too harsh?

From that moment on, the thought moves in and stays.

The next day he deliberately avoids that corridor. The day after, he slips out early after the meeting. A month later the two of them are still in the same church, still sitting in the same row of chairs — but a wall has gone up between them.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: no one lifted a hand to build that wall. No one quarrelled, no one fell out, no one said a single harsh word. The wall grew up inside, brick by brick. And it was built from only two materials: a suspicion never checked, and a hurt never dealt with.

That is the subject we have to face today.

In our last lesson we saw together the first root of separation — comparison. Comparison takes our eyes off Jesus and fixes them on other people, and then it is either pride or inferiority, and relationships begin to warp. Today we go further and look at the second and third roots: suspicion, and unforgiveness.

I have to be honest with you at the outset: these two are the quietest and the deadliest killers in the church.

They are quiet because they never need open conflict. They are deadly because they dissolve unity from the inside, and the people caught up in them usually go on believing, right to the end, that they are in the right.

Satan knows this. He knows it all too well.

In 2 Corinthians chapter 2, Paul happens to be dealing with a matter of forgiveness. He urges the Corinthian church to forgive a brother who had fallen, and then he says something very weighty: “that no advantage may be gained over us by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Corinthians 2:11).

Brothers and sisters, follow Paul’s logic carefully. He isn’t talking about spiritual warfare in the abstract. He’s talking about something very concrete: someone in the church has wronged everyone, and now — will they forgive him or not? Paul says that if they don’t forgive, Satan gains the advantage and gets the better of us.

In other words, unforgiveness hands the keys of the house to the enemy.

1 Peter 5:8 says, “Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). A lion on the hunt has a habit: it doesn’t chase the whole herd of antelope. It fixes on one — the one that has strayed off on its own. Satan’s strategy has never been a frontal assault on the whole church. It is to find a way to get you on your own.

How does he get you on your own? He doesn’t need to send you a disaster. He only needs to give you a thought.

“What did that look of his just now mean?”

“They must have been talking about me behind my back.”

“I’ve been so good to him, and this is how he treats me.”

A thought costs nothing, and yet it is the most expensive thing there is. If a thought is not handed over to Jesus, in three months it’s a wall, and in three years it’s a chasm.

So in this lesson we are going to do something very practical together: take up the Lord’s hammer and knock the wall down.

We’ll look at how two walls get built, and how they can be torn down. The first wall is called “suspicion,” and it goes up in this order: suspicion, misunderstanding, separation. The second wall is called “unforgiveness,” and it goes up in this order: hurt, unforgiveness, separation.

And then we’ll come back to our theme verse — the one and only secret for tearing walls down: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: That One Look on the Mountaintop
sections.html:
To feel the weight of this verse, we first need to climb a mountain.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, a disciple of the Lord Jesus, also called Levi, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum. It is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians. That is why Matthew keeps quoting the Old Testament and saying again and again, “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through the prophet.” He wants to prove one thing to his own people: Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah the Old Testament promised.

The Transfiguration in chapter 17 is the turning point of the whole book.

Just before it, in chapter 16, two great things happened. First, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, Peter confessed, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Second, the Lord Jesus said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed and rise on the third day. Peter took hold of him on the spot to talk him out of it, and was sharply rebuked by the Lord. In those few days the disciples’ hearts were in turmoil: up and down, understanding and confused all at once.

Then Matthew writes: “After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves. He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:1–2).

Suddenly Moses and Elijah appeared, talking with Jesus.

To the Jews, these two were no ordinary figures. Moses stood for the Law, and Elijah for the Prophets. The whole Old Testament is the Law and the Prophets. In that moment, the two greatest pillars of the Old Testament were standing there together, talking with Jesus.

Peter’s reaction is so typical of him. He said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at where Peter’s problem lay.

It wasn’t that he was ungodly — he was very godly. It wasn’t that he didn’t love the Lord — he loved him dearly. He was even willing to do the building with his own hands. His problem was just one thing: three tents.

Three tents mean three focal points. He put Jesus at the same height as Moses and Elijah — one tent each, all on an equal footing. And that is the mistake we most easily make: not throwing Jesus out, but bringing other things in and seating them side by side with Jesus.

The Father didn’t let Peter finish.

“While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.’” (Matthew 17:5)

The disciples fell on their faces, terrified. And then comes the tenderest verse in the whole chapter: “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 17:7).

Right after that comes our theme verse for today: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

Notice the two actions in this verse.

The first is “lifting up their eyes.” The original means to raise the eyes. They had been lying face down, eyes on the dirt, eyes on their own fear. The moment the Lord touched them, they lifted their heads.

The second is “they saw no one.” Moses was gone; Elijah was gone. The three-tent plan was cancelled of its own accord.

Brothers and sisters, this verse isn’t saying that Moses and Elijah don’t matter. It’s saying that only when Jesus is the one and only focal point do things fall back into their proper places. The Law was not abolished, the Prophets were not rejected; they simply returned to where they belong — pointing to Jesus.

That is the key to this whole lesson.

Why is there suspicion? Because when we lift up our eyes, what we see is people: their motives, their expressions, their tone of voice. Why is there unforgiveness? Because when we lift up our eyes, what we see is still people: what they owe me, how they hurt me, the apology they still haven’t made.

And the secret of unity, from beginning to end, is a single sentence: see no one else but Jesus.

The 321 way of putting it is this: the old self lives the self-centred life; the new self lives in selflessness. A self-centred person always has an “I” standing in the very middle of the picture; everyone else is cast as a supporting character, and everything is read as either good for me or bad for me. In the selfless person’s picture, only Jesus stands at the centre. That is how walls come down.

Satan’s tactic: getting people to choose separation because of the cracks in their hearts

Before we come to our two key points, we need to understand how the enemy fights.

Satan knows that the most effective way to destroy unity is not an open attack, but exploiting the breaches between people’s hearts: suspicion, distrust, hurt, unforgiveness.

Notice that word “breach.” The enemy doesn’t create the breach; the breach is already there. The enemy doesn’t need to build a wall. He only needs to find a crack and breathe into it.

Up in the north I’ve seen a phenomenon engineers call freeze–thaw damage. A concrete wall may look perfectly sound, but if it has a crack as fine as a hair, rainwater seeps in. When winter comes, the water freezes and expands by about nine per cent, forcing that tiny crack a little wider. In spring it thaws, and the water seeps in a little deeper. Winter after winter, and ten years on the whole wall comes down.

From start to finish, no one ever took a hammer to that wall. It was destroyed by one fine crack that was never dealt with.

Brothers and sisters, our relationships are just the same.

These feelings and experiences all seem perfectly reasonable — sometimes they even look like “a victim’s legitimate response.” He really did ignore me. He really did say that. He really did hurt me. All of that may be true. But if it isn’t handed to Jesus to deal with, the facts will ferment into a wall that blocks our unity with others, and our unity with God as well.

On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus prayed for his disciples. He didn’t pray for success, or gifts, or numbers. He prayed, “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

Unity is the deepest longing of the Lord’s heart. And so unity is bound to be the target the enemy most wants to destroy.

Now let’s see how he goes about it.

sections.heading: 2. Suspicion → Misunderstanding → Separation
sections.html:
Suspicion is a tiny seed, but it grows into enormous destruction.

Suspicion makes us twist the facts and read other people’s actions through negative assumptions. Suspicion is not just a psychological reaction; it is a killer of our unity in the Spirit.

One seed, a whole forest

Why do I call it “a tiny seed”?

Because when suspicion comes in, it is always absurdly small. It doesn’t arrive with drums and cymbals announcing, “I’m going to destroy your marriage.” It just asks quietly, “Why did he look at you like that?”

The Lord Jesus told the parable of the mustard seed, which “indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree.” That is how the kingdom of heaven grows, and it is how an evil thought grows too. Plant one thought and leave it unpulled, and it will grow into a tree in your heart. It will bear fruit and scatter seed, and it will teach your children to look at people with the very same eyes.

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase, “the wellspring of life.” Not what flows out over a single day, but over a whole lifetime. The seed you let into your heart today will decide whom you serve alongside, whom you walk with, and whom you go through the gates of heaven with, ten years from now.

An illustration: the faithful dog and his master’s tragedy

There is a heartbreaking story that has been told for more than a thousand years.

It is generally traced to a legend from Beddgelert in Wales, and earlier versions appear in the ancient Indian collection of fables, the Panchatantra. The story goes like this:

A young father had lost his wife and was raising his child alone, and he had trained a faithful dog to watch over the baby. One day the man came home from work to find the dog’s mouth covered in blood, blood in the room — and no child to be seen. His heart went cold. He immediately assumed the dog had eaten his child, and in his fury he drew his knife and killed it. Then he rushed into the inner room — and found the child sleeping safe and sound, and beside the bed a snake the dog had bitten to death.

The dog had saved the child, and died in his master’s suspicion.

The story has lasted a thousand years because it touches the most painful place in the human heart. Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: what did that father lack?

He didn’t lack love — he loved his child dearly. He didn’t lack decisiveness — he acted at once. He lacked only one thing: a question.

Had he taken thirty more seconds, walked a few more steps into the room and looked, the whole tragedy would never have happened.

The story shakes us, and it reminds us that suspicion can lead us to harm the most faithful people with our own hands. And what is even more frightening is that the damage done by suspicion is often irreversible. Once the knife falls, it can’t be taken back. Once the words are spoken, they can’t be taken back. Once the message is sent, it can’t be taken back.

A living lesson in Scripture: the tragedy of Hanun

The Bible records a true event almost exactly like that story.

2 Samuel chapter 10 tells us that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, died, and his son Hanun succeeded him. David remembered the kindness Nahash had once shown him and sent his servants to comfort Hanun. It was pure goodwill.

But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, “Do you think that David honors your father, in that he has sent comforters to you? Hasn’t David sent his servants to you to search the city, to spy it out, and to overthrow it?” (2 Samuel 10:3)

So Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved off half their beards and cut their garments short, and sent them away in deep humiliation.

And the result? A war that need never have happened broke out. The Ammonites hired the Arameans to fight for them, the alliance was crushed, and tens of thousands lost their lives.

Brothers and sisters, trace the line clearly: an act of goodwill, intercepted by one suspicious remark, became a slaughter. From start to finish, David did nothing wrong. Hanun didn’t even send someone to ask, “May I ask what the king meant in sending you?”

The most frightening thing about suspicion is this: it makes you react to the script in your own head rather than to the real person in front of you.

Supporting evidence from psychology: our brains are wired to tell stories

Psychology offers very clear supporting evidence for this.

In his 1958 book The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations, the Austrian-born psychologist Fritz Heider put forward what became attribution theory: human beings are natural “naive psychologists.” Whenever we see a behaviour, we automatically infer the cause behind it — and we won’t rest until we have.

Later, in 1977, the American psychologist Lee Ross gave a name to one of these patterns: the “fundamental attribution error.” When we explain other people’s behaviour, we overestimate their character and underestimate their circumstances; when we explain our own behaviour, we do exactly the opposite.

What does that mean?

Take the same thing — arriving late for a meeting. When someone else is late, we say to ourselves, “He’s just irresponsible.” When we’re late, we say, “The traffic was terrible today; there was nothing I could do.”

Add to that what the British psychologist Peter Wason’s 1960 experiment revealed — “confirmation bias”: once we form a hypothesis, we hunt hard for evidence that supports it and automatically ignore the evidence that overturns it.

Put those two together and you see why suspicion is so hard to stop. First I assume he has ill will towards me, and then my brain starts gathering evidence on my behalf. He didn’t reply to my message today — exhibit one. Yesterday he liked someone else’s post in the group chat — exhibit two. Last week he left early — exhibit three.

A month later I’m holding a thick case file. Every item in it is true, yet the conclusion of the whole file is entirely false.

Brothers and sisters, this is why Proverbs says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). And again, “He who pleads his cause first seems right; until another comes and questions him” (Proverbs 18:17).

When it comes to suspicion, the one who “pleads his cause first” is very often the voice in our own heart.

How suspicion builds a wall, step by step

In marriage, in friendship and in the church, suspicion always works through the same process:

Step one, suspicion breeds misunderstanding. The facts haven’t been checked, but the verdict is already in.

Step two, misunderstanding triggers defensiveness. I start protecting myself: saying a little less, giving a little less, coming a little less close.

Step three, defensiveness turns into distance. On the surface we’re still brothers and sisters; in reality there’s nothing left but politeness.

Step four, distance becomes separation. Two people in the same body, and no contact between them.

If it isn’t dealt with in time, even a healthy relationship will collapse.

The psychologist John Gottman of the University of Washington spent many years studying how married couples interact, and he identified the patterns that most reliably predict a marriage breaking down. One of them is “stonewalling” — when one partner can’t take any more, he doesn’t fight; he shuts down: no response, no eye contact, no reaction.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: what Gottman found is that the most dangerous thing isn’t fighting; it’s not fighting. It isn’t conflict; it’s withdrawal.

That fits exactly with what the Bible teaches. What makes separation so dreadful is not how fierce it is, but how quiet it is.

The way to tear down the wall: the example of Joshua 22

Thank God, the Bible doesn’t only diagnose the disease; it also writes the prescription.

Joshua chapter 22 records something that happened after the Israelites had received the land as their inheritance. The Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh were going home to the east of the Jordan. On the bank of the Jordan they built an altar, a great and imposing one.

When word reached the west of the Jordan, the whole congregation gathered at Shiloh, ready to go up and make war on them.

Notice: by this point suspicion had already completed its first three steps. The misunderstanding was there — they must be setting up a rival altar and rebelling against Yahweh. The defensiveness was there. The distance was there. One more step, and it would be brother against brother, with both sides ruined.

But they did one thing right. Before anything else, they sent Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, with ten leaders, across the river to find out what was really going on.

They asked, and the truth came out: the altar wasn’t for sacrifice at all. It was to stand as a witness — so that in time to come the children on the west bank would not say to the children on the east bank, “You have no portion in Yahweh.” They had built the altar precisely because they cared so much about unity and were afraid their descendants would be shut out.

And so the altar was given a name: “A Witness Between Us.”

Brothers and sisters, what stopped a civil war that was on the very point of breaking out?

Not a prayer meeting, not a prophecy, not anyone backing down. It was one conversation across the river.

Suspicion is the entrance to separation; conversation is the starting point of unity.

The Lord Jesus taught the same: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15).

Look at that one word: “go.” Not brood, not pass it on, not grit your teeth and bear it — go.

Applying 321: your focus determines your interpretation

Here the 321 vision gives us a very practical key.

We often say: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances.

At heart, suspicion is focus in the wrong place. When my focus is on myself, I see everything in terms of “Is this good or bad for me?” When my focus is on others, I start guessing, “What is he really up to?” When my focus is on my circumstances, I live in fear.

Only when my focus returns to Jesus can I stop rushing to a verdict. Because I know: this person is not my provider — Jesus is. This person is not my judge — Jesus is. I can’t see into this person’s heart, but Jesus can, and he is in control.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice.

Suspicion is the classic case of relying on the brain and ourselves. The whole thing happens inside my head from start to finish. Not a word is spoken aloud, nothing is checked; it all runs on inference. And the raw material of the inference is my wounds, my past, my insecurity.

What does it mean to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit? It means bringing that thought straight to the Lord: Lord, a thought has just risen up in my heart, and I don’t know whether it’s true or false. Shine your light on me, and give me the courage to go and ask one question.

Paul says love “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things” (1 Corinthians 13:7).

“Believes all things” isn’t naivety, and it isn’t foolishness. It means this: when the evidence is incomplete, I choose to give the other person the benefit of the doubt. Because I have been that person, the one who most needed someone else to give me the benefit of the doubt.

sections.heading: 3. Hurt → Unforgiveness → Separation
sections.html:
Hurts between people are unavoidable, but the way Satan exploits hurt is by getting us to choose unforgiveness, and so to fall into separation.

Notice the point of that sentence: the hurt itself is not the enemy’s goal; the hurt is only the enemy’s tool. What he really wants is your “response” to the hurt.

At the very moment the hurt happens, the enemy is standing beside you, handing you a key and whispering, “Lock it up. This time you’ve every right.”

And the Bible puts it very bluntly: “Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27).

Brothers and sisters, notice that word “place.” The original means a place, a space, a foothold. Letting the sun go down on your anger is marking off a plot of ground in your own heart and renting it out to the devil. Once he moves in, he won’t keep quiet. He’ll build a house on it, invite his friends, and start collecting rent.

An example from Scripture: Amnon and Absalom

2 Samuel chapter 13 records a heartbreaking family tragedy.

David’s son Amnon schemed to violate his half-sister Tamar. Tamar’s full brother Absalom found out.

Scripture then describes Absalom in one very quiet sentence: “Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad” (2 Samuel 13:22).

Neither good nor bad. On the surface all was calm — no quarrel, no falling out, no complaint. Even David thought the matter was over.

Then Scripture writes: “After two full years” (2 Samuel 13:23).

Two years. For two whole years Absalom ate his meals as usual, paid his respects as usual, attended the royal family feasts as usual. And in his heart, he never once put that knife down.

Two years later, at sheep-shearing time, Absalom held a feast and ordered his servants to kill Amnon when his heart was merry with wine.

And then? Absalom fled to Geshur and did not see his father’s face for three years. After he came back, two more years passed before David would see him. In the end Absalom raised a rebellion, forcing his old father to flee Jerusalem barefoot with his head covered, and he himself died in the forest of Ephraim.

Brothers and sisters, look at this chain of collapse: one hurt, two years of silence, a murder, three years in exile, a civil war, the deaths of two sons, a family shattered.

If hurt is not dealt with and forgiven, it turns into hatred, and in the end into destructive action.

And all of this could have been stopped at the first step. If in those two years Absalom had been willing to bring the matter to God, to bring it to his father, to bring it into the light and deal with it, the whole history of Israel would have been different.

The writer to the Hebrews uses a very vivid picture: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it” (Hebrews 12:15).

A root of bitterness. Roots are underground, out of sight. By the time you see it, it has already cracked the paving stones. And notice: it doesn’t trouble just you; “many” are “defiled by it.” One person’s unforgiveness pollutes the whole community. The root in Absalom’s heart ended up dragging down the whole nation.

Herodias and John the Baptist

Let’s look at another example.

Mark chapter 6 records that John the Baptist was thrown into prison for rebuking Herod’s unlawful marriage. What John said to Herod was short: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6:18).

The next verse is the key to the whole passage: “Herodias set herself against him, and desired to kill him, but she couldn’t” (Mark 6:19).

The word behind “set herself against” carries the sense in the original of holding on tightly inside. She gripped those words and would not let go of them, day or night.

And then she waited. She waited for Herod’s birthday, for the moment when the king, flushed with wine, swore an oath in front of his officials — and she had her daughter ask for the head of John the Baptist.

Brothers and sisters, I want you to notice something: Herodias didn’t kill on impulse. She waited a long time. The most frightening thing about unforgiveness is that it is patient. It is willing to wait; it schemes; it looks for its opportunity.

Here we see another truth: unforgiveness is a breach through which Satan takes control.

After that night, what did Herodias gain? She gained a platter. She silenced the mouth that had rebuked her, but her marriage was no better and her conscience no more at peace. History records that Herod Antipas was later stripped of his territory by the Roman emperor and sent into exile, and Herodias went down with him.

Unforgiveness never lets us win. It makes us push people out of our lives and into separation, and it blocks our relationship with God too.

What forgiveness really means: ἀφίημι

In connection with the Lord’s Prayer, the Lord Jesus taught, “For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). And in the next verse he said, “But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses” (Matthew 6:15).

Out of the whole Lord’s Prayer, there is only one line the Lord came back to and explained further — the line about forgiveness. That shows how much weight this carries in the Lord’s heart.

The Greek word for “forgive” is ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), which literally means “to let go, to release, to send away.” In commercial language it means “to cancel a debt”; in legal language it means “to drop the charges.”

So forgiveness is not “I pretend nothing happened.” It is “I let go.”

I’m holding an IOU that lists what he owes me. To forgive is to hand that IOU to the Lord and say: Lord, I’m not going to collect this debt myself any more. I’m handing it to you.

That is exactly what Romans says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19).

Brothers and sisters, forgiveness doesn’t say the thing doesn’t matter. It says the thing matters too much — so much that it can’t be left in the hands of someone as limited, as self-interested and as emotional as I am. I give the right of judgement back to the only righteous Judge.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

At its core, unforgiveness means I have climbed up onto the judgement seat. That seat isn’t mine. The moment I sit in it, I have left my originally intended position; I’m playing God. And anyone who plays God is bound to be crushed, because that burden was never one a human being could carry.

Forgiveness is stepping down from the judgement seat and returning to where a forgiven sinner ought to stand.

Peter’s arithmetic and the Lord’s answer

Once Peter came and asked the Lord, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”

According to the rabbis’ teaching at the time, forgiving three times was already going above and beyond. Peter said seven, and he thought he was being very generous.

Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).

The Lord didn’t mean four hundred and ninety times, so that on the four hundred and ninety-first you’re free to strike back. He meant: stop counting. As long as you’re still counting, you haven’t forgiven yet.

Then the Lord told a parable. A servant owed the king ten thousand talents, and the king, moved with compassion, cancelled the whole debt. The servant went out, met a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, seized him by the throat and had him thrown into prison.

Ten thousand talents against a hundred denarii — that’s the exchange rate the Lord himself set. He wants us to see clearly that what others owe me and what I owe God are simply not in proportion.

The parable ends very sternly: “So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds” (Matthew 18:35).

Notice “from your hearts.” Forgiving with the lips doesn’t count. Real forgiveness happens in the heart, and often it has to happen more than once.

Science and testimony: forgiveness is healing for yourself

The effect of forgiveness on people can now be measured scientifically.

In 2001, Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet, Thomas Ludwig and Kelly Vander Laan published a study in the journal Psychological Science. The researchers asked participants to recall, in turn, thoughts of “holding a grudge” and thoughts of “empathy and forgiveness,” while measuring their physiological responses. The results were clear: when people dwelt on unforgiving thoughts, their blood pressure, heart rate, skin conductance and facial muscle tension all rose significantly; when they moved into forgiving thoughts, those measures fell markedly.

Brothers and sisters, hear what this finding means: the person you hate is at home sleeping soundly, and it’s your heart and blood vessels that pay the price.

Professor Robert Enright of the University of Wisconsin–Madison began developing “forgiveness therapy” in the 1990s and is one of the pioneers of the field. He stresses one thing again and again: forgiveness is not condoning, not reconciliation, not forgetting. Forgiveness is a decision the injured person makes for themselves — the decision to stop using the other person’s wrong to go on punishing themselves.

There’s a widely quoted saying whose origin is much disputed: holding on to resentment is like drinking poison yourself and expecting the other person to die. It has spread because everyone who has tried it knows it’s true.

I also want to mention a real witness: Corrie ten Boom of the Netherlands. During the Second World War her family was arrested for hiding Jews, and her sister Betsie died in Ravensbrück concentration camp. After the war she travelled everywhere preaching — preaching forgiveness.

In 1947, after she had spoken in Munich, Germany, a man came up to her, held out his hand, and said with a broad smile: You’re right — the Lord has washed all our sins away.

She recognised him. He was one of the guards from the camp — the man in the corridor she and her sister had been forced to walk down naked.

She later described it herself: in that moment her hand seemed nailed to her side; she couldn’t lift it. She was seething inside; her blood ran cold. She prayed silently: Lord, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness.

Then, mechanically, reluctantly, she thrust her hand out. She said that at the very instant their hands clasped, a current of warmth ran from her shoulder down her arm and into her hand, tears sprang to her eyes, and she heard herself say: Brother, I forgive you with all my heart.

Corrie ten Boom is generally credited with saying: forgiveness is an act of the will, and the will can function regardless of the temperature of the heart.

Brothers and sisters, remember that. You don’t have to wait until it “feels right” to forgive. You hold out your hand first; the Lord takes care of the warmth.

Because the Lord on the cross has already shown us the way: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Stephen learned it too. As he was being stoned, he knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” (Acts 7:60)

Choosing to forgive cuts off the weapon Satan uses to destroy unity, and it is our ticket to keep walking on the road of love and unity.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: See No One Else but Jesus
sections.html:
Now let’s set today’s two key points back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: three pillars in the face of suspicion and unforgiveness

Jesus is my role model. On the cross he bore the greatest injustice in human history, and his response was: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Brothers and sisters, if forgiveness is possible, it is because he did it first.

The Bible is my standard. When the feeling in my heart says, “He doesn’t deserve it,” the Bible says, “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13). Feelings change; the standard doesn’t. I don’t follow my feelings; I follow the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Forgiveness doesn’t come by gritting your teeth; it comes by the Holy Spirit. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice: it’s “fruit,” not “product.” Fruit grows; it isn’t squeezed out.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. When I won’t forgive, who is reigning? My wound is. The wound sits on the throne giving orders — deciding whom I’ll speak to today, deciding whether I’m in a good mood or a bad one, deciding whether my prayers have any power. To forgive is to ask the wound to step down from the throne and to invite Jesus up onto it.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. A community full of suspicion cannot glorify God. The Lord said, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” The world won’t recognise us by our eloquence; it will recognise us by our relationships with one another.

Establish God’s system. A system is made up of relationships. If relationships are full of suspicion and unforgiveness, the system can’t be established — it’s just a pile of bricks heaped together with no mortar.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The most central statement of 321 is this: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

What is suspicion? Suspicion is the self-centred life. Because I’ve put myself in the very middle of the picture, I have to measure every move anyone makes: What does this mean for “me”? Is he looking down on “me”? Is he out to get “me”? If I weren’t at the centre of the picture, a great many things wouldn’t sting me at all.

What is unforgiveness? Unforgiveness is the self-centred life too. Because “I” have been wronged, “I” am in the right, “I” am the victim. The self-centred person clings to his rights and won’t let go; the selfless person has already handed himself over, so there’s nothing left to cling to.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living that fullness out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, here is the key: how can you offend someone who has already been crucified with Christ? Dead men don’t take offence.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Have you noticed that suspicion is contagious? I guard myself against him a little, and he guards himself against me a little; I give him the cold shoulder for three days, and he gives it back to me for a week. That is pride provoking pride, and both sides losing. Turn it around: when one person speaks first, reaches out first, apologises first, the wall in the other person’s heart begins to loosen too. That is humility drawing out humility.

The fivefold change and a shift in perspective

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice that relationships come before ministry. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The problem in many churches is that the order has been reversed. To get the job done, we put up with relationships staying broken. The job gets done — and the people scatter.

Today’s lesson is working at the level of “relationships,” and the way in is through “mindset.”

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective: not asking, “Why is he treating me like this?” but, “Lord, what do you want to teach me through this?”

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly one: on earth, I’m the creditor; in heaven, I’m the one who owed ten thousand talents and had it all cancelled.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal one: do I mean to let this relationship stay frozen as it is today, or do we walk on together into eternity?

From a worldly perspective to a godly one: worldly wisdom says, “Always hold something back”; God’s wisdom says, “Believes all things.”

The 920 practice and 235 relationships

The 920 practice says: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; in our dealings with them we are to practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: the person you’re most suspicious of, the person who once hurt you deeply, is the very “2” God has given you. He isn’t your obstacle; he’s your training ground.

Of the nine graces, three are tailor-made for today’s lesson: patience, kindness and faithfulness. Patience means not rushing to a verdict; kindness means giving the other person the benefit of the doubt; faithfulness means my commitment to this relationship doesn’t change with how he behaves.

235 relationships means: with selfless people, become a “2” — a spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Someone gripped by suspicion and unforgiveness can never build 235. Because 2 needs openness, 3 needs trust, and 5 needs people standing shoulder to shoulder. Once the wall goes up, all three grind to a halt.

So tearing down walls isn’t a private matter. It is the key to whether God’s system can be established at all.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Tearing Down the Walls of Suspicion and Unforgiveness
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s take them one at a time and go deep with them using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Stop guessing, start talking

This week, when something happens that makes you uneasy or suspicious, don’t let your mind run wild first. Instead:

First, find a suitable moment to talk to the person directly.

Second, ask what they meant, rather than assuming their motives.

Third, learn to say, “I felt that … is that what you meant?”

Brothers and sisters, notice how that sentence is built. The first half says “what I felt” — that’s my responsibility, and I’m not pushing it onto you. The second half is a question mark — it hands the right to define what happened back to the other person. That one question mark is the thirty extra seconds that father never took; it’s Phinehas’s trip across the river.

Suspicion is the entrance to separation; conversation is the starting point of unity.

Work through it with the eight stages:

Information: Today you’ve learned a fact — suspicion moves through misunderstanding, defensiveness and distance into separation; you’ve also learned that the fundamental attribution error makes us overestimate other people’s ill will.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show you whom you are “writing a script” about right now. Ask the Lord to lay that name on your heart.

Conviction: Admit before the Lord — my inferences are not facts, and I have no right to pass judgement on anyone’s heart.

Implementation: This week, pick one matter and go and ask that question. Don’t pass it on by message; face to face is best, or at least a phone call.

Evaluation: After you’ve asked, write it down — was the truth what I imagined? What did I discover?

Correction: If I guessed wrong, confess it to the Lord and, where needed, apologise to the person. If the other person really was in the wrong, then follow Matthew 18:15: show him his fault between you and him alone.

Repetition: Make “ask first” a habit. Once doesn’t count as practice; a month does.

Multiplication: Teach this habit to your small group, your family, your children. Make “In our family we don’t guess, we ask” a house rule.

Practice 2: Each day, pray to forgive someone who has hurt you

This week, set aside time every day to speak, in prayer, the name of someone who has hurt you, and say to the Lord:

“Lord Jesus, you have forgiven me, and I too choose to forgive ______. Heal me, and set me free.”

At first you may not be able to get the words out, but this is the beginning of a road to freedom. Forgiveness isn’t denying the hurt; it’s refusing to let the hurt go on controlling your life.

Notice the order of this prayer: first, “you have forgiven me,” and only then, “I too choose to forgive.” The order can’t be reversed. Very often the reason people can’t forgive is that they’ve forgotten they were let off a debt of ten thousand talents.

Notice that word too: “choose.” Forgiveness is an act of the will, not the result of an emotion. You make the decision first, and the feelings catch up afterwards — sometimes a long time afterwards. That’s all right; keep saying it every day.

Work through it with the eight stages:

Information: The word for forgiveness in the original means “to let go, to cancel a debt”; unforgiveness gives place to the devil and makes your own body pay the price.

Revelation: Be still, and let the Holy Spirit bring that name before you. Usually the first one that comes to mind is the one the Lord most wants to deal with.

Conviction: Acknowledge that “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay” is the Lord’s word, not my job.

Implementation: Pray once every day, speaking that name out loud.

Evaluation: After a week, when you think of this person, has the temperature of your heart changed?

Correction: If it all wells up again, don’t lose heart, and don’t condemn yourself. Seventy times seven includes forgiving the same thing seventy times seven times.

Repetition: Make it part of your morning prayers every day.

Multiplication: Once you’ve truly been set free, go and pray alongside someone who is still bound. Those who have been healed are the best at healing others.

Practice 3: Mend a relationship broken by misunderstanding

This week, take the initiative and contact someone you have misjudged, or who has misjudged you. Even a text or a simple greeting can be the start of a relationship being restored.

You don’t need to explain everything. Just say sincerely, “I’ve been thinking of you lately — I hope all is well.”

Let God’s love replace the walls people build, and let unity be restored once again.

The Lord Jesus said, “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24).

Brothers and sisters, see how astonishing the Lord’s order is: even the offering can be put on hold. God would rather you leave your gift in front of the altar and go and put the relationship right first.

And notice that it says “your brother has anything against you” — it’s someone else who has a grievance against me, not me against them. The one the Lord asks to move first is me.

Work through it with the eight stages:

Information: A broken relationship hinders our worship; the one the Lord asks to take the first step towards reconciliation is often the one who hears this message first.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to bring a name to mind — the name you avoid the moment you think of it.

Conviction: Believe that taking the initiative isn’t losing face; taking the initiative is being like the Lord. Humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Implementation: Send that message today. No explanations, no raking up the past, no demanding a reply.

Evaluation: Once it’s sent, hand your heart to the Lord. Whether the other person replies isn’t up to me.

Correction: If they aren’t ready yet, give the timing to God and keep praying blessing over them.

Repetition: Once every quarter, take a quiet look — are there still any names hanging on my relationship ledger?

Multiplication: Share your testimony in your small group, so that others find the courage to send that message too.

A Gentle Reminder: choosing to trust and choosing to forgive are the shortcut to unity

Satan is always whispering in our ear: You can’t trust him.

But Jesus says to us: Forgive him.

Satan is always whispering in our ear: He’ll hurt you again.

But Jesus says to us: Not until seven times, but until seventy times seven.

Brothers and sisters, choose to trust — not because people are reliable, but because you believe Jesus is in control. Choose to forgive — not because the other person has done nothing wrong, but because you yourself have already been forgiven.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Tear Down the Walls of Separation, and Let the Love of Christ Bind Us Together
sections.html:
Unity doesn’t happen naturally; it is a choice we make every day: the choice not to be suspicious, the choice to talk, the choice to forgive.

These choices aren’t emotional reactions; they are decisions made in the spirit.

Paul says, “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3).

Notice “being eager to keep.” Unity doesn’t maintain itself. It’s like a boat: if you do nothing, it won’t stay where it is; it will drift away.

I want to finish with a single drop of water.

Put a drop of water on a table, and before long it has dried up. Let that same drop fall into the ocean, and it will never dry up — because it is no longer “a drop”; it is the sea.

Brothers and sisters, suspicion reinforces our boundaries, and unforgiveness thickens them. Unity is letting those boundaries dissolve in the love of Jesus.

Let’s choose to be that drop which becomes one with all the waters — seeing not ourselves, but Jesus alone.

Let’s go back to that verse on the mountain: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

This morning, may the Lord touch us too and say to us: Get up, and don’t be afraid. May we lift up our eyes and see that the one standing behind that wall is not an enemy, but a brother who needs grace just as much as I do — and that standing between him and me is Jesus.

When we are one, the body of Jesus will shine with his glory. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)
practices: Stop guessing, start talking
Each day, pray to forgive someone who has hurt you
Mend a relationship broken by misunderstanding
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that this morning your word has shone a light on the walls in our hearts.

Lord, we confess that we so often put guessing in place of talking, silence in place of facing things, and retreat in place of forgiveness. We thought we were protecting ourselves, but in fact we were giving place to the devil. Please forgive us.
Shine your light on us. Show us the person we have been writing a script about in our hearts, and show us the name we have never been willing to let go of.
Lord, on the cross you said: Father, forgive them. Put your forgiveness within us. Our strength is not enough, but your grace is sufficient. Our hearts are still cold; let your love go to work first.
In the name of the Lord we tear down the wall of suspicion, we tear down the wall of unforgiveness, and we take back every place we have given to Satan.
When we lift up our eyes, let us see no one else but Jesus. Make us truly one in your body; reign as King among us, and receive all the glory.
May the Lord’s peace come upon every brother and sister, and may the Lord’s healing come to every wound that is still bleeding.
We pray in the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
discussion: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” (Proverbs 18:13) Think back to the last time an unchecked thought about someone rose up in your heart. What did that thought grow into? If you could do it over, at which step would you call a halt, and how would you go about asking?

“Be angry, and don’t sin. Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil.” (Ephesians 4:26–27) Is there a name in your life that, “after two full years,” you still haven’t let go of? What is stopping you from forgiving? Would you be willing to let your brothers and sisters in the small group stand with you in prayer as you make that choice?
l018.title: Tearing Down the Walls of Suspicion and Unforgiveness
l018.subtitle: Why Separation Happens (Parts 2 and 3)
l018.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: Walls Are Built from the Inside
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

The small hours of Sunday, 13 August 1961. The people of Berlin went to sleep as usual, and when day broke they found a barbed-wire fence running down the middle of their streets. The same city, the same people, the same lanes — cut in two overnight. Later the barbed wire became concrete, and the concrete became a wall 3.6 metres high and 155 kilometres long. That wall stood for twenty-eight years, until it finally fell on 9 November 1989.

On the day it fell, the whole world cheered in front of their television sets. But historians later reminded us of something: the truly frightening thing about that wall was never the concrete. Concrete takes only a few months to put up, and only a few nights to knock down. What is truly hard to tear down is the wall that remains in people’s hearts after the concrete has gone. The Germans even coined a phrase for it: “the wall in the head.” The wall came down, but the wall in the heart was still there.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what we’re going to talk about today. Every separation you can see on the outside was first built on the inside.

We don’t need to go to Berlin for examples. A husband and wife under one roof who barely exchange three sentences a day. Brothers who grew up together, now facing each other in court over an inheritance. Brothers and sisters in the same small group who nod and smile at the door while in their hearts they’ve long since taken a detour around each other. Two groups in a church who both love the Lord, yet for ten years haven’t sat at the same table. A wall doesn’t need concrete. One thought is enough.

How high is the cost of separation? In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad, a psychology professor at Brigham Young University, and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine. It pooled 148 studies and more than 300,000 participants, and found that people with weak social connections had roughly a 50 per cent higher risk of dying during the follow-up period than people with strong social connections. The researchers noted that the effect is comparable to well-known health risks such as smoking and obesity.

There’s an even longer study. Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, making it one of the longest studies of happiness in human history. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has distilled decades of data into one sentence: the best predictor of a person’s health and happiness in later life is not wealth, not fame, not cholesterol, but the quality of their relationships.

Brothers and sisters, what science has measured, the Bible said long ago. In the Garden of Eden, looking at the newly made Adam, God said the first “not good” since creation began: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Human beings were not made to live alone. Separation damages the health of our bodies, damages the unity of the church and damages the bonds between people; and Satan tries every means he can to drive us apart from one another, and even to cut us off from God.

We need to see Satan’s methods clearly. The first thing he did in Eden was not to get people to kill or commit arson; it was to create separation. He said to the woman, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). With one sentence he planted suspicion of God in the human heart, and humanity was separated from God. Then Adam pushed the blame onto Eve, and Eve onto the serpent, and people were separated from one another too. From that day on, separation has been Satan’s speciality.

Separation is Satan’s scheme; unity is Jesus’ mission.
