On the night he was betrayed, the heart of the Lord Jesus’ prayer for his disciples was one thing alone: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

We’ve already looked at the first three causes of separation: comparison, suspicion and unforgiveness. Today we go on to three more key factors that destroy relationships: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding.

These three look quite different from one another: one is about advantage, one about attitude, one about the way we see. But brothers and sisters, they grow from the same root — that “self.” Live the self-centred life, and there is a wall; live in selflessness, and the wall comes down.

So today’s theme verse is the answer to the whole lesson: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

sections.heading: Scripture Background: That Moment on the Mountain, When Only One Remained in View
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of this verse, we first need to stand on that mountain.

The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, also called Levi, one of the twelve apostles. He had been a tax collector in Capernaum (Matthew 9:9; Mark 2:14). In the Jewish society of his day, tax collectors collected money for the Romans and were regarded as traitors — people shut out by the synagogue, by their relatives and by the whole community. Brothers and sisters, notice this: the man who wrote this book had once been on the other side of that wall himself. It was Jesus who walked past the tax office, said to him, “Follow me,” and tore the wall down. Someone who has been shut out knows better than anyone how precious unity is.

Matthew is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jewish Christians. The theme of the whole book is “Jesus is King” — the Messiah King promised in the Old Testament.

Now look at the context. The Transfiguration in chapter 17 doesn’t come out of nowhere. It follows straight on from chapter 16.

In the region of Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asked his disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). What a lofty confession! Yet only a few verses later, when Jesus said plainly for the first time that he must go up to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed and rise on the third day, Peter took hold of him and tried to talk him out of it. The Lord turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Brothers and sisters, the same mouth spoke heavenly revelation one moment and earthly thinking the next. What made the difference? Whether or not “self” had stepped aside. And straight after that the Lord gave his great summary: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain. “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2). Moses and Elijah appeared as well, talking with Jesus. Moses stood for the Law, Elijah for the Prophets; in that moment the whole Old Testament stood beside him as a witness.

Then Peter spoke up: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you want, let’s make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4).

Peter’s words sound very devout, but they hide a serious problem. Three tents put Jesus on a level with Moses and Elijah, making the Lord one-third of the picture. And as the Chinese Union Version renders it, “I will make them here” — he was putting his own arrangements above the Lord’s plan. Brothers and sisters, this is the self-centred life in its most typical form: not open rebellion, but zealously arranging God’s place for him.

God responded at once. “While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him’” (Matthew 17:5). The moment the cloud covered them, the three-tent plan was gone. The Father said only one thing: listen to him — not to them, to him.

The disciples fell on their faces, terrified. “Jesus came and touched them and said, ‘Get up, and don’t be afraid’” (Matthew 17:7). And then comes today’s theme verse:

“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

In the original this sentence is very forceful. “Lifting up their eyes” is literally “raising their eyes”; the second half, translated literally, says, “they saw no one, except Jesus himself alone.” The Greek uses μόνον (monon), meaning “solely, only, alone.” Moses withdrew, Elijah withdrew, the three-tent plan withdrew, Peter’s opinions withdrew — and when everything else had withdrawn, the one who remained was everything.

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the key to tearing down walls. The walls in our hearts are all there because too many people are standing in front of our eyes: my interests stand there, other people’s faults stand there, my own sense of superiority stands there. The moment we “see no one,” the wall collapses. The focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances: that is the most central statement of 321, and it is the very picture of Matthew 17:8.

sections.heading: 1. Self-Interest → Advantage and Selfish Desire → Separation
sections.html:
The first cause the lesson gives us is “self-interest.” When someone cares only about what benefits him and pursues only his own advantage, it becomes all too easy to sacrifice relationships and sever unity.

A culture of self-interest: advantage becomes the measure of relationships

People often say, “In business there are no permanent friends, only permanent interests.” The saying is generally traced to the nineteenth-century British Prime Minister Lord Palmerston. In a speech to Parliament on 1 March 1848 he said: we have no eternal allies, and we have no perpetual enemies; our interests are eternal. The saying moved from diplomacy into business, and from business it has quietly moved into the family and the church.

When people live for “self,” even the closest relationships can be cut off. The lesson lists four scenes we know all too well:

1. Siblings falling out over an inheritance. As children they slept in the same bed; grown up, they haven’t spoken for twenty years over a plot of land.

2. A marriage growing cold through self-protection. Both are afraid of being hurt again, so both close their hearts away; the house is still there, but the home is gone.

3. Small-group servants quarrelling over position. What they fight about often isn’t truth, but “who gets the final say.”

4. A church dividing because people compare their gifts. Gifts were meant for working together, but they’ve become a ruler for measuring who stands higher.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: not one of these four begins with outward circumstances. Every one of them begins on the inside.

Selfish desire pitches its camp within us

The letter of James puts this very bluntly:

“Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members? You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” (James 4:1–2)

There are two important words in the original here. “Pleasures” is ἡδονή (hēdonē), meaning “pleasure, enjoyment”; the English word hedonism comes from it. James isn’t saying that having desires is sin. He’s saying that when “make me happy” becomes the highest rule, the war begins.

The other word is even more vivid. “War” is στρατεύομαι (strateuomai), whose root is the word for “army”; its basic meaning is “to encamp, to draw up in battle array, to wage war.” James is saying that selfish desire isn’t an occasional visitor; it has pitched its camp and dug in among our members. Brothers and sisters, do you hear that? The battlefield isn’t the church meeting room; the battlefield is inside us. The quarrels on the outside are only the smoke from the war within.

Then James adds the line that cuts deepest: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask.” People who live for self share one trait — they fight very hard, but they seldom ask quietly. Fighting is relying on ourselves; asking is relying on God. Rely on the brain and on ourselves, and you worry; rely on the heart and on the Holy Spirit, and you rejoice.

The most dangerous self-interest is the kind dressed in the robes of piety

The lesson reminds us that the Pharisees were the classic example of self-interest.

To protect their spiritual image, they chose to associate only with people “of standing,” shutting sinners out and living in a spiritual separation. The Lord Jesus recorded a prayer of theirs: “The Pharisee stood and prayed to himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men, extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector’” (Luke 18:11).

What makes this prayer so frightening isn’t how wicked it is, but how much it sounds like a prayer. It opens with “God,” but its whole content is “I.” He stood in the temple, but his eyes were on other people; his mouth said thank you, but his heart was measuring who stood higher.

So when Jesus sat at table with tax collectors and sinners, they couldn’t bear it: “The Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, ‘This man welcomes sinners, and eats with them’” (Luke 15:2). In Middle Eastern culture, sharing a table is not as simple as a meal; it is a sign of acceptance, of identification, of covenant. Jesus chose to sit down; the Pharisees chose to stand further off. One was tearing a wall down; the other was building one.

Paul, late in life, sighed in the same way: “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21).

Paul also foretold that this would be the condition of the last days: “For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:2). Brothers and sisters, look closely at the order of Paul’s list. He lists nineteen marks of end-time corruption one after another, and the very first is “lovers of self.” The original φίλαυτοι (philautoi) literally means “those who love themselves.” Every other corruption grows out of this one. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Where self-interest ends: both sides lose

In 1950 two researchers at the RAND Corporation in the United States, Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher, devised an experimental scenario that the Princeton mathematician Albert Tucker later named the “Prisoner’s Dilemma.” The scenario is simple: two people are questioned separately. If both stay silent, both receive a light sentence; if one betrays the other, the betrayer goes free; if they betray each other, both receive a heavy sentence.

And the result? When each person calculates only his own maximum advantage, the most common outcome is that the two betray each other, and both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Let me give you an even smaller picture. Two mountain goats meet on a narrow log bridge, wide enough for only one goat. Each thinks it has the right to cross first, so they butt heads, and in the end both fall into the water. If one were willing to lie down and let the other step over it, both goats could cross. Whoever lies down makes it possible for both. Brothers and sisters, the one willing to lie down isn’t the loser; it is the bridge.

Applying 321: from the self-centred life to selflessness

The cure for self-interest isn’t “living for yourself a little less”; it’s changing the centre.

The Lord Jesus pointed the way very clearly: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). “Deny” in the original is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown, to renounce, to say I don’t know him” — the very word used when Peter denied the Lord three times. The Lord means: say to that old self, “I don’t know you.”

Paul states the positive side of selflessness: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living that fullness out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Pour a cup of water into the ocean, and that water hasn’t vanished; it has gained the whole ocean.

And our highest role model is the Lord himself: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” is κενόω (kenoō) in the original, meaning “to empty out.” Brothers and sisters, the way the Lord of the universe set about tearing down walls was to empty himself. He isn’t asking us to do anything he hasn’t done.

So Paul goes straight on to write the prescription for unity: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4).

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The self-interested person has the order upside down — he grabs the ministry first, then counts the advantage, and only at the end discovers that his life is empty and his relationships are gone. But shift the perspective, and everything changes: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. That plot of land, that position, that word of vindication — all of them are temporary. The person sitting across from you is eternal.

sections.heading: 2. Accusation → Condemnation → Separation
sections.html:
Another killer of unity is an attitude of “accusation” and “condemnation.”

The lesson asks a very good question: when we face someone who has done wrong, do we want to “lift him up,” or to “distance ourselves from him”? Do we, like the Pharisees, pick up stones ready to stone the sinner to death, or do we, like Jesus, choose forgiveness and acceptance?

Accusation is Satan’s line of work

Brothers and sisters, there’s something we need to know first: accusation is not a neutral habit. Accusation has a pedigree.

The name “Satan” in Hebrew is שָׂטָן (satan), meaning “adversary, accuser”; in Greek it is rendered διάβολος (diabolos), meaning “slanderer, one who sows discord.” The root of the word carries the sense of “throwing across, tearing apart” — his work is to throw words back and forth and pull people apart.

Revelation couldn’t put it more plainly: “I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, ‘Now the salvation, the power, and the Kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ has come; for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night’” (Revelation 12:10).

“The accuser of our brothers … who accuses them … day and night” — that is Satan’s job description. Brothers and sisters, we need to take this to heart: when we pick up a magnifying glass and count up a brother’s faults day and night, spreading word of a brother’s failures everywhere we go, whose shift are we working? We may be sitting in church doing Satan’s work.

By contrast, what does the Bible say Jesus is doing? “Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us” (Romans 8:33–34).

Brothers and sisters, there are two voices in heaven: one accuses day and night, the other intercedes day and night. Every day, when we open our mouths, we are in fact choosing which side to join.

Jesus our role model: no condemnation, only love and redemption

John chapter 8 records a scene that will never go out of date. The scribes and Pharisees brought a woman caught in adultery and set her in the middle, stones in their hands and the law of Moses on their lips. What they really wanted wasn’t justice; it was to trap Jesus.

Jesus said only one thing: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her” (John 8:7).

Scripture tells us that when they heard this, they went out one by one, beginning with the oldest. Brothers and sisters, why did the oldest leave first? Because the longer you’ve lived, the better you know that your own hands aren’t clean.

Then comes that conversation so beautiful it brings tears to the eyes: “Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, ‘Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?’ She said, ‘No one, Lord.’ Jesus said, ‘Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more’” (John 8:10–11).

Notice: the one person there who had every right to pick up a stone was the one person who didn’t. “Condemn” in the original is κατακρίνω (katakrinō), meaning “to pass sentence.” The Lord didn’t say, “You have no sin” — he said, “Neither do I condemn you,” and then, “From now on, sin no more.”

Brothers and sisters, here is an order we so often get backwards. It isn’t that Jesus doesn’t care about sin; he cared enough to go to the cross. But his order is: first forgiveness, then change; first acceptance, then teaching. Our order is often the reverse: first condemn, then demand the other person change, and only accept them once they’ve sorted themselves out. The result: the wall goes up, and the person walks away.

Scripture states plainly why the Lord came: “For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him” (John 3:17).

He ate with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 15:2), showing that he wanted unity, not separation; he came to seek and to save the lost, not to judge the world.

The lesson puts it superbly: Jesus knew that only in love do people repent; only in acceptance do people turn back; only in unity can teaching and change truly take place.

Confirmation from psychology: contempt is the number one killer of relationships

From the 1980s onwards, John Gottman, a psychology professor at the University of Washington, and Robert Levenson of the University of California recorded hundreds of couples talking in the laboratory, then followed their marriages for more than a decade afterwards. They identified four of the most destructive patterns of interaction, which they called the “Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, defensiveness, stonewalling and contempt.

The research found that the single strongest predictor of divorce among them is “contempt” — looking down on the other person from a position of superiority. And the word “stonewalling” is wonderfully apt: it literally means “building a wall of stone” — no response, no reaction, shutting the other person out.

Brothers and sisters, psychology has given this attitude a name; the Bible gave us its origin long ago. Contempt is the attitude of condemnation; stonewalling is the act of separation.

Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying, “If you judge people, you have no time to love them.” We only have so much time. Spend it on judging, and there’s none left over for loving.

Judging is a usurpation

The Bible speaks very seriously about judging, because judging is in fact usurping a position that isn’t ours.

“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

“Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge. Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?” (James 4:11–12)

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. To judge is to climb up onto the judgement seat, and that seat isn’t ours.

And the gospel declares: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Brothers and sisters, we ourselves are people who have been forgiven. Someone who has just been let off a debt of ten thousand talents really has no business seizing a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii (see Matthew 18:23–35).

Applying 321: from the hand of judgement to the shoulder of Barnabas

So when we come across a brother who really has done wrong, what should we do? The Bible doesn’t ask us to pretend we haven’t seen it. It gives us a completely different action:

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

“Restore” in the original is καταρτίζω (katartizō). In Matthew 4:21 this word describes the sons of Zebedee in the boat “mending” their nets, and in medicine it was used for “setting a dislocated bone back in place.” Brothers and sisters, this is the action we are meant to take: not throwing away the torn net, but mending it; not complaining that the arm is dislocated, but setting it back into the body.

And in the same verse Paul adds a warning: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” The one mending the net has to handle it gently, because you and I are part of the net too.

The Bible gives us a living role model — Barnabas. When Saul had just come to faith, all the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him, and only one man stood up for him: “When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus” (Acts 9:26–27).

Later, when Mark had turned back halfway at Pamphylia, Paul thought they should not take him again, but Barnabas still wanted to take him (Acts 15:37–39). Years later, Paul himself wrote: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). Brothers and sisters, had there not been someone back then willing to give him another chance, the church might have been without a Gospel of Mark.

The lesson says it so well: we don’t need more hands of judgement; we need more shoulders like Barnabas’s.

When a doctor sees a wound, he doesn’t say to the patient, “How could you be so careless?” He stops the bleeding first, cleans the wound and dresses it. The church is a hospital, not a courtroom; what we should be holding in our hands is gauze, not stones.

sections.heading: 3. Seeing Others’ Faults → Seeing Our Own Strengths → Separation
sections.html:
The third cause the lesson gives us is a distortion in the way we see: we’re in the habit of looking at other people’s faults through a “magnifying glass” and at our own strengths through a “flattering filter.” And separation quietly arises in the gap between the enlarging and the shrinking.

Three familiar attitudes

The lesson lists three common forms this attitude takes:

1. Feeling that others are never quite good enough — not as good as me.

2. Being unable to stand someone’s personality or way of doing things.

3. Being unwilling to work with people who think differently.

Brothers and sisters, all three of these sound so slight — so slight that we often think we’re simply “a person of principle.” But that’s exactly how walls get built: one sentence at a time.

The beam and the speck: a carpenter’s humour

The Lord Jesus said something wonderfully vivid about this:

“Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.” (Matthew 7:1)

“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye;’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:3–5)

The wording here paints a picture. “Speck” in the original is κάρφος (karphos), a tiny chip of wood or a bit of straw; “beam” is δοκός (dokos), the great timber that holds up a whole house. The Lord Jesus was a carpenter’s son and had worked as a carpenter himself; he knew exactly how different those two things are in size. A man with a roof beam sticking out of his eye leans in to pick a wood chip out of someone else’s — what an absurd picture!

Notice the Lord’s point: he didn’t say, “Never mind the speck in your brother’s eye.” What he spoke about was the order: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly.” Only when you see clearly can you actually help. Only when you’ve dealt with yourself first have you any right to come close to someone else.

Psychology: our eyes are crooked by nature

Social psychology has left a solid record of this distortion.

First, there is the “fundamental attribution error.” The term was coined by the social psychologist Lee Ross in 1977. Put simply: when someone else is late, we say he has no sense of time; when we’re late, we say the traffic was bad today. We explain others by their character, and ourselves by our circumstances. The same event, two different rulers.

Second, there is the “better-than-average effect.” A study by the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson, published in Acta Psychologica in 1981, found that about 88 per cent of the American drivers surveyed believed they drove more safely than the median driver. Brothers and sisters, mathematically that’s impossible. But that is the human heart: the magnifying glass points outwards, the flattering filter points inwards.

These studies are not meant to replace the Bible, but to confirm from the side what the Bible has long made plain — the eyes of the human heart are crooked by nature. So what we need is not to look harder, but to be given a new pair of eyes.

The mystery of the body: we are different precisely so that we can work together

The lesson reminds us that God made each of us different precisely so that we would work together and make up for one another’s lack. If we only want to change others and are unwilling to adjust ourselves, we fall into pride, criticism and judgement.

Paul explains it using the body:

“But now they are many members, but one body. The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:20–21)

“No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” (1 Corinthians 12:22)

“that there should be no division in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:25–26)

Brothers and sisters, follow Paul’s logic: the eye and the hand can need each other precisely because they are different. If the whole body were an eye, it wouldn’t be a body; it would be a heap of eyes. The church is a body precisely because we are different and yet one, imperfect and yet making up for each other.

The natural world tells us the same thing. California’s coast redwoods are the tallest trees on earth and can grow to more than a hundred metres, yet their roots go down only two or three metres. How can such shallow roots hold them up? Because redwoods never grow alone. Underground, their roots intertwine and knit together into a web; the whole grove stands hand in hand, and that’s how it stands against the wind.

Then there are flocks of geese. An analysis by the aerodynamicists P. B. S. Lissaman and C. A. Shollenberger, published in the journal Science in 1970, showed that twenty-five birds flying in a V formation, riding the upwash from the wingtips of the bird ahead, could in theory fly about 70 per cent further than a bird flying alone. Brothers and sisters, not one of them had stronger wings. They were simply in the right position.

The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in Life Together, left us a piercing sentence: whoever loves his dream of community more than the real people in the community in front of him will end up destroying that community. Brothers and sisters, it often isn’t that we don’t love the church. It’s that we love “the church of my ideals” too much, and so the real, flawed brothers and sisters in front of us fail the test one by one.

Applying 321: the 920 practice and 235 relationships

321’s 920 practice is exactly the medicine for this way of seeing. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; in front of every “2” we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: every one of these nine graces needs an “other person” in order to grow. Patience needs someone difficult to get along with; kindness needs someone unlovable; gentleness needs someone who makes you angry. That brother you “don’t quite get along with” isn’t your obstacle; he’s your training ground. God hasn’t put him beside you to wear you down, but to grow fruit.

One step further on are 235 relationships: with selfless people, become a “2” — a spiritual companion; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, a web of relationships like that can only be built on “seeing the other person’s gifts,” never on “staring at the other person’s faults.”

This is also the road of the fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. If today we change just one mindset — from “Where does he fall short?” to “What has God placed in him?” — the whole chain will move along with it.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: See No One Else but Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, put today’s three causes side by side and you’ll discover something: they grow from the same root.

Self-interest puts my own advantage at the centre; accusation puts me up on the judgement seat; fault-finding makes me the standard. Three roads, all leading to one word — “self.”

321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

So the way to tear down the wall isn’t to try harder to love that difficult person; it’s to let “self” step aside. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Back to the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, he didn’t condemn, he sat at table with sinners. The Bible is my standard — not my feelings, not my standards, not my face. The Holy Spirit is my guide — only the Holy Spirit can make me see the beam in my own eye.

Then to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — in this relationship, he has the final say, not me. Let Jesus receive all the glory — so I don’t need to win, and I don’t need to prove I’m right.

And finally the Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system is built on advantage and rank; God’s system is built on life and relationships.

321 says our perspective must shift four times: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. Brothers and sisters, that matter between you and that brother — seen with earthly eyes, it’s a quarrel; seen with heavenly eyes, it’s training. Seen with temporary eyes, the question is who came off worse; seen with eternal eyes, the question is who is being made complete.

The Path of Serving is walked the same way: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The order can’t be skipped. Many people skip life and go straight to ministry, and so the ministry becomes yet another wall.

And all of this is distilled by our theme verse into a single sentence: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone” (Matthew 17:8).

They saw no one — not my interests, not other people’s faults, not my own superiority.

Jesus alone — he is my role model, he is my standard, he is my King, he receives all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, the moment there is no one left in our eyes but Jesus, the wall falls by itself. Because the wall was built by “self,” and once “self” is gone, the wall has no foundation.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Steps to Tearing Down the Wall of Self-Centred Separation
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s walk through them step by step using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Recognise the motive of self-interest

This week, reflect on a relationship of yours that is strained or has gone silent, and honestly ask yourself three questions:

1. Do I care too much about my own interests?

2. Am I unwilling to give up even a little of my own sovereignty?

3. Am I only willing to associate with people who are “useful” to me?

When you find traces of self-interest, turn to Jesus at once and say, “Lord, for your sake I am willing to lay myself down.”

The hardest part of this practice isn’t answering the questions; it’s being still and letting the Holy Spirit shine his light. Information is what we’ve learned today: that self-interest brings separation. Revelation is the Holy Spirit pointing to one particular face and saying, “This is the one.” Conviction is when I stop defending myself and admit that it wasn’t principle — it was my own interest.

Practice 2: Put down the stone, pick up the rope

When others do wrong, this week practise the “three don’ts”: don’t condemn, don’t gossip, don’t judge by your own standards.

Instead, learn the “three do’s”: cover with love, build up with words, support with action.

“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

This step is Implementation. Implementation means this: at least once this week, when that comment is already on the tip of your tongue, swallow it and turn it into a word of blessing; when someone starts talking about a brother in front of you, don’t join in — say instead, “Let’s pray for him.”

After Implementation come Evaluation and Correction. Each evening, take three minutes to ask yourself: Did I pick up a stone today? Did I pick up a rope today? Which word came out too quickly? If I meet the same situation tomorrow, what will I say?

We don’t need more hands of judgement; we need more shoulders like Barnabas’s.

Practice 3: Practise appreciating someone you “don’t quite get along with”

This week, deliberately observe someone you have tended to criticise in the past, and then list three of their strengths. You might pray silently, “Lord, help me see him as you see him, and teach me to respect and accept him.”

This won’t only change your attitude towards him; it will also break down the wall your own self-made standards have built in your heart.

Brothers and sisters, this step is Repetition. The way we see people doesn’t change after one look. It changes slowly, by looking again and again, counting again and again, giving thanks again and again. You can go one step further: tell him to his face one of the strengths you’ve seen. You’ll find that the moment you say it out loud, the wall has one brick fewer.

The last step is Multiplication. Once your way of seeing has changed, pass these new eyes on — in your small group, in your home, take someone with you and practise this together. One person tearing down their own wall is salvation; a whole group tearing down walls together is revival.

A Gentle Reminder: Jesus is not a Lord of condemnation, but a Lord of unity

If Jesus dealt with us by the law, not one of us could stand. But he chose to redeem us and accept us with love, and he teaches us to treat others in the same way.

“being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) Brothers and sisters, notice the words “being eager to keep” — unity doesn’t happen automatically; it has to be guarded with effort.

sections.heading: Closing Word: From Self at the Centre to Christ at the Centre
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to Berlin.

On the evening of 9 November 1989, the wall fell. But the Germans tell us that the real rebuilding took far longer, because “the wall in the head” is not something a bulldozer can knock down.

We have walls in our hearts too. Today we’ve seen three of their bricks: self-interest, accusation and fault-finding. And every one of those bricks is stamped with the same word — “self.”

The root of separation lies not in the differences between people, but in whether “self” takes first place in our hearts. Let’s choose to leave the culture of self-centredness behind, follow Christ’s example, and live a life of unity.

Unity isn’t forced endurance; it is a decision made out of love. If only we are willing to let Jesus be Lord, he can make us children of peace and vessels of unity.

“See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1)

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s lift up our eyes together. Put down our interests, put down the stones, put down the magnifying glass. When all of that has withdrawn, we will see the Lord who has been standing there all along.

“Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

May Jesus reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our small groups, reign as King in our church; may all the glory go to him.

keyVerses: “Lifting up their eyes, they saw no one, except Jesus alone.” (Matthew 17:8)

Put down the stone, pick up the rope
Practise appreciating someone you “don’t quite get along with”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. You are the Lord who broke down the middle wall of separation; in your own body you made the two one.

Lord, we confess that there are walls in our hearts. We have sacrificed relationships for our own interests; we have picked up stones to condemn our brothers; we have looked at others through a magnifying glass and at ourselves through a flattering filter. Please forgive us.

Lord, we don’t ask you to change others first; we ask you to change us first. Holy Spirit, shine your light and let us see the beam in our own eye. Give us gentle hearts to restore brothers who have fallen. Give us new eyes to see the gifts you have placed in every person.
Lord, may my interests withdraw, may my standards withdraw, may my pride withdraw. When I lift up my eyes, may I see no one, but you alone standing there.
discussion: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1) Think of a relationship of yours that is currently strained or distant. If you face it honestly, is there a motive of self-interest in it? This week, what specific interest or sovereignty are you willing to lay down for the Lord?

“First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:5) Think of a brother or sister you “don’t quite get along with,” and name three of their strengths. In your small group, how can you practically become “the shoulder of Barnabas” to support someone who is going through a time of weakness?

sections.heading: Introduction: A Drop of Water, and an Ocean
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Tomorrow morning, when you wash your face, try one small thing. Turn the tap down as low as it will go, and let the water slowly gather into a single drop that hangs at the mouth of the tap. You will see a bead of water, crystal clear; the light passes through it, and it shines brighter than a diamond.

That one drop holds about 0.05 millilitres, and inside it are some 1.7 × 10²¹ water molecules. Every molecule clings tightly to its neighbours by hydrogen bonds, and that is why the drop can hold itself up as a round, full bead instead of spreading out flat.

It is beautiful. It is also pure.

But if you let it fall onto the kitchen counter and go and have your breakfast, by the time you come back it is gone. A little sun, a little breeze, and in less than half an hour it has evaporated without leaving a trace.

A drop of water, however pure, however precious, so long as it insists on remaining a single drop, has only one possible end: it disappears.

And yet it is the same water. At its mouth, the Amazon pours roughly two hundred thousand cubic metres of water into the Atlantic every second. That is the volume of eighty standard swimming pools, every second. It cuts across an entire South American continent and sustains the richest ecosystem on earth.

The water of the Amazon and that drop on your tap are the same thing. The molecular formula is identical: H2O. There is only one difference — one chose to stay inside itself, the other chose to flow out and to flow in.

Brothers and sisters, that is the whole of today’s lesson.

The lesson opens with a sentence that cuts to the heart: the separation between people is very often not because of different languages, different habits or different backgrounds, but because “I am not willing to lay myself down.”

Look at the brothers and sisters who have not spoken to each other for years, the ministry teams that in the end no longer have anything to do with one another, the families who live under one roof and yet each go their own way. Ask them why, and every one of them will give you a set of reasons: what he said back then, how she handled that matter, how I simply cannot cope with his personality.

But keep listening, listen right to the end, and you will hear the same sentence every time: “Why should I be the one to back down first?”

Separation never comes from the distance being too great. Separation comes because an “I” is standing in the middle.

When we cling to our own feelings, our interests, our opinions, our grievances and our hurts, we are like that drop of water that refuses to flow in. We guard ourselves, but we also guard our own loneliness; we keep ourselves intact, and leave ourselves out in the sun, waiting to evaporate.

So the key to unity has never been “changing other people”.

The key to unity is “laying ourselves down”.

The lesson puts it very clearly: when we are willing to place ourselves in Jesus’ hands and let him become our centre, we are no longer an isolated drop of water; we can be one with the body of Christ and enter his abundant kingdom.

Today we are going to look at three things together: first, to lay ourselves down is to choose to be separated no longer; second, what it actually means to lay ourselves down; third, how Jesus himself laid himself down. Then we will step together into three very concrete practices.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter of Unity Sent from Prison
sections.html:
Our theme passage comes from Philippians chapter 2.

The writer is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally dated to AD 61–62, during Paul’s first imprisonment in Rome. He says in the letter itself, “so that it became evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my bonds are in Christ” (Philippians 1:13). In other words, this letter, so full of joy, so full of unity, so full of hope, was not written on the lawn at a retreat. It was written in chains.

The church that received it was in Philippi. Philippi was a city in the province of Macedonia. In 42 BC Octavian and Antony defeated the forces of Caesar’s assassins there, and afterwards the city was raised to the rank of a Roman colony. What did it mean to be a colony? It meant that although the people of this city lived far away in northern Greece, they held Roman citizenship, enjoyed Roman law and freedom from certain taxes, and took great pride in being Romans.

This was a city that set enormous store by “status” and “standing”.

The Philippian church was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). In it were Lydia, the wealthy dealer in purple cloth; a slave girl possessed by a spirit, of the very lowest standing; and a jailer and his household from inside the Roman system. A businesswoman of high society, a slave girl once treated as a money-spinner, a military man in charge of a prison — sitting at the same table breaking bread. In the Roman society of the day, those three kinds of people could never have shared a table.

So from its very first day, the church at Philippi was a church that “could only exist because people laid themselves down”.

But people are people. By the time Paul wrote this letter, this church — the one he loved most and gave thanks for most — had developed cracks. In chapter 4 Paul names names: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.” (Philippians 4:2) Two sisters who had laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel were at odds.

It was in exactly this situation that Paul wrote, in chapter 2, the passage that has come to be called the “Christ hymn”. Scholars widely believe that Philippians 2:6–11 may have been a hymn sung in the early church. Paul brings this song out not to teach some lofty Christology, but to deal with a very practical matter —

he is dealing with separation in the church.

Look at what comes just before the passage: “If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ, if any consolation of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any tender mercies and compassion, make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind; doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:1–4)

Do you see it? The prescription Paul writes is not “you need to communicate more”, nor “you need to spend more time together”, but “each counting others better than himself” and “not just looking to his own things”.

Then he says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 2:5)

And straight after that comes the hymn: who, existing in the form of God … emptied himself.

Brothers and sisters, please remember this order. Faced with a church that had cracks in it, Paul did not first tell people to go and repair their relationships. He first turned their eyes to Jesus. Because unity is not a technique; unity is a life. And the name of that life is “emptying oneself”.

sections.heading: 1. To Lay Ourselves Down Is to Choose to Be Separated No Longer
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point uses a very beautiful picture: the picture of water — choose the ocean, and be no longer just a drop.

Two endings for a drop of water

The lesson says: if a drop of water insists on itself and refuses to merge, then however pure and however precious it may be, in the end it will still evaporate and vanish. But when that drop is willing to let itself go, to flow into a great river and on into the sea, it is no longer small; it becomes one with a mighty current and has enormous influence and worth.

There is a very deep truth in this picture: the nature of the water does not change; what changes is where it is.

The same you, placed inside “yourself”, is a drop of water that may evaporate at any moment; placed inside “the kingdom of God”, you are part of a river of living water.

The Bible really does have such a river. God took the prophet Ezekiel to see the temple, and he saw water flowing out from under the threshold of the house, growing deeper and deeper — ankle-deep, then knee-deep, then waist-deep, and at last “a river that could not be walked through” (Ezekiel 47:5). This river flowed eastward all the way down and into the Dead Sea. Scripture says: “It will happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes.” (Ezekiel 47:9)

Why is the Dead Sea called the Dead Sea? Here is a real geographical fact: the Dead Sea has an inlet but no outlet. The water of the Jordan flows in and can never flow out again; it can only evaporate. Day after day, year after year, the salt keeps concentrating, until today the Dead Sea is close to ten times as salty as ordinary sea water — so salty that fish cannot live in it, and not a blade of grass grows on its shores.

Brothers and sisters, the Dead Sea did not die for lack of water. The Dead Sea died because “everything goes in and nothing comes out”.

Some Christians are like that. They come to the meetings, they hear the messages, they receive the grace — but nothing ever flows out of them: no serving, no giving, no forgiving, no welcoming. Over time the grace in them does not become living water; instead it crystallises into something salty and bitter — fault-finding, comparing, judging, defensiveness.

Take in and never give out, and you become a Dead Sea. Be willing to flow out and to flow in, and you become a river of living water.

The one thing that was “not good”

Why must people be one? Because God laid this down when he made humankind.

In Genesis chapter 2, when God had finished making the heavens and the earth and everything in them, he called each thing “good” — until he looked at Adam on his own. Scripture records: “Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’” (Genesis 2:18)

Notice: there was no sin yet. Everything in Eden was perfect. And yet God said, “Not good.” In Genesis chapters 1 and 2, “not good” appears only this once; the one and only thing God called “not good” was being alone.

Separation is not a neutral state. Separation is the state God called “not good” from the very beginning.

So when did separation really come in? In Genesis chapter 3. Satan said to them, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) The moment humankind reached out and grasped at “I can be like God”, three layers of separation appeared at once. They hid from God — separation from God. Adam said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree” — separation from one another. They sewed fig leaves together to cover themselves — separation from themselves.

Isaiah puts it with great precision: “But your iniquities have separated you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he will not hear.” (Isaiah 59:2)

So the root of separation is sin, and the core of sin is the self-centred life. We want to grasp hold of ourselves, to leave our originally intended position, to take God’s place. This is exactly what 321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

By Genesis chapter 11, humanity’s collective self-centredness reached its peak: “They said, ‘Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.’” (Genesis 11:4)

Brothers and sisters, look at the motive behind the tower of Babel — “let’s make a name for ourselves”. And the result? Their language was confused, and humanity was scattered over the whole earth.

This is one of Scripture’s weightiest lessons: any unity built in order to “make a name for ourselves” will in the end always turn into separation. Because a crowd of self-centred people, even when they are packed onto the same building site, are not one; they simply happen to share the same interests for a while. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

There is only one kind of true unity: a company of people who have laid themselves down, before one and the same Lord.

Supporting evidence from science and psychology

The harm that isolation does to people is not just a matter of mood.

In 2010, Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine, drawing together 148 studies and data on more than 300,000 participants. They found that people with stronger social connections had about a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period. The research team pointed out that the health risk of weak social connection is comparable to well-known risk factors such as smoking and heavy drinking.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, sums up its conclusion in one sentence: what keeps people healthy and happy through life is neither wealth nor fame, but good relationships.

What science has measured is exactly what God said at the very start: “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

The English poet John Donne, who was also Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, wrote some words in 1624 that are still quoted today: “No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.”

No one is an island. And no drop of water can become an ocean on its own.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

Notice that the order itself deals with the self-centred life.

Why am I willing to lay myself down? Because Jesus is my role model; he laid himself down first. On what basis do I judge whether I ought to lay something down? Because the Bible is my standard, not my feelings. By what power can I let it go? Because the Holy Spirit is my guide, not my willpower. Once I have laid myself down, who takes the seat? Jesus reigns as King. Once I have laid myself down, who gets the glory? Jesus receives all the glory — not me, earning a fine reputation as someone “so big-hearted”.

A drop of water enters the ocean not because it has suddenly become great, but because it has finally agreed to leave the cup.

sections.heading: 2. What Does It Mean to “Lay Ourselves Down”?
sections.html:
This is the lesson’s second key point, and the most practical part of it.

The lesson begins with a very important definition: laying ourselves down does not mean denying our own worth; it means choosing not to make “self” our starting point.

This has to be made clear, or it is very easy to go astray.

The Bible never tells us to despise ourselves. God says we are made in his image, and to the people he chose he says, “you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). So “laying ourselves down” is not low self-esteem; it is not trampling ourselves underfoot; it is not becoming someone with no voice, no boundaries and no worth.

321 puts it exactly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out.

What does Paul say? “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“It is no longer I who live” — that is laying down. “But Christ lives in me” — that is entering into fullness.

A drop of water placed in the sea has not disappeared; it has become the sea.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing with another picture: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat that clings to itself will only ever be one grain. A grain of wheat that lets itself go bears much fruit.

Very well — so what, concretely, are we to lay down? The lesson lists six things. Let’s take them one at a time.

(1) Lay down comparison; stop trying to prove yourself by what you achieve

Comparison is one of the most draining things there is.

Because comparison never has a finish line. Beat this person, and there is another one ahead. Win this time, and next time you have to win again. Your worth turns into a proof that never ends.

Paul says: “For I say through the grace that was given me, to every man who is among you, not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3)

“To think reasonably” is the Greek sōphronein — to be clear-headed, sound-minded, to think in line with reality. The most frightening thing about comparison is that it robs us of clear thinking: it magnifies others and distorts ourselves, until in the end there is no truth left in our eyes, only rankings.

The cure for comparison is not “actually I’m not so bad”, but “my worth is not found here”.

Brothers and sisters, your worth is not what you have achieved; it is what the Lord has done for you. The cross has already put a price on you — the life of God’s only Son. That price will not go up because you had a good year at work, and it will not go down because you were weak this quarter.

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life. When your mindset turns from “I have to prove myself” to “I have already been proved”, your life loosens. Only someone who no longer needs to prove himself can truly rejoice at someone else’s good news.

(2) Lay down suspicion; put both yourself and others into God’s hands

Suspicion is separation’s favourite building material.

Psychology has a very well-known phenomenon called the “fundamental attribution error”, formally named by the social psychologist Lee Ross in 1977. It describes how, when we explain other people’s behaviour, we tend to put it down to their character, but when we explain our own, we tend to put it down to our circumstances.

He hasn’t answered my message because he’s a cold sort of person. I haven’t answered his because I’ve just been so busy lately.

The same thing, measured with two rulers.

Brothers and sisters, a great many of the misunderstandings in the church grow in exactly this way. We mean no harm; it’s just that without realising it we explain others by the worst assumption and ourselves by the best excuse.

What is the Bible’s standard? “Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

The Lord Jesus says it more sharply still: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

Laying down suspicion does not mean naively believing there is nothing wrong with anyone; it means handing the judgement seat back to God. Suspicion is so exhausting because we are holding three jobs at once: prosecutor, judge and victim. 321 says: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The judgement seat is God’s place; no wonder we can’t sit comfortably when we climb into it.

So put yourself into God’s hands, and put that person into God’s hands too. You will find that you have not only let him go; you have let yourself go as well.

(3) Lay down hurt; choose to forgive and to reconnect

This is the hardest of them all, because the hurt is real.

Let me first say something as a pastor: the Bible never says “that was nothing”. Forgiveness actually starts by admitting there is a debt. If there is no debt, there is nothing to cancel.

Paul teaches us: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” (Colossians 3:13)

Look at the standard at the end — “even as Christ forgave you”. The measure of our forgiving is not whether the other person deserves it, but how the Lord has already treated me.

One frequently cited study is an experiment by Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and colleagues, published in 2001 in the journal Psychological Science. The researchers asked participants to call to mind, in turn, an unforgiving frame of mind and a forgiving one, while measuring their physiological responses. They found that when people dwelt on grudges and imagined revenge, their blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose markedly; when they entered a frame of mind of empathy and forgiveness, these measures settled down.

Brothers and sisters, this shows one thing: when you will not forgive, you are the one bearing the consequences of the other person’s sin. Someone has put it well — refusing to forgive is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to drop.

But the lesson does not stop at “forgive”. What it says is “forgive and reconnect”.

Forgiveness is one-sided; I can complete it on my own before God. Reconnection is two-sided; it takes time, it takes wisdom, and sometimes it takes boundaries. But a Christian should not use “I’ve already forgiven him” as a reason to put that person in the freezer of his heart for good. Forgiveness with no willingness to move towards reconnection can easily become nothing more than a more respectable form of separation.

What did the Lord Jesus do on the cross? He came that he “might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility through it” (Ephesians 2:16). He did not only pardon; he made the two into one body.

(4) Lay down self-interest; learn to think of others

Paul’s words are still ringing in our ears: “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” (Philippians 2:4)

Notice that Paul did not say “don’t look to your own things”; he said “not just”. The Bible is not asking us to be irresponsible; it is asking us to widen our field of vision.

Adam Grant, an organisational psychologist at the Wharton School, divides people in his 2013 book Give and Take into three types: givers, takers and matchers. He points out a fascinating finding: in many workplace performance rankings, the people at the bottom are often givers — but the people who climb to the very top are givers too. The difference is that successful givers know how to give wisely and give with boundaries, rather than being drained until they run dry.

That bears out exactly the Bible’s order: life first, then ministry; first be connected with God, and then you can keep on giving.

Brothers and sisters, 321 says: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

When our service goes wrong, it is often not because we are not trying hard enough but because the order has been turned upside down. We put ministry ahead of relationships, so to get the job done we are willing to hurt people; we put relationships ahead of life, so to keep the peace we refuse to face ourselves.

Laying down self-interest means putting the order back where it belongs.

(5) Lay down your standards; stop criticising and finding fault with others

This one needs careful discernment, so we must say it precisely.

“Laying down standards” in the lesson never means giving up the standard of biblical truth. The Bible is our standard; that will never change. What the lesson means is the standards we make up ourselves and then use to measure other people — how I think worship should be sung, what time I think children should go to bed, how many minutes I think a co-worker should take to reply to a message, what I think a spiritual person should look like.

Faced with arguments over eating or not eating, keeping days or not keeping them, Paul says: “But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.” (Romans 14:10)

The Lord Jesus also says, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.” (Matthew 7:1)

Fault-finding has a secret: the people who find fault with others are in fact the least forgiving towards themselves. They carry a very strict ruler in their hearts; they measure themselves with it first, and then everyone else. They spend all day doing God’s performance reviews for him, yet they have never once enjoyed God’s grace.

Brothers and sisters, if you notice that lately you are especially quick to find other people irritating, don’t rush to deal with that person. First come before the Lord and ask: Lord, is there a place in me that your grace has not yet touched?

(6) Lay down pride; be willing to make up what others lack, and work hand in hand

The last one is really the root of the other five. Comparison, suspicion, holding grudges, self-interest, fault-finding — behind every one of them is the same thing: pride.

Scripture says, “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice.” (Proverbs 13:10) And again, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

And God’s attitude towards these two kinds of people is very clear: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Notice the word “resists”. The original, antitassomai, is a military term for an army drawn up in battle array against an enemy. It is not merely that God does not like proud people; God has drawn up his battle lines and stands facing them. A proud person finds that every effort he makes has to face God’s army.

So what does humility actually look like in the church? Paul says, “For as the body is one, and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.” (1 Corinthians 12:12) “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you.’” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

Here is the mystery of the body: no member is complete, so every member needs the others. The hand is deft, but the hand cannot see; the eye can see, but the eye cannot pick anything up. God deliberately made us incomplete, so that we cannot do without working hand in hand.

The phrase the lesson uses is “make up what others lack”. What a beautiful phrase that is. When a humble person sees a brother’s lack, his first reaction is not to comment on it, but to fill it.

Ecclesiastes says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10) “A threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12)

When three strands are twisted around one another, the friction makes them hold each other up, and their strength is far more than three times that of one. This is exactly the principle of 321’s “235 relationships”: two selfless people becoming spiritual companions — that is your “2”; bringing forth spiritual parents and spiritual children — that is the “3”; the fivefold ministries working hand in hand to become a team of spiritual comrades — that is the “5”.

One person can go fast; only a company of people can go far. And what keeps a company of people walking together is not ability but humility.

sections.heading: 3. Jesus Our Role Model: He Laid Himself Down, and It Was for Us
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point takes us to the highest place, which is also the lowest — the cross.

The lesson quotes Philippians chapter 2. Let us read the whole passage now:

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

Seven steps down

Brothers and sisters, walk down with me, one step at a time.

The first step: “existing in the form of God.” The Greek word for “form” is morphē. It does not mean outward appearance but the expression of one’s essential nature — he was God from the beginning, and all the glory of God’s very being was his.

The second step: “didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped.” The original word, harpagmos, means a prize to be clutched tightly and kept for oneself. What Satan grasped at in the beginning, what Adam and Eve grasped at in the beginning, was precisely “equality with God”. Yet the One who was equal with God from the start did not treat it as something he had to cling to.

The third step: “but emptied himself.” The original is ekenōsen, from the verb kenoō, “to empty”. Notice that what he emptied was not his divinity — he never stopped being God. What he emptied himself of was his way of using his rights, the display of his glory, his entitlement to be served.

The fourth step: “taking the form of a servant.” Here again is morphē. He did not “play the part” of a servant; he truly and really took on the nature of a servant — from Lord of all things to doulos, a slave.

The fifth step: “being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form.” He became truly human, knowing weariness, hunger and tears.

The sixth step: “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death.” He obeyed to the very end, until his last breath. In Gethsemane he said, “not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42)

The seventh step: “yes, the death of the cross.”

To the Philippians, this seventh step landed like a hammer blow.

In the Roman Empire the cross was a punishment reserved for slaves, rebels and non-citizens. By law, Roman citizens could not be crucified. The Roman statesman Cicero, in his speech in defence of Rabirius, said that the very word “cross” should be kept far not only from the body of a Roman citizen, but even from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears.

What the Philippians were proudest of was their Roman citizenship; and one of the greatest guarantees of that citizenship was “I will never have to go to a cross”.

Yet Paul tells them: the One you worship came all the way down from the highest place there is, right down to the place you dare not even think about.

Brothers and sisters, this is the perfect answer to what it means to “lay ourselves down”.

The way down is the way up

But the story does not stop at verse 8. Paul goes on:

“Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” (Philippians 2:9–11)

Do you see it? When the seven steps down were complete, God himself raised him to the highest place.

This is an unchanging law in the kingdom of God: God does not compete with those who grab for power; God lifts up those who let go.

The Lord Jesus said it himself: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28)

And he lived it out before our eyes. At the Last Supper, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he got up, laid aside his outer garments, wrapped a towel around his waist, and washed his disciples’ feet one by one — including the feet that were about to walk out and betray him.

He let go, and we gained. He came down, and we were lifted up. He was shut out from his Father’s face and cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46) — so that we would never be separated again.

Ephesians puts it in the plainest terms: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation.” (Ephesians 2:14)

In the temple in Jerusalem there really was a stone wall between the Court of the Gentiles and the inner courts, and on it was carved a warning: any foreigner who passes this barrier will have himself to blame for his death. That wall was the most concrete symbol of human separation.

On the cross, the Lord Jesus tore that wall down.

Brothers and sisters, what are all our separations today compared with that wall? The Lord has already torn down the greatest wall of all, the wall between God and humankind — and here we are, over one remark, one incident, one misunderstanding, building new walls between brothers.

The lesson says: if we say we want to follow Christ’s example, we must learn to lay ourselves down. Not in order to disappear, but in order to take part in a greater, eternal plan.

321 says: Jesus is my role model. A role model is not something you hang on the wall to admire; a role model is someone you follow. The way he walked is the way we walk.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness, from Separation to Unity
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us look at today’s message once more within the framework of 321.

First, the heart of this lesson is the very heart of 321’s message: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

The root of separation is the self-centred life. The door to unity is selflessness. The whole Bible, from Genesis chapter 3, “you will be like God”, to the New Jerusalem in Revelation, where “God himself will be with them”, is about one thing: when people snatch themselves back, God is pushed out; when people lay themselves down, God moves in.

Second, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

One of Satan’s specialities is manufacturing separation. In Eden he set humankind against God; in Cain he set man against man; in the church he sets brother against brother. His strategy is always the same: first make you feel you have been wronged, then make you feel you have every right to hold on to that grievance.

And there is only one way to break it: lay yourself down. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Third, the fourfold shift of perspective.

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — not “how could he treat me like this?” but “Lord, what do you want to do in this?” From the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal — however great this grievance, it lasts a few decades at most; but if this relationship is reconciled, it will stretch on into eternity. From the worldly to the godly — not settling it by human methods, but overcoming by God’s methods.

Fourth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Notice the order. Unity belongs to “relationships”, the fourth item. You cannot skip the first three and go straight to it. Someone whose mindset has not changed will not have a changed life; someone whose life has not changed will not have changed daily living; and someone whose daily living has not changed will never manage to mend their relationships.

So today’s real lesson is not “whom do I need to make peace with?” but “will I let my mindset be changed?” Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Fifth, the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Many people who cannot get along with others actually cannot get along with themselves; and they cannot get along with themselves because they have not yet truly come into line with God.

Sixth, the 920 practice.

Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. The 920 practice is this: in front of that “2”, live a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice: of those nine graces, at least six can only grow within relationships. Shut away in a room on your own, you cannot learn patience, you cannot learn kindness, you cannot learn gentleness. God has placed that “difficult” person beside you not to wear you down, but so that you will bear fruit.

Seventh, the 235 relationships.

With a selfless person, become a “2” — spiritual companions who hold each other up; build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working hand in hand. “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

Eighth, the Goal: establish God’s system.

The lesson’s closing words put it superbly: the kingdom of God is not a human organisation, not someone’s personal platform, but the realm where Jesus reigns as King. God’s system is not about gathering people under a name; it is about gathering people under a King.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Steps into a Life of Unity
sections.html:
The lesson gives three practices. We’ll take them one by one, and we’ll go deeper with each by using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: Where will I put this drop of water that I am?

The lesson asks us to meditate on three questions every day and pray over them:

First, am I still “clinging to myself”?

Second, is my choice to protect my feelings, my reputation, my position, my church — or am I willing to lay myself down and enter the kingdom of God?
