Third, am I willing to say, “Lord, I want to put myself into your ocean, to be one with you and one with my brothers and sisters”?

The lesson also gives a very concrete action: draw a drop of water on a piece of paper, write inside it one thing you are willing to lay down today, and offer it to God.

Brothers and sisters, don’t underestimate this action. Writing it down turns something vague into something definite. Vague repentance never changes anything; repentance that has been written down gives the Holy Spirit something to work on.

Now let’s walk it through the eight stages.

Information: you have heard it today — separation is clinging to yourself; unity is laying yourself down.

Revelation: information does not change people; revelation does. So please stop and pray: Lord, show me what it really is that I am clinging to right now. When the Holy Spirit points out in your heart that name, that matter, that scene, you have received revelation.

Conviction: once you have seen it, you must say “yes”. Not “but he was in the wrong too”, but “Lord, on this one I submit.”

Implementation: write it inside that drop of water and offer it up concretely.

Evaluation: a week later, look back — did I really let it go, or did I only push it down for a while?

Correction: if you find you have taken it back again, don’t condemn yourself; simply let it go once more.

Repetition: do it again every morning. Laying yourself down is not a one-time decision; it is a daily choice.

Multiplication: when you have truly experienced it, go and tell someone else. Let the story of your drop of water become someone else’s invitation into the ocean.

Practice two: Choose unity, not independence

The lesson asks us this week to do one thing deliberately that will bring us into unity:

First, take the initiative to contact someone with whom you have had a misunderstanding.

Second, in your team, take the initiative to cooperate rather than insisting on your own way.

Third, at home or in your service, choose to “take a step back” so that someone else can flourish.

Fourth, refuse to complain; choose praise and thanksgiving.

The lesson says: you will find that the moment you lay down “self”, God’s glory and power begin to flow.

On that last point, psychology offers good confirmation too. In 2003 Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Participants were divided into three groups, which each week wrote down, respectively, things they were grateful for, things that troubled or annoyed them, and neutral events. After several weeks the group that wrote about gratitude not only rated their lives as a whole more positively, but also complained of fewer physical symptoms.

Complaint and gratitude look at the same world, but they end up with two different lives.

Brothers and sisters, please pay special attention to the words “take the initiative”. Unity never happens by itself. Unity always needs someone to move first.

And the one who moves first is very often the one who is more like Jesus.

How do the eight stages work here? Revelation: Lord, whom do you want me to step out towards first this week? — usually a name comes to mind at once, and you will very much want to swap it for another. Conviction: all right, it is him. Implementation: within this week, send that message, make that phone call. Evaluation: am I going to repair the relationship, or to prove that I am the more spiritual one? Correction: if my motive is not pure, I adjust it before God first, and then go. Multiplication: carry this culture of taking the initiative into your small group, your family, your team.

Practice three: Live for the kingdom of God

The lesson asks us to meditate on two questions:

First, am I willing to give myself for the kingdom of God, and not only for my church or for myself?

Second, am I willing to lay down the boundaries between churches and the labels on ministries, and to work for the vision of unity?

Then the lesson gives a crucial sentence: the kingdom of God is not a human organisation, not someone’s personal platform, but the realm where Jesus reigns as King. When you live for the kingdom, you will bring about limitless influence.

Brothers and sisters, there is a very important distinction here.

The prayer the Lord Jesus taught us does not begin with “May my ministry flourish”, but “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) He also said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33)

Social psychology has a famous experiment. In 1954, at a camp called Robbers Cave in Oklahoma, Muzafer Sherif divided a group of boys who did not know one another into two teams. After a few competitions, fierce hostility quickly sprang up between the two teams — calling each other names, fighting over territory, damaging each other’s belongings.

Next the researchers had the two teams eat together and watch films together, hoping that “spending more time together” would dissolve the hostility. It failed. Simply putting people together only gave them more opportunities to attack each other.

What really turned things around was a “higher shared goal” that the researchers deliberately set up: the camp’s water supply line broke, and the two teams had to work together to fix it; the truck bringing the food broke down, and the two teams had to pull on the rope together to get it moving. Only when the two teams had a shared goal that neither could achieve alone did the hostility begin to crumble.

Brothers and sisters, this experiment tells us one thing: unity does not come from “spending more time together”; unity comes from “a shared, higher goal”.

Unity between churches is the same. We will not become one just by holding a few more joint meetings. We are one because we have one King, one kingdom, and one charge that will not change until death.

“There is one body and one Spirit, even as you also were called in one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all, and in us all.” (Ephesians 4:4–6)

Going deeper with the eight stages here: Revelation — Lord, have I secretly mistaken my platform for your kingdom? Implementation — this month, pray specifically, at least once, for another church and another ministry. Evaluation — when someone else is flourishing more than I am, what is my first reaction inside? Correction — bring the envy to the cross. Repetition — until rejoicing at someone else’s revival becomes your instinct.

A Gentle Reminder: To choose unity is to choose to let Jesus be King

After the practices, the lesson adds a gentle reminder. I want to read it out in full:

You are no longer that lonely drop of water, but the drop that is willing to enter the ocean. You no longer live for yourself, but for Christ. Jesus will be glorified in you.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the logic here.

Unity is not a social goal; unity is a question of kingship.

Why can two people not get along? Because inside each of them sits a king. When I let Jesus be King, and you let Jesus be King, there is only one King left between us — and then unity is not something forced; it simply happens.

Paul says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

These are the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

John the Baptist summed up the lesson of a whole life in a single short sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

sections.heading: Closing Word: Only by Laying Ourselves Down Can We Enter True Revival
sections.html:
The lesson closes with very powerful words: revival is not an event, nor an atmosphere, but a company of people willing to let Jesus be Lord, willing to lay themselves down, to enter God’s kingdom, to be one with each other and to walk with God.

But what does revival look like in the Bible? Acts chapter 2 tells us: “All who believed were together, and had all things in common.” (Acts 2:44) “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” (Acts 2:46–47)

Look at the order: first “together”, first “with one accord”, and only then “the Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved”.

Unity comes first; revival comes after.

The Lord Jesus’ own prayer runs the same way: “that they may all be one … that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) The key to the world believing is not our eloquence, nor our venues, but our unity.

The psalm says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” And then, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:1, 3)

The blessing God commands comes down “there” — on the place where brothers live together in unity.

So the lesson says: if each of us is willing to lay ourselves down, separation will have nowhere left to stand, and the glory of Jesus will be greatly revealed.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord sets a very simple choice before you.

Will this drop of water that you are stay in the cup, or flow into the ocean?

Will you go on being the one who says, “Why should I be the one to back down first?” — or will you be the one who steps out first?

Will you live for your own name, or for the kingdom of Jesus?

A drop of water placed in the ocean does not disappear. It becomes part of the ocean, and goes to places it could never have reached on its own in a whole lifetime.

May each of us say to the Lord today: Lord, I am willing. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)
“that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21)
practices: Choose unity, not independence
Live for the kingdom of God
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and were obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. You laid everything down, and it was for us. You broke down the middle wall of separation, reconciling us to God and reconciling us to one another.

Lord, forgive us. So often we cling to our own feelings, our interests, our opinions, our grievances and our hurts, and will not let go. We wear ourselves out with comparison, judge others with suspicion, build high walls out of our hurts, and condemn our brothers by our own standards. Have mercy on us, we pray.
Holy Spirit, shine your light on me and name it plainly; show me the one thing I must lay down today. Give me the courage to write it down, to offer it up, and never to take it back.
Lord, I want to put this drop of water that I am into your kingdom. Let me be separated no longer, but bear witness to your glory in unity.
Make me the one who takes the initiative first, the one who makes up what others lack, the one who rejoices for the kingdom.
Let your kingdom come; let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The lesson says, “The separation between people is very often not because of different languages, different habits or different backgrounds, but because ‘I am not willing to lay myself down.’” Set this beside Philippians 2:3–4: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” Share: of the six things the lesson lists — comparison, suspicion, hurt, self-interest, standards and pride — which one has the Holy Spirit touched most deeply in you today? What, specifically, are you willing to lay down?

The Lord Jesus prayed, “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) Share: towards which brother or sister will you take the first step this week? How do you plan to do it? Ask the group to pray together about this, and follow up with one another at the next meeting.
l020.title: Lay Down Self, No More Separation
l020.subtitle: Separation Is Holding On to Self; Unity Is Letting Go of Self
l020.partTitle: Unit 2 · Jesus — The Focus of Revival

sections.heading: Introduction: One Question Can Change a Whole Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to learn together a question that is very short, yet carries great power. It is only three words long: “Whose is it?”

One day the Pharisees laid a trap for Jesus. They asked him: is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not? It was a question that would offend someone whichever way he answered. But Jesus did not fall into their snare. He did just one thing — he had them bring him a coin, and then he asked the simplest of questions.

Scripture records: “He asked them, ‘Whose is this image and inscription?’ They said to him, ‘Caesar’s.’ Then he said to them, ‘Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’” (Matthew 22:20–21)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord Jesus did not debate politics with them, nor argue about tax law. He simply held up that coin and asked, “Whose is this?” The moment the question was asked, the answer appeared; and once the answer appeared, it was clear what to do.

“Whose is it?” — this is a question the Lord Jesus himself used. Today he wants to place this same question into the hands of each one of us.

What are you holding in your hands right now? A job, a marriage, a child, some savings, a position, a dream? This morning, in the early light, the Lord Jesus gently asks you: “Whose is this?”

The reason we live under such weight is often not that what we are holding is too heavy, but that we have hoisted onto our own shoulders things that do not belong to us. We treat God’s estate as our own property, and what God has entrusted to us as something we own; so at the first rustle of trouble we tense up, we clutch, we cannot sleep.

This is a question of focus.

Brothers and sisters who take photographs know this: with the same lens and the same view, focus on the foreground and the mountains behind dissolve into a blur; focus on the distant mountains and the flowers in front melt into a haze of light. The lens hasn’t changed, the light hasn’t changed; only the focus has changed. But change the focus, and the whole picture is completely different.

Life is like that too. What we see depends not on what is in front of us, but on where our focus is.

Psychology has a very famous experiment that bears this out. In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris of Harvard University published a study in the journal Perception entitled “Gorillas in Our Midst”. They asked participants to watch a short video and count how many times the team in white passed the ball. Halfway through, someone in a gorilla suit strolled into the scene, beat their chest, and stayed there for several seconds. And the result? About half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all.

It was not that their eyes were faulty; their focus was completely taken up with something else. Psychologists call this “inattentional blindness”.

Brothers and sisters, this is a sobering reminder: get the focus wrong, and even the most obvious fact becomes invisible. How often the Lord Jesus is standing right in the middle of our lives, waving to us, while we are busy counting our own passes, doing our own sums, guarding our own face — and we do not see him at all.

So today’s lesson is not asking us to try harder; it is asking us to refocus.

Today we are going to ask the same question four times: Whose is my life? Whose is my family? Whose is my wealth? Whose is the church I give myself to? When the answer to all four questions comes back to Jesus, our focus is set true; and once our focus is set true, our whole life comes into alignment.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, Two Settings, One Lord
sections.html: Before we turn to the four areas, let us first get to know today’s two theme passages. Once we understand their settings, we will better understand their weight.

sections.heading: 1. Romans 14: Declaring Who Is Lord amid the Tension of Judging One Another
sections.html:
Romans was written by the apostle Paul. It is generally thought that Paul wrote this letter towards the end of his third missionary journey, around AD 56–57, in Corinth in Greece, intending to send it to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited in person.

The Roman church was in a very particular situation: it had believers from a Jewish background and believers from a Gentile background. In AD 49 the Roman emperor Claudius had ordered the Jews expelled from Rome (Acts 18:2 records this). A few years later the ban was relaxed, and Jewish believers gradually returned to Rome, only to find that Gentile believers were now the majority in the church, and that the way they met, their eating habits and their rules about keeping days were no longer what they had been.

So friction set in. Some ate everything; some ate only vegetables. Some esteemed one day above another; some esteemed every day alike. They could not stand the sight of each other, and so they began to judge and to despise.

How did Paul deal with it? He did not begin by ruling on who was right and who was wrong. He began by pulling everyone’s eyes away from “what I think” and back to “who the Lord is”. He said, “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” (Romans 14:7–8) Then verse 9 at once gives the grounds: “For to this end Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.”

Brothers and sisters, look closely at Paul’s logic. He does not say “you need to love each other a bit more”. He says “you are not your own”. Once the question of ownership is settled, the question of judging settles itself. For since I am not my own, my brother is not mine either; to his own lord he stands or falls (Romans 14:4).

“We are the Lord’s” — here the original uses a simple but powerful possessive: we “belong to the Lord”. This is not a sentimental phrase. It is a title deed.

sections.heading: 2. Acts 17: Declaring the Source of All Things in a City of Idols
sections.html:
The second passage comes from a completely different setting. Acts 17 records Paul in Athens. Athens was the intellectual capital of the world at the time, and a city of idols as well. Scripture says that Paul’s “spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols” (Acts 17:16).

The Athenians brought him to the Areopagus to hear this new teaching of his. How did Paul begin? He did not start by denouncing idols. He started from an altar “to an unknown god”, and then declared: the God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands; nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all people life and breath and all things.

Then he spoke today’s second theme verse: “‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’” (Acts 17:28)

Brothers and sisters, this verse pushes “Whose is it?” as far as it can go. It is not only that my possessions belong to God; my very breath belongs to God. It is not only that my achievements belong to God; the fact that I can still sit here at this moment, with my heart still beating, depends entirely on him.

Our bodies breathe about twenty thousand times a day, and we never have to remind ourselves to breathe. The earth beneath our feet is racing around the sun at about 29.8 kilometres a second — about 107,000 kilometres an hour — and yet we sit here perfectly steady. None of this is to be taken for granted. It is grace. We are simply living in God’s world, using God’s air, counting God’s days.

Two passages: one says, “whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s”; the other says, “in him we live, move, and have our being”. One speaks of the Lord’s ownership by redemption; the other, of his ownership by creation. Like two hands, they set us upright together: we belonged to him from the beginning, and we have been bought back at a great price and become his once again.

In his Institutes of the Christian Religion, Calvin wrote words that have been quoted ever since: “We are not our own … we are God’s.” That is the foundation of today’s lesson.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Teaching on Focus — Where Is Your Focus?
sections.html:
Everyone has a focus. It is whatever we care about most, pay most attention to, think about most often. Our focus is not something that crosses our mind now and then; it is the thing that surfaces automatically the moment we grow quiet. It is the first name we worry about when we wake in the night, the first problem we think of when we open our eyes in the morning.

The Lord Jesus said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:21) Where your heart is, there your focus is; and where your focus is, there your life is heading.

The lesson gives us three very practical diagnoses:

sections.heading: 1. Focus on Yourself, and You Easily Become Self-Pitying, Boastful and Selfish
sections.html:
Psychology has a phenomenon that has been confirmed again and again, called the “self-reference effect”. In 1977 T. B. Rogers and his colleagues published research in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology showing that people remember information related to themselves especially well and process it especially fast. In other words, we are born gathering up the world with ourselves at the centre.

This is not some new discovery of psychology; it is the fall that the Bible described long ago. In the 321 vision we say: the root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and the root of the problem is pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights that are not ours, wanting to take God’s place.

People whose focus is on themselves boast when things go well, pity themselves when things go badly, and turn selfish when others are blessed. On the surface these look like three different emotions, but they spring from one and the same root disease — I have put myself in the dead centre of the frame.

sections.heading: 2. Focus on People, and You Easily Become Dependent, Hurt and Disappointed
sections.html:
People are loved by God, but people cannot be our God. When our focus is on people, we let one remark from someone decide our mood for the whole day, and let the look on someone’s face decide our worth for a whole lifetime.

The prophet Jeremiah warned of this long ago: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.” (Jeremiah 17:5) And a little further on: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh.” (Jeremiah 17:7)

Between blessing and curse, the only difference is a focus.

sections.heading: 3. Focus on Your Circumstances, and You Will Waver and Be Anxious
sections.html:
Peter once walked on the surface of the sea. Scripture records: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:30)

Brothers and sisters, notice that the wind had been there all along, and so had the waves. While Peter was walking on the water, the wind and waves were just as strong. What changed was not the wind and waves but the focus — he went from looking at the Lord to looking at the wind.

We are the same today. When we fix our eyes on exchange rates, on medical test results, on our children’s report cards, on changes in staffing, our hearts rise and fall with those numbers. Circumstances are the waves; focus is the feet. Stand on the waves and you will surely sway; stand on the Lord and the waves become a road.

sections.heading: 4. The Real Answer: Whether We Live or Die, We Are the Lord’s
sections.html:
But the Bible does not stop at a diagnosis; it gives us the answer: “If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” (Romans 14:8)

What this means is that all ownership of our lives belongs to Jesus. We do not live for ourselves; we live for the Lord.

Paul says it even more clearly elsewhere: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:15)

Brothers and sisters, Christ died for us not only so that we would be forgiven, but so that we would change bosses, change centres, change focus.

In the 321 vision, this is exactly the key step from the old self, which is self-centred, to the new self, which is selfless. Selflessness is not wiping ourselves out, not becoming worthless; selflessness is no longer having ourselves at the centre, so that the boundless Lord can live out his boundless life in us. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Our focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. This is the most basic and the most vital practice in 321.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Whose Is My Life?
sections.html:
The scriptural basis

“Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)

There are two sentences here, like two nails, that fix the question “Whose is my life?” firmly in place.

The first: “You are not your own.” The second: “You were bought with a price.”

For “bought with a price”, the Greek uses the word for buying a slave in the marketplace: someone pays the full price and takes a slave away from the market, so that he now belongs to a new master. The price paid for us was not silver or gold, but the precious blood of Christ. Peter says: “knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things, with silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ.” (1 Peter 1:18–19)

Scripture interpreting Scripture: from creation to redemption, all points to one conclusion

From creation: “For in him we live, move, and have our being.” (Acts 17:28) Our life was received in the first place. Paul’s question cuts deep: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

From redemption: “Christ died, rose, and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.” (Romans 14:9)

Add the authority of creation to the authority of redemption, and there is only one answer: my life belongs to Jesus.

An example from daily life

A sister once told me that every morning when she opened her eyes, the first words in her heart used to be: “What do I need to get done today?” Later she began learning to change them to something else: “Lord, what do you want me to get done today?” She said the two sentences differed by only a few words, yet her whole day became completely different. Her diary used to be her master; now her diary is her tool.

It’s like transferring ownership of a car. It’s still the same car, and still the same road map, but someone else is now holding the steering wheel.

Supporting evidence from science and psychology

In 1966 the psychologist Julian Rotter put forward the theory of “locus of control”, distinguishing between an internal and an external locus. Research has found that people who are overly convinced that everything depends on their own control actually feel stronger stress and frustration when they face situations beyond their control.

What our faith offers is a third way: it is not I who am in control, nor fate, but the Lord who loved me and gave himself for me who reigns. Handing him the steering wheel is not abandoning responsibility; it is returning to our originally intended position.

Not far into the opening of his Confessions, Augustine wrote: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” For more than sixteen hundred years these words have been proved true again and again.

Applying the 321 Vision

In 321 we say, “let Jesus be King”. Letting him be King is not a slogan; it is a whole series of concrete handovers: letting him be King of my time, King of my choices, King of my work, King of my future.

When we make decisions, we no longer act on our own authority or do what we please; we first grow quiet and ask: “Lord, this is yours. How do you want to use it?”

This is the shift of perspective — from the human perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly perspective to the heavenly, from the temporary perspective to the eternal, from the worldly perspective to the godly.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Whose Is My Family?
sections.html:
The scriptural basis

“Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” (Psalm 127:3)

Notice the words “of Yahweh” and “his”. Whatever is given has a Giver. Children are a heritage, a trust — not a possession.

Hannah understood this. She pleaded bitterly for a son, and God gave her Samuel. Yet she said: “I prayed for this child, and Yahweh has given me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I have also given him to Yahweh. As long as he lives he is given to Yahweh.” (1 Samuel 1:27–28)

Brothers and sisters, the child Hannah had prayed for so long to receive — she was willing to give him back. Because she knew from the start: this child had always been the Lord’s.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: Abraham’s mountain, Job’s ash heap

In Genesis 22 God told Abraham to offer up his only son, Isaac. After three days on the road, at the very moment the knife was raised, the angel stopped him and said: “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” (Genesis 22:12)

What God wanted was not Isaac’s life; what God wanted was the place Isaac held in Abraham’s heart. When Abraham let go, Isaac was safer than ever.

Job lost ten children in a single day. He fell to the ground and said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.” (Job 1:21)

The lesson puts it well: learn to cherish when you have, and still give thanks when you lose. The first half is Hannah; the second half is Job.

Supporting evidence from psychology: the tighter you hold, the more it hurts

In 2014 Holly Schiffrin and colleagues published a study in the Journal of Child and Family Studies entitled “Helping or Hovering?” It found that “helicopter parenting” — parents who over-involve themselves and over-control — was associated with lower autonomy, lower life satisfaction and higher levels of depression among university students.

This is not telling us not to love our children; it is reminding us that when love is joined to “he is mine”, it turns into control, and when love is joined to “he is the Lord’s”, it turns into blessing.

An example from daily life

Anyone who flies a kite knows that the string needs tension, but you also have to be willing to let it out. Grip it tight and the kite won’t fly high; let go completely and the kite falls to the ground. The person who really knows how to fly a kite keeps the string in hand and their eyes on the sky.

It is the same with our families. In our hands we hold the bond of love, but our eyes must be on the Lord who commands the wind.

Applying the 321 Vision

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The pain in many families comes from turning this order upside down — first demanding that things be done right, then demanding peaceful relationships, and only last of all giving any thought to life.

When something goes wrong with someone in our family, our first move is not to scramble in a panic or rush to correct them, but first to entrust them to Jesus and let him work in person. Scripture says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:7)

This is also the most real training ground for the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; our family members are the “2” closest to us. In front of them, live a selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. What a home needs most is not someone better at arguing their case, but someone who humbles themselves first.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: Whose Is My Wealth?
sections.html:
The scriptural basis

When David was old, he gathered materials for the temple, and the whole people gave willingly and gladly. David prayed before Yahweh:

“Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head above all.” (1 Chronicles 29:11)

“But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” (1 Chronicles 29:14)

Brothers and sisters, read verse 14 once more: “we have given you of your own.”

So giving was never “me giving to God”; giving is “me returning to God what is God’s”. From first to last, we are only the ones it passes through.

The psalm puts it even more directly: “The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.” (Psalm 24:1)

Scripture interpreting Scripture: no one can serve two masters

The Lord Jesus said: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

Notice that the Lord Jesus did not say, “Don’t love money too much”; he said, “You cannot serve two masters at once.” Once money takes the master’s seat, it is no longer just a tool. It becomes the master; it gives orders; it keeps us awake at night.

The Lord also said: “Beware! Keep yourselves from covetousness, for a man’s life doesn’t consist of the abundance of the things which he possesses.” (Luke 12:15)

So the question has never been “How much do I have?” The question is “Whose is it?”

The attitude of giving

“Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)

“Cheerful” — the Greek word here is the root of our English word “hilarious”, carrying the sense of joyful, wholehearted willingness. What God wants is not giving that has been squeezed out of us, but giving that flows out of joy.

Proverbs also says, “Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase.” (Proverbs 3:9) The words “first fruits” matter a great deal — not what is left over, but what comes first.

Supporting evidence from psychology: those who give are happier

In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn and Lara Aknin of the University of British Columbia, with Michael Norton of Harvard University, published a study in the journal Science entitled “Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness”. They gave participants a sum of money; one group was told to spend it on themselves, the other to spend it on someone else. They found that by the end of the day the group that had spent the money on others was markedly happier.

When God made us, he built this circuitry into us. The Lord Jesus said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35) This is not merely an exhortation; it is the design of the universe.

Examples from daily life, and a famous saying

In his journal in 1949 the missionary Jim Elliot wrote: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Six years later he was martyred for the gospel in Ecuador.

Brothers and sisters, the money in our hands will one day all be left behind on this earth; only what has been exchanged for eternity can truly be taken with us.

One brother described it vividly: we are only God’s bank card, not God’s vault. The card has our name printed on it, but the money in the account belongs to the Owner.

Applying the 321 Vision

In 321, “let Jesus be King” has to reach all the way to our wallets. Because the wallet is the doorway of the heart — “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:21)

When the Lord moves us to give, being able to let go gladly and willingly is a concrete sign that selflessness has overcome the self-centred life. The self-centred life holds on; selflessness lets go. Pride hoards; humility shares.

And this is a shift of perspective: from the temporary to the eternal. Money kept in our hands is temporary; money given to the Lord is eternal.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: Whose Is the Church?
sections.html:
The scriptural basis

“He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18)

“I also tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the Lord Jesus’ words: “my assembly” — my church — and “I will build”. The owner of the church is Jesus, and its chief engineer is Jesus too.

Paul said to the elders of Ephesus: “Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.” (Acts 20:28)

The church was bought by the Lord with his own blood. And what has been bought with blood, no one dares call “mine”.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: the head and the body

Paul repeatedly uses “the head and the body” to describe the relationship between Christ and the church. Since Christ is the head, the church does not belong to any leader, any system, any family, any tradition.

The church in Corinth had exactly this problem in its day: “each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” Paul immediately fired back: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:12–13)

Straight to the heart of it. Every faction and party in a church grows from the same root — someone has treated what is not theirs as their own.

An example from daily life

The difference between a steward and the owner of a house lies in what the keys mean. The steward has keys too; he can open doors, manage the house, make many decisions. But the steward knows full well that the house is not his, and that one day he must give an account.

When a steward forgets that he is a steward, he starts remodelling the house, turning guests away, and replacing the owner’s name with his own. A great deal of the rivalry and hurt in the church begins at exactly that moment.

Supporting evidence from a famous saying and from history

The Dutch theologian Abraham Kuyper, who also served as prime minister of the Netherlands, spoke immortal words in 1880 in his address at the founding of the Free University: “There is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’”

Church history bears this out again and again: the church has been persecuted, divided and misused, yet never destroyed. Because the One who builds it is the Lord, and the One who keeps it is the Lord. “The gates of Hades will not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)

Applying the 321 Vision

When the church faces difficulty, conflict or challenge, our first reaction is not to find someone to blame or to take sides, but to turn our eyes to Jesus — “looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

In 321 this is called “let Jesus receive all the glory”. If the church is mine, I have to be seen; if the church is the Lord’s, I gladly step back behind the scenes.

This is also what the 235 relationships look like in practice: with a selfless person, become a “2”, holding each other up; build spiritual parents and spiritual children into a “3”, passing it on from generation to generation; join with the fivefold ministries to become a “5”, fighting side by side with one heart. We are not building our own kingdom; we are establishing God’s system.

A Gentle Reminder: When the focus is right, life comes into alignment

The lesson reminds us of something very important: we are not the centre of the world, nor the lead character of our own story.

The history of astronomy records a famous revolution. People once believed the earth was the centre of the universe, with every heavenly body revolving around us. To make that model hold together, they had to keep adding “epicycles”, circle upon circle; the more they calculated, the more complicated it became, and the less accurate. Then in 1543 Copernicus put the sun back at the centre, and the whole system suddenly became simple and harmonious.

Brothers and sisters, our lives are the same. As long as we keep ourselves at the centre, we have to keep adding circle upon circle of explanations, excuses, defences and comparisons; life grows ever more complicated, and we grow ever more tired. But when we put Jesus back at the centre, everything suddenly comes into alignment.

Only when Jesus becomes our focus will we see true direction, meaning and glory.

Scripture says: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36) Of him, through him, to him — that is alignment.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From “Mine” to “His”
sections.html:
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Today’s lesson happens to lay out the whole framework of 321.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — while on earth he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34); he himself is the most perfect demonstration that “everything belongs to the Father”. The Bible is my standard — the answer to “Whose is it?” is not something we work out for ourselves; the Bible tells us plainly. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who turns the words “you are not your own” from knowledge into conviction in our hearts.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — since everything is his, of course he has the authority to be Lord. Let Jesus receive all the glory — since all things come from him, of course the glory must return to him too.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Not establishing my household, my career, my church — but establishing God’s system.

The self-centred life and selflessness

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life: my life, my family, my money, my church. The mark of the new self is selflessness: the Lord’s life, the Lord’s family, the Lord’s money, the Lord’s church.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out. When I say, “This is the Lord’s”, I have not lost anything; on the contrary, I have gained a boundless Lord who takes responsibility for me.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The four questions in today’s lesson are really four returns to our originally intended position.

The fivefold change

321 says: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

“Whose is it?” is precisely a mindset. Once this mindset changes, the way we treat ourselves changes (life); our diaries and our wallets change (daily living); our grip on our families loosens (relationships); and our posture in the church bows lower (ministry).

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The shift of perspective

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: no longer asking, “What do other people think of me?” but “How does the Lord see this?”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly perspective: no longer measuring worth by earthly possessions. “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2)

From the temporary perspective to the eternal perspective: everything in our hands must one day be put down; only what has been offered up lasts for ever.

From the worldly perspective to the godly perspective: the world says, “This is mine”; the Bible says, “This is the Lord’s.”

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves

Brothers and sisters, so often the moment something happens, we start calculating with our heads: How do I hold on to this? How do I win it back? And the more we calculate, the more we fret. 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will have joy, rely on the brain and you will have worry. For out of the heart is the wellspring of life.

When we grow quiet and ask, “Lord, whose is this?”, we are relying on the heart, not on the brain.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Three Actions to Refocus
sections.html:
If faith stops at being moved, the feeling evaporates. So the lesson gives us three very concrete practices. We will use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take these three practices deeper and make them real.

Practice one: Remind yourself every day — I belong to the Lord

Every morning when you get up, make this declaration:

“Lord, my life belongs to you; today I live for you.”

A declaration like this will help you focus on the Lord’s sovereignty from the very start of the day, rather than on your own ideas.

Working through the eight stages:

Information — first memorise the verse: “If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” (Romans 14:8) Put it on your phone’s lock screen, or stick it on the mirror.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to make these words no longer just a verse, but a light in your heart. You can pray like this: “Lord, let me truly see that I am not my own.”

Conviction — say “Amen” to these words in your heart. Conviction is not mere understanding; it is putting your full weight on it.

Implementation — for seven days in a row, make this declaration the first thing you say when you get up. Before you are even out of bed, declare it.

Evaluation — every night before you sleep, ask yourself: at what moment today did I live as my own master again?

Correction — bring that moment to the Lord and say, “Lord, I took that back again; now I hand it over to you once more.”

Repetition — it doesn’t end after seven days; after seven days, do seven more, until it becomes a habit. The psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, who study emotion and gratitude, published research in 2003 showing that people who deliberately practised gratitude over several weeks showed clear positive changes in their sense of well-being and their outlook on life. Spiritual practices likewise need time to build up.

Multiplication — find a brother or sister, teach them this declaration, and remind each other. This is what 321 calls your “2”.

Practice two: Entrust your family to Jesus

This week, pray for the family member you are most anxious about, and say these words:

“Lord, he (she) is your heritage, not my responsibility. Please watch over and guide him (her) yourself.”

And practise letting go — no longer using your own methods to control or change them.

Working through the eight stages:

Information — memorise this verse: “Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” (Psalm 127:3)

Revelation — be still before the Lord, and let him show you the person, the matter, you are gripping most tightly.

Conviction — admit a fact: I cannot control his heart; only the Lord can.

Implementation — this week, pray for him more often than you lecture him. Every time you think of him, entrust him once more.

Evaluation — write down the things you held back from saying this week, and the things you said and then regretted.

Correction — if you said the wrong thing, go and apologise. Humility draws out humility, and both sides win; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

Repetition — make “entrusting” a daily action, not something you only do in a crisis.

Multiplication — share your experience with another brother or sister who is also worried about their family, and become an encouragement to them.

Brothers and sisters, please take special note of the weight of this sentence in the lesson: “He is your heritage, not my responsibility.” This is not shirking responsibility; it is putting down a burden that is not ours to carry. We must still do our part — to love, to be there, to set an example — but changing a human heart is the work of the Holy Spirit, not our work.

Practice three: Make one real gift, and practise handing over ownership

If your income has recently increased, or you feel prompted, practise giving a sum of money gladly to the church, a ministry or someone in need, and as you give, pray like this:

“Lord, this was always yours; I gladly give your money back to you.”

Working through the eight stages:

Information — memorise this verse: “For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” (1 Chronicles 29:14)

Revelation — grow quiet, and let the Holy Spirit show you a specific amount. Not someone else’s amount — the amount the Lord gives you.

Conviction — acknowledge in your heart: this money was never mine.

Implementation — do it within this week; don’t put it off. Delay lets the prompting cool.

Evaluation — after you have given, face your heart honestly: is it joy, or is it a pang? Is it willing, or reluctant?

Correction — if there is a struggle in your heart, don’t pretend; bring it to the Lord and ask him to renew you. “God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)

Repetition — let giving become a settled pattern rather than an occasional impulse.

Multiplication — there is no need to make a show of it, but at the right moment you can pass on to the next generation this mindset: “This was always yours.”

sections.heading: Closing and Call: From “Mine” to “His”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have asked “Whose is it?” four times. Now let us look at where it leads.

When we think our life is our own, we will be constantly anxious, grasping and comparing. Anxious, because we are afraid of losing; grasping, because we are afraid there won’t be enough; comparing, because we are afraid of losing out. All three are the fruit of the self-centred life.

But when we recognise that everything belongs to Jesus, we will let go, trust and obey. Let go, because it was never mine to begin with; trust, because the Lord is far better at managing it than I am; obey, because he is the Lord and I am the servant. All three are the fruit of selflessness.

The same matter, the same situation — two completely different lives. The only difference lies in one question: Whose is it?

From now on, let us learn to ask: Whose is it? If it is the Lord’s, let us hand it to the Lord, and let the Lord reign, let the Lord guide, let the Lord receive the glory!

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s call: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Not letting him be King of one corner of our lives, but King of all of it; not letting him have whatever glory is left over, but all the glory.

Paul says, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21)

This morning, may each of us be able to open our hands, give up the steering wheel, and set our focus on him. When the focus is right, life comes into alignment; and when life is aligned, we will see God do in our families, our work and our church exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think.

keyVerses: “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” (Romans 14:7–8)
“‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’” (Acts 17:28)
declarations: Lord, my life, my family, my wealth and my church all belong to you!
I choose to set my focus on you, and let you have first place in me.
practices: Remind yourself every day — I belong to the Lord
Entrust your family to Jesus
Make one real gift, and practise handing over ownership
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. This morning you have shone your light on us with one simple question: “Whose is this?”

Lord, we confess that we often treat what you have given as what we own; we often live as stewards with the airs of the owner of the house. We are anxious, we grasp, we compare; we wear ourselves out and crush the people around us. Forgive us, we pray.
Lord, today we give our lives back to you — our time, our choices, our work and our future are all in your hands, because you are the Lord of our lives.
We give our families back to you — they are your heritage. Please watch over and guide them yourself, because you are the head of every household.
We give our wealth back to you — all things come from you, and we give you of your own, because you are the Lord of our wealth.
We give the church back to you — you are the head of the whole church. Please build it yourself, because you have promised that the gates of Hades will not prevail against your church.

Holy Spirit, remind us every day, so that our focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances, but on Jesus alone. Let our old self, the self-centred life, be crucified, and our new self, selflessness, be lived out; make us humble, that humility may overcome pride.
Have first place in us; reign as King; and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.” (Romans 14:8) Take three minutes of silence and ask yourself: what am I gripping most tightly right now? Is it mine, or is it the Lord’s? Am I willing to hand it over to the Lord in front of the group?

“Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.” (Psalm 127:3) Of the four areas — life, family, wealth and church — which is the hardest for you to say, “This is the Lord’s”? Why? Share with one another, pray for one another, and practise becoming each other’s “2”.

l021.subtitle: Adjusting Our Focus from “Mine” to “His”
