sections.heading: Introduction: A Ship Needs Two Things
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

For this morning’s devotion, I’d like to begin by asking you to picture a scene.

An ocean-going sailing ship sails at night into unfamiliar waters. The wind begins to rise, the waves roll in one after another, and the hull pitches from side to side in the darkness. At a moment like this, an old sailor on board will do two things.

The first thing: he lets down the anchor. The anchor isn’t tossed onto the surface of the water, nor hooked onto another boat alongside; it has to sink all the way to the bottom of the sea and lock onto the immovable bedrock beneath the seabed. Once the anchor holds, the waves can’t sweep the ship away.

The second thing: he looks up for a star. In the days before satellite navigation, every sailor in the northern hemisphere knew the same star — the North Star. Because the axis of the earth’s rotation points almost directly at it, however the night sky wheels around, the North Star stays fixed in its place in the north. Find it, and the ship knows where it is heading.

Brothers and sisters, for a ship to survive wind and waves it needs two things: an anchor and a star.

The anchor answers one question: on whom am I relying?

The star answers another: for whom am I living?

These are exactly the two questions today’s lesson puts to us.

Our daily living is so often pulled about by circumstances, by people, events and things. When the stock market rises we’re happy; when the medical report comes back we can’t sleep all night. Someone praises us and we soar; someone misunderstands us and we sink. Our emotions rise and fall like the waves, and our faith rocks like the ship. Why? Not because the waves are too big, but because the anchor has been dropped in the wrong place and we’ve mistaken the star we’re steering by.

So the Lord reminds us today: the real key to overcoming is not a change of circumstances but putting our focus back where it belongs.

Right now, in your heart, ask yourself two questions honestly:

First, on whom am I relying to live?

Second, for whom am I living?

If what I rely on is not Jesus but people, resources, circumstances or my own methods, then I will surely be disappointed. Because people leave, resources dry up, circumstances change, and methods stop working.

If my aim is not Jesus but achievement, applause, control or other people’s approval, then I will surely grow weary. Because achievement is never enough, applause never lasts long enough, and control can never be held firmly.

But brothers and sisters, when our focus is adjusted back to Jesus — when the anchor is locked onto the Rock, when our eyes are fixed on that unmoving star — our life gains both stability and direction.

The writer of Hebrews says, “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil” (Hebrews 6:19).

This anchor isn’t locked onto the seabed; it is locked within the veil — in the Most Holy Place, onto Jesus, who has already gone in and is seated on the throne.

Today, let us together cast our anchor in the right place and lift our eyes in the right direction.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: That One Sentence on the Areopagus
sections.html:
Our theme verse today comes from Acts chapter 17.

The author of Acts is Luke. He was a doctor (Colossians 4:14 calls him “Luke the beloved physician”), and also Paul’s co-worker on his missionary journeys. He wrote both the Gospel of Luke and Acts to a man named Theophilus (Luke 1:3; Acts 1:1), and they are generally thought to have been written around AD 60.

And the scene of this passage is Athens.

It was Paul’s second missionary journey, around AD 50 to 51. Paul first went to Thessalonica and was persecuted; then to Berea, and was hounded out again; so the brothers sent him south, and he arrived in Athens. The text says, “Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols” (Acts 17:16).

What kind of place was Athens? It was the centre of ancient Greek philosophy, the city of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle. The liveliest activity in the city at the time was debate. Luke describes them with a line touched with gentle irony: “(Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing.)” (Acts 17:21)

They brought Paul to the Areopagus — the council hill of Athens, the city’s highest court and the place where ideas were put on trial. Paul stood there, facing a crowd of philosophers.

Notice how Paul opens. He doesn’t begin by scolding them for idolatry, nor by quoting the Old Testament — because they didn’t accept the Old Testament. He starts from their own altar: “For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you” (Acts 17:23).

Then Paul builds his case step by step: this God made heaven and earth, and does not live in temples made with hands; he is not served by human hands, as though he needed anything; from one man he made every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth. And at this point Paul speaks the words of our theme verse today:

“‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’” (Acts 17:28)

This one short sentence, just a handful of words, says everything about what a human being really is.

“Live” in the original is zōmen — to be alive; “move” is kinoumetha — to move, to act; “have our being” is esmen — to exist, to be. Being alive, acting, existing — the three most basic things a human being possesses, and not one of them did we give ourselves.

And the “poets” Paul quotes are the Greeks’ own poets. The first half is generally thought to come from the Cretan poet Epimenides, and the line “For we are also his offspring” from the long poem Phaenomena by the Cilician poet Aratus. Paul used lines they knew well to bring them before the God they did not know.

Brothers and sisters, feel the tension of this scene: a crowd of the world’s finest thinkers, people who relied on their own minds more than anyone, standing on the summit of human reason, hear one sentence — you don’t even breathe by your own power.

This is the first lesson we have to learn today.

sections.heading: 1. On Whom Do We Rely? Hold Fast to Jesus and No Longer Be Dismayed
sections.html:
1. Whatever you lose sends you into panic; whatever sends you into panic is what you were relying on

Let’s begin with a very practical observation.

Many people, the moment they lose a certain relationship, a certain resource or a certain opportunity, fall completely into confusion and panic. Lose a job, and the sky falls in; lose one person’s support, and they can’t go another step; lose a sum of savings, and they can’t sleep at night.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a question of weakness; it’s a question of focus. Whatever you panic about losing shows what you were relying on to live all along.

The prophet Jeremiah puts this very bluntly:

“Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land.’” (Jeremiah 17:5–6)

“Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” (Jeremiah 17:7–8)

Notice that Jeremiah doesn’t say, “If you’re a tree, you’ll never meet the heat.” The text plainly says “when heat comes,” and plainly says “the year of drought.” The heat will come, the drought will come; that is certain. Where is the difference? The difference is where the roots go down.

The desert bush has its roots in salt land; the tree by the waters has its roots by the river. The same sun beats down on both: one withers, one stays green.

That is the question of whom we rely on.

2. Jesus is the source of wisdom, the guarantee of protection, the wellspring of power

So what exactly is Jesus to us?

First, Jesus is the source of our wisdom, because he knows all things.

Paul speaks of Christ, “in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Colossians 2:3).

Brothers and sisters, at life’s crossroads we so often scramble for methods, for advisers, for information. Information isn’t a bad thing, but information isn’t the same as wisdom. The amount of data humanity produces in a single day today far exceeds the total of the past several thousand years, and yet our anxiety hasn’t shrunk because of it. Why? Because wisdom isn’t found in data; wisdom is found in that One.

Second, Jesus is the guarantee of our protection, because he is present everywhere.

The psalmist says, “Where could I go from your Spirit? Or where could I flee from your presence? If I ascend up into heaven, you are there. If I make my bed in Sheol, behold, you are there! If I take the wings of the dawn, and settle in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 139:7–10).

Have you noticed that this passage starts out sounding like “there’s no escape,” and by the end it has become “you can never run out of his hand”? The same truth sounds like a threat to the rebellious and like a guarantee to the obedient.

Third, Jesus is the wellspring of our power, because he can do all things.

Jeremiah prayed, “Ah Lord Yahweh! Behold, you have made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm. There is nothing too hard for you” (Jeremiah 32:17).

And Paul says, “I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

This verse is often misused to mean “whatever I want to do, I’ll succeed at.” But look at the context: Paul is talking about having learned to be brought low and having learned to abound. He says, “I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need” (Philippians 4:12). Paul’s “I can do all things” doesn’t mean he can obtain all things; it means he can bear all things and stand firm in all things. It’s a matter of whose power he relies on, not of his own resources.

3. No need to chase the anointing — just hold fast to Jesus

There’s a sentence in our lesson that I love: we don’t need to strain after the anointing, we don’t need to depend on circumstances changing, we don’t need to cling to our connections; if we simply hold fast to Jesus, we have everything.

It sounds simple, but it deals with a very deep-rooted disease: we keep wanting “the things of God” more than we want God himself.

We ask for the anointing because we want power; we ask for doors to open because we want things to go smoothly; we ask for connections because we want security. None of this is wrong, but if our focus stops at “things,” we will always be chasing, and it will never be enough.

What does Paul say? “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (2 Corinthians 6:10).

“As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” — brothers and sisters, this isn’t some trick of positive thinking; it is a spiritual fact. Because when you have the Lord who owns all things, in him you possess all things.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a prayer that has echoed down the centuries: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” That sentence says everything about the human heart — what we lack isn’t things; what we lack is that One.

4. Confirmation from psychology: the secure base

In psychology there’s a well-known concept called the “secure base.”

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and his colleague Mary Ainsworth confirmed it further in the 1970s with her “Strange Situation” experiments: when a small child knows there’s a stable, predictable, always-responsive caregiver behind him, his courage to explore an unfamiliar environment clearly increases; but when the caregiver is there one moment and gone the next, warm one moment and cold the next, the child withdraws, grows anxious, or behaves in contradictory ways.

Listen carefully to the heart of this finding: how far a child dares to venture out depends on how stable he believes the base behind him is.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the spiritual reality. Do we dare to stand on the truth at work? Do we dare to forgive the person who has hurt us deeply? Do we dare to offer up our time, our money, our gifts? It depends on how stable the “base” behind us is.

If my base is other people’s opinion of me, I will certainly shrink back, because opinions change.

If my base is my savings, I will certainly calculate, because savings run down.

If my base is Jesus, then I can go forward — because he is the same yesterday, today and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

Isaiah puts this steadfastness most warmly: “Don’t you be afraid, for I am with you. Don’t be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you. Yes, I will help you. Yes, I will uphold you with the right hand of my righteousness” (Isaiah 41:10).

“Don’t be dismayed” — so the cure for dismay isn’t better circumstances; it’s “I am your God.”

5. Applying the 321 vision: the Three Foundations are our anchor

The 321 vision says: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These are the Three Foundations.

Brothers and sisters, the word “foundation” matters. A foundation isn’t decoration; a foundation bears the load. How high a building can rise depends not on how good the outer walls look but on how deep the foundations go.

When I take Jesus as my role model, I no longer need to imitate other people’s success;

when I take the Bible as my standard, I no longer need to be pushed around by public opinion and the latest trends;

when I take the Holy Spirit as my guide, I no longer need to rely on my own cleverness to guess the road ahead.

That is the concrete answer to “on whom do we rely.”

And 321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Because the outcomes of our whole life flow from the heart (Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life”).

A Gentle Reminder

How can you tell whether you’ve put your focus in the wrong place? There are two very simple indicators:

First, are you often disappointed by people?

Second, are you often anxious because of circumstances?

If so, there’s no need to condemn yourself, but you do need to adjust. Because disappointment and anxiety aren’t the enemy; they are warning lights on the dashboard, telling you: the anchor is in the wrong place.

sections.heading: 2. For Whom Do We Live? No Longer for Ourselves, but Only for the Lord
sections.html:
1. Two probing questions: for whom do we live? For whom do we serve?

The first question is asked; the second follows close behind.

Are we living for ourselves, or for the Lord?

Are we serving to please people, or to please the Lord?

Brothers and sisters, these two questions cut deeper than the first. Because “on whom do we rely” can still be forced out of us in times of trouble; but “for whom do we live” is the thing most likely to drift when life is going smoothly.

When a person is ill, it’s easy to rely on the Lord; when a person is being praised, it’s easy to forget the Lord.

The apostle John divides the pull of the world on us into three directions:

“Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:15–17)

Notice the three phrases John uses.

“The lust of the flesh” is my wanting to “feel” — I want pleasure, I want comfort, I want to be satisfied.

“The lust of the eyes” is my wanting to “have” — I’ve seen it, so I want it.

“The pride of life” — in the original alazoneia tou biou, literally “the boasting of life” — is my wanting to “be seen”: I want people to know I’ve got it, I can do it, I’m right.

These three are precisely the threefold temptation of that tree in the Garden of Eden: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6). Good for food is the lust of the flesh; a delight to the eyes is the lust of the eyes; desired to make one wise is the pride of life.

And when the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, Satan used these same three: turn stones into bread; throw yourself down from the pinnacle of the temple so that people will see; bow down and worship me and you’ll have the glory of all the kingdoms. Three times Jesus answered, “It is written…” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? From Eden to the wilderness, from the wilderness to today, the content of temptation has never changed. They have only one thing in common — “self.”

2. “No longer living for ourselves” is the inevitable fruit of the gospel

So what is it that the gospel means to accomplish in us?

Paul states it with absolute certainty:

“For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15)

Look at the logic here. Christ died for me — so I no longer live for myself. This isn’t a heavy-handed command; it’s the conclusion that love draws.

Paul says again, “For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Romans 14:7–8).

The deepest word of all is in Galatians:

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“It is no longer I who live” — 321 puts it well: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless.

But listen carefully: selflessness doesn’t mean erasing yourself, it doesn’t mean having no worth, it doesn’t mean becoming a person with no feelings. Selflessness is “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” It is exchanging a limited “I” for an infinite Lord; it is a small cup of water being poured into the vast ocean.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

3. Pleasing people is a road that never ends

Paul has another sentence that everyone who serves ought to read again and again:

“For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10)

The Lord Jesus also warned, “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

Why is “pleasing people” so dangerous? Because it never has an end.

In 1985 the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan put forward “self-determination theory,” distinguishing intrinsic motivation from extrinsic motivation. A series of their studies showed that when something a person once did out of love comes to be driven mainly by external rewards or evaluation, intrinsic motivation actually falls; and people driven chiefly by outside approval are more prone to burn out and give up when the feedback dries up.

Brothers and sisters, can you hear how this echoes the Bible? If what drives my service is other people’s applause, then on the day the applause stops, I won’t be able to keep serving. If my sense of worth is built on being affirmed, then one cool response can knock me flat.

But what if I do it for the Lord?

“And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.” (Colossians 3:23–24)

“As for the Lord” — adjust this one phrase, and the whole weight of your service changes. Because the Lord sees the parts no one else sees: that phone call no one knows about, that early-morning prayer no one hears, that silence when you were misunderstood and chose not to defend yourself.

4. An example from daily living: two people mopping the floor

There’s a picture I often come back to.

Two people are mopping the floor of the church corridor at the same time. The first gets halfway, looks up to see whether anyone’s coming, and thinks: when the pastor comes by in a moment, will he notice? The second keeps his head down and even mops spotless that corner no one ever walks across.

The same work, the same time, the same sweat. But the first is polishing for “people’s eyes,” and the second is cleaning “the Lord’s house.”

When no one comes by that day, the first will feel it was all for nothing; the second will still be full of joy, because from start to finish the one he was serving was never the person passing by.

Brothers and sisters, this is the difference: focus on people and you’ll be drained; focus on the Lord and you’ll be filled.

Even if others don’t understand, don’t support me and don’t respond, I still press on steadily, because my aim is to please the Lord, not to please people.

5. Applying the 321 vision: the Two Core Values and the 920 practice

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

The answer to “for whom” is, in fact, these Two Core Values.

To let Jesus be King means I no longer sit on the throne of my own life. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

And the 920 practice of 321 reminds us: every person we have a relationship with is our “2.” Before them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that not one of the nine graces exists to make ourselves look good. Love is given to others, patience is shown towards others, gentleness is lived out before others. Fruit was never meant for the tree itself.

An apple tree never eats its own apples.

A Gentle Reminder

When you’re downcast because no one praised you, or want to give up because you see no results, it may well mean that the focus of your service has quietly shifted from Jesus to yourself.

Don’t condemn yourself, but refocus. Because refocusing is the very key to recovering your joy.

sections.heading: 3. For Whom Is Revival? Only When the Focus Is on Jesus Does Revival Stay on Course
sections.html:
1. Revival is not those three things

We all long for revival. But we need to ask a more fundamental question: for whom is revival?

Our lesson reminds us that the focus of true revival is not growing numbers, not social change, and not signs and wonders.

Please don’t misunderstand. Growing numbers are good, a society being changed is good, and signs and wonders are also gifts from the Lord. All three may be results of revival, but none of them can be the focus of revival.

Because once the focus is on numbers, we begin to compare;

once the focus is on social change, we begin to measure results by worldly methods;

once the focus is on signs and wonders, we begin to chase phenomena rather than seek the Lord.

The Lord Jesus himself dealt with this. After the five thousand had eaten their fill, the crowd was about to come and take him by force to make him king, but he withdrew to the mountain (John 6:15). The next day the crowds found him, and the Lord said, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled” (John 6:26).

The sign was right in front of their eyes, yet all they remembered was the taste of the bread.

2. The focus of revival: Jesus glorified

So what is revival for? There is only one answer — that Jesus be glorified.

When the Lord Jesus spoke of the Holy Spirit, he said, “He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine, and will declare it to you” (John 16:14).

Brothers and sisters, this is the touchstone for discerning every spiritual work. Whatever truly comes from the Holy Spirit will in the end give the glory to Jesus. The Holy Spirit never promotes himself; the Holy Spirit always exalts Christ.

The Lord also said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).

Notice the order: first he is lifted up, and only then are all people drawn. It isn’t that we find ways to attract people; it’s that when Jesus is lifted high, people are naturally drawn.

Yet we so often do it the other way round. We work hard designing events to attract people and forget to lift up Jesus. The result: people come, but they don’t stay; because what drew them wasn’t the Lord, what keeps them won’t be the Lord either.

The psalmist’s prayer should become our prayer: “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake” (Psalm 115:1).

Paul says of Christ, “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Colossians 1:18).

“That in all things he might have the preeminence” — that is the definition of revival.

3. The witness of history: every revival is a return to Jesus

Church history gives us the clearest confirmation.

In 1727, at Herrnhut in eastern Germany, a group of brothers and sisters who had fled there from Moravia were on the verge of splitting apart over their differences and disputes. Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf went from house to house, visiting and reconciling them, and led them back before Christ. On 13 August that year, during a Communion service, the Holy Spirit was poured out; the disputes ceased and the brothers were reconciled. After that they began a round-the-clock prayer watch, one shift after another, day and night without a break, which continued for more than a hundred years; and the Moravian Brethren went on to send out a great number of missionaries, influencing the later Methodist movement and the modern missions movement.

There is a famous saying generally attributed to Zinzendorf: “I have one passion: it is he, he alone.”

Brothers and sisters, see the order here: not strategy first, not method first, not numbers first, but first a “return to Jesus,” first reconciliation, first the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The starting point of revival is putting the focus back where it belongs.

In 1857 Jeremiah Lanphier, a lay missionary serving a church near Wall Street in New York, started a midday prayer meeting on Fulton Street. On the first day only six people came; a few months later, thousands of people all over New York were stopping work during their lunch break to pray, and it spread across America and to Britain.

No revival has ever been set in motion by a secret formula. Every revival is a group of people seeing Jesus afresh.

4. A scientific picture: the focus determines the orbit

The seventeenth-century astronomer Johannes Kepler set out his first law of planetary motion: a planet’s orbit around the sun is an ellipse, and the sun sits at one of the ellipse’s two focal points.

Notice the word “focus.” The reason the earth has neither flown off nor fallen in for four and a half billion years, but has traced a stable orbit, is not that the earth tries hard enough; it’s that the sun sits at its focus.

Brothers and sisters, your life is just the same. Whether your orbit is steady depends not on how hard you try but on who is at your focal point.

Get the focus right, and the orbit is steady; let the focus drift, and the faster you go, the further off course you end up.

If an aeroplane’s heading is off by a single degree, after an hour’s flight it will be more than ten kilometres off target. An error in direction is magnified by distance.

So if revival doesn’t adjust its focus, it will go off course; if the church doesn’t adjust its focus, it will lose focus; if a life doesn’t adjust its focus, it will wither.

5. Applying the 321 vision: the Goal and a shift of perspective

The Goal of 321 is: establish God’s system.

What is God’s system? It is an order of life and a network of relationships in which Jesus truly reigns as King and the glory truly goes to Jesus.

This also requires us to make four shifts of perspective:

from the human perspective to God’s perspective;

from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective;

from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective;

from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Paul says, “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

“Set your mind on the things that are above” means lifting our focus from the horizontal line to the vertical.

321 also reminds us of the 235 relationships: become a “2” with others who are selfless, serving as one another’s spiritual companion; build a “3,” as spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Revival is never a one-person affair; revival is a group of people with a shared focus, joined together by the Lord.

A Gentle Reminder

When you pursue revival, don’t look for a secret formula; look for Jesus.

Without him, all the methods in the world are in vain. With him, even the most ordinary group of people can be used by the Lord.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: When the Focus Returns to Its Place, Life Returns to Its Place
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we’ve said today within the 321 framework and look at it once more.

“On whom do we rely” corresponds to the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. These three are our anchor. If the anchor holds, wind and waves can’t capsize the ship.

“For whom do we live” corresponds to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. These two are our star. If we take our bearings by it accurately, our direction will not go wrong.

And the anchor and the star together point to the Goal: establish God’s system.

From beginning to end, this lesson is really dealing with one thing — “self.”

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. When I rely on myself, that is one form of pride; when I live for myself, that is another. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

And 321 reminds us that change is fivefold: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships, and only then can ministry truly change.

Notice the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Today’s lesson works at the very headwaters. “On whom do we rely, and for whom do we live” is a question of mindset; once the mindset is adjusted, life is adjusted; once life is adjusted, our service changes from “performance” into “overflow.”

Finally, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not circumstances. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Exercises in Turning Our Focus
sections.html:
Our lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We’ll deepen them using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: Write down your list of dependencies

Take a sheet of paper and list three things you most easily lean on. It might be money, it might be connections, it might be reputation, it might be some method or talent of your own.

Once they’re written down, hand them back to the Lord one by one in prayer, and declare: “Lord, I’m not relying on these; I’m relying on you.”

Information: Today I’ve learned a principle — whatever loss sends me into panic shows what I was relying on all along.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light and show me the thing I’ve never been willing to let go of.

Conviction: I acknowledge that Jeremiah 17:5–8 is true; whoever relies on the arm of man will wither, whoever relies on Yahweh will stay green.

Implementation: This week, write these three things down and entrust them to God in specific prayer — don’t just think about it.

Evaluation: At the weekend, look back: this week, did I grab hold of any of them again?

Correction: Pray a prayer of surrender over that one again, and find a spiritual companion to walk with me.

Repetition: Rewrite the list once a month, and you’ll find its contents changing.

Multiplication: Teach this exercise to someone else, and write the list alongside them.

Exercise 2: Realign your heart for service

In your service, if you feel discouraged, weary, or start comparing yourself with others, stop at once and ask yourself one question: “For whom am I doing this?”

Then pray silently: “Lord, I serve only you; I don’t live for people’s opinions.”

Information: Pleasing people is a road that never ends; the research of Deci and Ryan confirms how fragile extrinsic motivation is.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to point out the hidden motive in my service that wants “to be seen.”

Conviction: I believe the standard of Galatians 1:10 — if I am pleasing people, I am not a servant of Christ.

Implementation: This week, before every act of service, first pray silently: “This is for the Lord.”

Evaluation: This week, whose words sent my emotions up and down?

Correction: Bring that matter before the Lord, and declare afresh whom I am serving.

Repetition: Let “This is for the Lord” become your opening prayer every time you serve.

Multiplication: Share your experience of this exercise once in your small group.

Exercise 3: A daily exercise of focusing on Jesus

Spend at least five minutes each day not praying about your needs, not praying about your service, not interceding for any project; simply worshipping Jesus and gazing on Jesus.

Read a passage from the Gospels, watch him speak, watch him act, see his heart, and then say to him, “Lord, you are so good.”

Information: Psalm 27:4 says, “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.”

Revelation: In those five minutes, let the Holy Spirit reveal the Lord’s beauty to me.

Conviction: I believe that gazing on Jesus is in itself the most fruitful thing I can do, not a waste of time.

Implementation: Fix one time and one place; begin with five minutes and don’t overreach.

Evaluation: How many days this week did I actually do it? What made me stop?

Correction: Move the time to the part of the day when I’m least likely to be interrupted.

Repetition: Keep it up for forty days in a row and let it become a habit.

Multiplication: Invite family members or a companion to do it with you, and remind one another.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Return to the Focus, Enter into Victory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the two questions we started with.

Whom you rely on decides how far you can go;

whom you live for decides whether the journey is worth it.

Some rely on themselves and go very fast, but not very far; some live for themselves and do a great deal, but it isn’t worth it.

But when we hold fast to Jesus and live for him, we can walk securely on the heights, overcome difficulties, and live out revival.

In the darkest hour of his nation, the prophet Habakkuk wrote these words: “For though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines; the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food; the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in Yahweh. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation! Yahweh, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places” (Habakkuk 3:17–19).

Notice that Habakkuk’s circumstances didn’t change — the fig tree still didn’t flourish, the flocks were still cut off from the fold. What changed was his focus: “Yet I will rejoice in Yahweh.”

That “yet” is the sound of a focus returning to its place.

So this morning, let us adjust our focus together: not to satisfy ourselves, not to please people, but simply and solely for Jesus.

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’” (Acts 17:28)
“For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:
Lord, I do not rely on circumstances, and I do not live for myself; I live relying on you and living for you.
practices: Write down your list of dependencies
Realign your heart for service
A daily exercise of focusing on Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you. In you we live, move and have our being; yet so often we live as though everything depended on ourselves.
Lord, forgive us for casting our anchor on things that move, and forgive us for fixing our eyes on people who change.
Today we are willing to adjust our focus afresh. We declare: I do not rely on circumstances, I rely on you; I do not live for myself, I live for you.

May your Holy Spirit work within us, taking away our dismay and taking away our hunger for applause. Let us serve without comparing, without growing weary, without losing focus; let us stand in trouble without being shaken, without fear, without turning back.
Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our work, reign as King in our church, and have the preeminence in all things.
May all the glory be yours, for ever and ever.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Read Acts 17:28: “For in him we live, move, and have our being.” Recently, what loss or change has sent you into particular panic? From that panic, what do you see you have actually been relying on all along?

Read 2 Corinthians 5:15: “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” In your current service or work, which part most easily turns into living “for yourself”? This week, what concrete action will you take to refocus it on Jesus?
